therefore, fools become attached to sense objects for the sake of experiencing that feeling.
Others maintain that not only feeling, but also the apprehension of an object, constitutes enjoyment.
Furthermore, that [experience] is not sensation (*vedanā*), because it would contradict the commentary.
Nor is the apprehension of an object (*arthopalabdhi*) anything other than consciousness (*vijñāna*); therefore, it is not appropriate for it to be a mental factor (*caitasika*).
Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the discernment of what is felt, because its nature consists in the grasping of specific qualities such as pleasure and so forth.
The formative forces (saṃskāra) that impel both experience and perception are volition (cetanā), attention (manaskāra), and so forth.
Alternatively,
experience is sensation (vedanā), because it consists in the individual experiencing of objects and the experiencing of karma to be felt as pleasure and so on.
Thus, feeling (*vedanā*) is the enjoyment (*upabhoga*) of objects and their karmic results;
perception (*saṃjñā*) is the discernment (*pariccheda*) that delimits the signs of objects as the basis for conventional designation;
and formations (*saṃskāra*) are the mental application (*ābhoga*) toward the objects of other consciousnesses.
Consequently, through the predominance of volition and the other [mental factors], consciousness follows immediately after the object.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), desire and the rest are included.
Thus it has been explained from what cause, in what manner, and for what purpose the process of activity occurs.
In this context: because of "concealing," since ignorance obstructs the vision of things as they truly are;
because of "planting," since the formative forces establish the latencies of karma within consciousness;
and because of "leading," since consciousness brings about arrival at the place of rebirth.
Because the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is fully grasped by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);
because it is completed by the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*);
and because there is a threefold discrimination by contact (*sparśa*).
Through feeling, there is enjoyment;
through craving, there is the drawing forth of renewed existence projected by karma;
and through the appropriations, there is the binding of consciousness to the objects of desire and so forth that are conducive to its arising.
Because it brings about the manifestation of karma performed through becoming (*bhava*) so that it yields its maturation (*vipāka*) in a future existence, [it is called *abhinirvṛtti*].
The world is afflicted by birth, which is suffering, and by aging and death;

thus, it is said to "proclaim the characteristic of affliction" (*saṃkleśalakṣaṇa*). This refers to the characteristic of affliction in the sense that the afflictions of defilement (*kleśa*), karma, and birth, as they proceed, result in the thorough affliction of the world.
And thus, in order to demonstrate that even in the absence of a self (*ātman*), cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) arises from mere unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpamātra*),
it is explained: "Because of concealing, because of sowing, because of leading, and because of grasping," and so forth.

Thus, this twelvefold dependent origination has been shown with respect to the side of active involvement (*pravṛtti*). In that context, the final statement, "the world is afflicted because of concealment" (*chādanāt*), is to be connected with every [member].

By what means is there obscuration, or in what way does one become afflicted through obscuration? To this he says: "Because of the obstruction of seeing things as they truly are by means of ignorance.

For since ignorance consists in non-seeing, when the object of seeing reality is obscured by ignorance, the vision of reality does not arise; thus, because it obstructs the arising of the vision of reality, ignorance is the obstruction to the vision of reality.

Furthermore, the vision of reality (*bhūtadarśana*) is primarily supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-prajñā*); because it arises subsequent to that [wisdom], because it is attained subsequent to that, and because it is understood through that, its preparatory application—consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation—is called the "vision of reality.
Because ignorance is an obstruction to the vision of reality, it is the condition for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*); thus, by means of such concealment, the world is afflicted by ignorance.
This connects to the statement: "The world is afflicted by way of planting [the seeds of existence]."
To explain by what, where, and whose planting occurs, it says: "by the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), [the planting] of the latent impression of karma (*karmavāsanā*) in consciousness (*vijñāna*).
In this context, "formative forces" refers to bodily, vocal, and mental action—whether meritorious, non-meritorious, or imperturbable—which "forms" (*saṃskaroti*) a future existence;
the meaning is that they cause it to sprout without being directed toward a specific aim.
And that alone is expressed by the term "formations" (*saṃskāra*), but not everything.

Furthermore, it becomes capable of projecting renewed existence (*punarbhava*) through the predominance of ignorance (*avidyā*), and not merely by its own existence; thus, it is said that "ignorance is the condition for formations.
For indeed, those [formations] fashion renewed existence for one in whom knowledge has not arisen, but not for one in whom knowledge has arisen.

Furthermore, ignorance is not called the condition for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) merely by way of its predominance (*adhipatya*); rather, it is also their general condition of origination (*samutthāna-pratyaya*).
For just as ignorance, through its association, is generally the condition of origination for all afflictions (*kleśa*), so too is it for the volitions (*cetanā*) that originate from them.

Moreover, regarding the origination of the formative forces—which follow from the seeking of various forms of existence and enjoyment—ignorance, being co-existent with them, is their general condition.

Regarding the immovable [karmas] as well, which arise from the view of escape regarding those stages, the ignorance co-arising with them is stated to be the "general condition" (*sāmānyapratyaya*) for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
As for "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), what is intended here is the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), and not the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*);

because it is impossible for the storehouse consciousness to lead the place of rebirth for one whose active consciousnesses have ceased, and because there is no simultaneous occurrence of wholesome and afflicted states, and thus the latencies of karma cannot be established therein by the formative forces.
Regarding the phrase "of the karmic impression" (*karmavāsanā*):
what, then, is this so-called "karmic impression"? It is the seed, the causal state, of future birth.

For example, just as a grain of rice, undergoing transformation in dependence upon specific conditions such as soil, ash, and manure, becomes the seed that serves as the cause for the arising of a sprout.

"By means of establishing" (*pratiṣṭhāpanāt*) expresses "planting" (*ropaṇa*) by way of another synonym. Furthermore, "establishing" here refers to the initial infusion (*āpyāyana*) of that seed into the continuum of consciousness (*vijñānasantāna*).
For no impure (*sāsrava*) dharma has a previously non-existent seed deposited within it, as is the case with the pure (*anāsrava*) dharmas.

Thus, through the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), the world is afflicted because they deposit the seed of renewed existence (*punarbhava*) within consciousness (*vijñāna*). Regarding the statement "the world is afflicted by leading," it is not understood by what means, to where, or whose leading it is; therefore, he says: "by consciousness, because of the dispatching [of the being] to the place of birth."

By means of consciousness permeated by karma, through its continuous succession, there is the bringing forth and leading of the latent impression—which serves as the seed for renewed existence—from the place of death to the place of rebirth.

This being so, it is demonstrated that the consciousness at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi-vijñāna*) does not have formations (*saṃskāra*) as its condition; rather, it is only the consciousness of the prior existence that has formations as its condition.
For it is not logical that an effect should arise from a cause that has already perished.

For those who have attained the formless absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti), since they die in one place and are reborn in that very same place, how can there be "reaching a place of rebirth" in the formless realms? This should be understood according to the circumstances, as in the case of name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
Regarding the statement "the world is afflicted by way of grasping" (samparigraha):
by what grasping, and of what? To this he says: "by name-and-form, of the personal existence" (ātmabhāva).
Name-and-form consists of the five aggregates.

From the moment of rebirth-linking (pratisaṃdhi) onwards, through the stages of the embryo as a mass of cells (kalala), a bubble (arbuda), a fleshly lump (peśī), a solid mass (ghana), and the limbs (praśākhā), before the six sense bases have arisen, this is "name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.
Indeed, through the cultivation of specific qualities, its distinctness is established within other homogeneous classes of beings (nikāyasabhāga).

And when that [consciousness] has arisen, the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is differentiated according to the distinctions among the homogeneous classes (*nikāyasabhāga*) such as humans, animals, and so forth; thus it is said that "personal existence is grasped by name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
Alternatively, it grasps the entire personal existence up until death, because from the very beginning it is established as the causal state for everything.
Or else, even though name-and-form is not yet differentiated, it is said to grasp it through name-and-form because from the very beginning it is established as the causal state for everything.

Alternatively, even though name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is not distinct [from the self-entity], he shows how that self-entity is grasped as something separate, just as it is said that "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are comprised within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

However, for those of miraculous birth (*aupapāduka*), the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have consciousness (*vijñāna*) as their condition; therefore, name-and-form should be understood as having consciousness as its condition according to what is possible.
It is said that "one is afflicted because of filling [the body]."
By what is it filled, and of what?
By the six sense bases;
[it fills] the body comprised of name-and-form.
For in the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the body is said to be incomplete due to the absence of the sense-bases such as the eye.

And in that stage, although the body-base (*kāyāyatana*) and the mind-base (*manāyatana*) exist, they too are indeed incomplete because of the absence of the completion of both the supported and the support.
However, in the stage of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), once the eye and so forth have been produced, the supported becomes complete.
The sense-base of the body (*kāyāyatana*) is also complete because of the completeness of those [faculties] such as the eye upon which it depends.
How does that eye and so forth depend [on them]? Because their functioning is bound to them.
The mind-base (*manāyatana*), which is comprised of the six consciousnesses, is also complete at that time due to the completion of its basis without remainder.
And the completion of the major and minor limbs occurs precisely at the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Because the basis is thus fulfilled by means of the six sense bases, it should be understood that the world is afflicted;
this is connected to the statement that "the world is afflicted through the threefold discrimination."

When the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness comes together, contact (*sparśa*) is the discernment of that threefold modification of the faculty which is conducive to the arising of sensations such as pleasure.
For this very reason, it is called "contact" because it touches upon the similarity of the faculty's modification by assuming its aspect (*tadākāratayā*).
Alternatively, contact, conditioned by the six sense bases, produces a threefold modification of the faculty that is conducive to sensations such as pleasure.
"By enjoyment, through feeling":
for feeling is enjoyed—that is, tasted—by craving;
or alternatively, the enjoyment of feeling consists in the enjoyment of meritorious and other types of karma.
Alternatively, "enjoyment" here refers to the experience of feeling (*vedanā*).
When pleasure and so forth are being experienced, the world is afflicted by attachment, aversion, and delusion due to the intensification of that pleasure and so forth.
[The phrase] "because of cultivation" means this.
Since it is not understood by whom or what is being drawn forth, he says: "By craving, of the renewed existence projected by karma.

When the renewed existence—projected by the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) through the nourishment of the seed within consciousness—is moistened by craving, which acts like water and consists of a desire for personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) without distinction across all realms of rebirth, then that renewed existence is employed for arising and its arising is established; that is "drawing forth" (*karṣaṇa*). [This occurs] because of binding (*nibandhana*).

To the question of by what means, where, and for whom [this occurs], he himself provides the answer: "By means of the appropriations (*upādāna*), in the desire-realm and so forth that are conducive to rebirth.

By means of the four appropriations characterized by desire and attachment (*chanda-rāga*), consciousness (*vijñāna*)—which has been projected by karma—is bound and established within the desire-realm, views, ascetic rules and observances, and the doctrine of self, which are conducive to its arising; for consciousness functions therein through the power of desire and attachment.

Regarding the phrase "due to facing toward" (*ābhimukhyāt*), here too, in response to the opportunity for another's question, he himself says: "Because existence (*bhava*) brings about the confrontation [of the result] so that the karma previously performed may again yield its maturation (*vipāka*). Just as consciousness (*vijñāna*)—which is bound by its cause, being the karma performed in a previous life existing in the state of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—obtains its functional activity toward the fruit of maturation, so too does existence become truly present and, having projected a new birth, faces toward its actualization. Thus, because it is brought face-to-face by existence, the world is afflicted:
it suffers through birth, and through old age and death.
What? It is that "the world is afflicted.

Thus, when there is the production of renewed existence from becoming, one is afflicted from the very beginning at the moment of conception due to the coagulation of consciousness with the semen and blood;
likewise, one is afflicted by being turned about within the mother’s stomach and intestines.
Furthermore, it suffers from the inability to abandon its mother’s cramped and difficult mode of feeding;
likewise, it emerges through a narrow and impure passage.

The world that has been born suffers again through old age, characterized by baldness, graying hair, and so forth, and through death, characterized by the dissolution of name-and-form, as it falls away from the two beloved things: youth and life.
"The world is afflicted" means that it "goes"; the meaning is that it goes from a homogeneous interval to a momentary interval.

"It is afflicted" (kliśyate) means that one is tormented by birth, aging, sickness, death, and so forth, within the three realms through a succession of moments and by way of the state of constant coming and going (ājavañjavībhāva).
Others say that "it is afflicted" means "it is not purified.
Thus, this twelve-linked dependent origination, characterized by defilement (saṃkleśa), is the opposite of purification by means of the eleven meanings beginning with concealment.
The sequence of origination beginning with ignorance [proceeds] because each preceding factor brings about each succeeding one.
Defilement is threefold: the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), the defilement of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), and the defilement of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*).
Among these, the defilement of afflictions consists of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*);
the defilement of karma consists of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*).
The defilement of birth consists of the remaining members [of dependent origination].
Defilement is twofold: defilement as cause and defilement as fruit.
Among these, defilement as cause consists of those members whose intrinsic nature is affliction and karma.
And the defilement of the fruit is by means of the remaining [factors].

Defilement is sevenfold, corresponding to the sevenfold cause: the cause of perversion (*viparyāsa-hetu*), the cause of projection (*ākṣepa-hetu*), the cause of leading-on (*upanaya-hetu*), the cause of appropriation (*parigraha-hetu*), the cause of enjoyment (*upabhoga-hetu*), the cause of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa-hetu*), and the cause of agitation (*udvega-hetu*).
Among these, the cause of perversion is ignorance (*avidyā*).
The projecting cause is the formative forces (*saṃskāra*);
the bringing-into-existence cause is consciousness (*vijñāna*);
the grasping causes are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Contact and sensation are the causes of enjoyment;
craving, grasping, and becoming are the causes of attraction;
birth, aging, and death are the causes of distress.
And this defilement proceeds from unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*).

Furthermore, in how many ways is defilement shown in brief by means of this twelvefold dependent origination? For this very reason, it is said: "This twelvefold dependent origination is defilement in three ways, in two ways, and in seven ways.
The word *ca* (and) has the sense of conjunction and the sense of enumeration.
Affliction itself is defilement; thus, there is the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*).
Likewise, there are the defilements of karma and birth.
For when affliction arises, it is called "defilement" because it causes harm to both oneself and others.

As it is also said in the Sūtra: "One who is lustful and overwhelmed by lust intends for his own harm, intends for the harm of others, and intends for the harm of both. The same should be understood for hatred and delusion as well."
It is called "defilement" (*saṃkleśa*) because it produces both the defilements of karma and birth.

For it is through the sovereignty of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that karma projects birth; for one who has seen the truths, even though karma exists, there is no further projection of existence (*punarbhava*), because the seed of future existence is made to become actual existence by the manifestation of the afflictions, and because the connection to rebirth occurs only for one whose mind is afflicted.
Therefore, for an Arhat, there is no connection to rebirth due to the absence of an afflicted mind.
Action, whether wholesome or unwholesome, is a defilement because it causes weariness of body and mind in the present and because it yields maturation in the future.
Birth, too, is a defilement because it is the locus of all calamities.
Thus, defilement is threefold.
This is because the cause is divided into two types:
the defilement of afflictions (*kleśasaṃkleśa*), which consists of the triad of ignorance, craving, and grasping, since all three have the nature of affliction;
and the defilement of karma (*karmasaṃkleśa*), which consists of the two, namely formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*), since both have the nature of karma.

However, there is this distinction: karma in its state as essential nature (*svarūpāvastha*) is "formative predispositions" (*saṃskāra*), while in its state as a seed (*bījāvastha*) it is "existence" (*bhava*).

As for the defilement of birth (*janmasaṃkleśa*), the remaining members—consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*)—are included within birth because they are comprised therein. Thus, the two-fold defilement is distinguished by way of cause and fruit.
The defilement of cause consists of those factors whose intrinsic nature is affliction and karma;
the defilement of result consists of the remaining factors.

In this context, karma and afflictions constitute the "defilement of cause" because they are engaged in bringing about birth—which, consisting of the factors from consciousness through feeling and characterized by the calamities of birth, old age, and death.
And the defilement of the fruit consists of the remaining factors beginning with consciousness, because they are the fruits of karma and afflictions.

Furthermore, this very dependent origination is a sevenfold defilement; it is a sevenfold cause because it serves as the cause for perversion, projection, leading, grasping, enjoyment, attraction, and agitation.
Among these, the cause of perversion is ignorance.
For one who has fallen into ignorance, due to delusion regarding reality, perverts the impermanent and so forth by way of the permanent and so forth.

The formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are the projecting cause, because they establish the seed of birth—which consists of four factors—within consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consciousness is the leading cause, because it leads [the being] to the sphere of rebirth after having passed away from here.

Name-and-form and the six sense-bases are the cause of appropriation because, for one who has been led [into birth], there is the appropriation of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) by means of name-and-form and the six sense-bases.

Previously, appropriation was stated to be by name-and-form alone with reference to the womb-born (*jarāyuja*) and other modes of birth; now, with reference to the spontaneously born (*upapāduka*), appropriation is also stated to be by the six sense-bases.
Alternatively, it is intended that by name-and-form, the inclusion of the mere personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is first expressed at the outset.
In this case, however, there is no contradiction between [the state of] being incomplete and being complete.
Contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are the causes of experience;
for through experience accompanied by its cause, one experiences the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome and unwholesome karma.
Craving, grasping, and becoming are the causes of attraction.
That fool, having experienced the ripening of karma, craves for this or that sensation;
and with craving increased, he grasps at sensual pleasures and so forth through the craving for union with them.

And because of that grasping (*upādāna*), his previously existing karma pertaining to rebirth—which exists in the state of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—undergoes transformation; having obtained its activity through the yielding of its projected maturation (*vipāka*), it becomes "existence" (*bhava*).

Since that existence—consisting of craving, grasping, and becoming—is drawn forth and brought face-to-face for the production of renewed existence, as projected by the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), craving, grasping, and becoming are the cause of attraction.

Alternatively, because one particular latent impression of karma, corresponding to desire and attachment, is brought face-to-face through the power of craving, craving, grasping, and becoming are the cause of attraction.

Birth and old age and death are the cause of agitation; thus, by drawing out [the meaning] here, one experiences the suffering of birth, old age, and death within each respective class of beings, as well as other sufferings—sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair—which have infinite varieties.
In that context, by the mention of the threefold defilement (*saṃkleśa*), the fact that afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma are the common and uncommon causes of birth is demonstrated.
For affliction is the common cause of the sprout of birth, like the earth and so forth.
The specific cause of karma is like a seed for a sprout, because there is a difference in birth corresponding to the difference in that [cause].

Alternatively, he demonstrates here that there are not three sections consisting of the prior limit, the posterior limit, and the middle limit, but rather [the three] are karma, afflictions, and fruit;
by this twofold designation, he shows that this is merely cause and fruit, and that no other agent or experiencer is defiled here.
Alternatively, in this context, karma and afflictions alone are the cause;
for it is observed that birth occurs or does not occur depending on the presence or absence of those two.
Therefore, birth is indeed their fruit.
Therefore, it is shown that here there is neither cause nor fruit, but rather in every case a state consisting of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandhika-avasthā*).

Furthermore, by the exposition of the sevenfold causes, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is shown to be twofold: characterized by projection (*ākṣepa-lakṣaṇa*) and characterized by actualization (*abhinirvṛtti-lakṣaṇa*).

Among these, dependent origination characterized by projection is explained by means of seven members (*aṅga*), because this demonstrates that by what it is projected, how it is projected, and what is projected.

The characteristic of manifestation (*abhinirvṛttilakṣaṇa*) consists of five factors: that by which there is manifestation, the manner in which there is manifestation, what the manifestation is, and the disadvantage (*ādīnava*) within that manifestation. By what is it projected? It is projected by the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*); for, having become deluded regarding reality, one perceives erroneously and constructs wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable (*āniñjya*) formative forces. In what way is it projected by those formative forces? By nourishing the seeds within consciousness (*vijñāna*), thereby establishing it in a state of potentiality for arising.
What is projected? It is name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling pertaining to future existence, as appropriate.

Once thus projected, by what is it brought to completion? By means of clinging, which arises with craving as its condition—that craving which has arisen here in dependence on feeling produced from what was previously projected, according to the stated sequence.
How is it brought to completion by that? Because, through that [clinging], karma—which exists in the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) within consciousness—is made into becoming (*bhava*).
For various kinds of karmic latencies reside within consciousness because it is permeated by diverse formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
That which, through the grasping of specific types of appropriation (*upādāna*), causes renewed existence (*punarbhava*) to occur here, is called "existence" (*bhava*) in this context.
What, then, is that "arising" (*abhinirvṛtti*)? It is the birth in the future of that projected [continuum] consisting of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth.
Furthermore, when that [existence] exists, what is the disadvantage? It is old age and death, resulting from the loss of beloved youth and life, and so forth.
If it is argued that the cause for leading [to this state] is purposeless here, it is not purposeless;
it is for the sake of refuting the attainment of the occurrence of existence (*bhava*) through the arising of existence (*upapatti-bhava*) following a severed death.

And all these defilements proceed from unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), because defilement has the mind and mental factors as its basis. For it has been said: "Unreal imagination consists of the mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms."
The Summary Meaning of Unreal Imagination: Furthermore, the summary meaning of unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is illuminated through nine kinds of characteristics:

the characteristic of existence, the characteristic of non-existence, the specific characteristic, the characteristic of inclusion, the characteristic of the means for entering the characteristic of non-existence, the characteristic of differentiation, the characteristic of synonyms, the characteristic of manifestation, and the characteristic of affliction.

Regarding the phrase "the summary meaning of unreal imagination," this detailed explanation of the meaning is provided for the sake of easy comprehension, while the presentation of the summary meaning is for the sake of not forgetting it.
Therefore, two points are stated here:
the characteristic of existence, namely that "unreal imagination exists," and the characteristic of non-existence, namely that "duality is not found therein."
Thus:
consciousness arises manifesting as the particular characteristics of objects, sentient beings, self, and representations.
Thus:
"The characteristic of inclusion consists of the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected."

The characteristic of the means for entering the characteristic of non-existence: "Relying upon perception, non-perception arises," and so forth. The characteristic of differentiation: "Unreal imagination consists of the mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms."
Thus:
"The definition of the synonyms is that consciousness is the perception of the object itself, while the mental factors [perceive] its specific qualities."
The characteristic of active engagement consists of one, the consciousness of conditions (*pratyayavijñāna*), and a second, that which pertains to experience (*aupabhogika*).
The characteristic of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) is described as "due to concealing, planting, leading, and grasping," and so forth.

Having thus explained the ninefold unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), what is the connection here for explaining how emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is to be understood? By this, two things have been asserted: unreal imagination and emptiness;

as well as purification preceded by affliction (*saṃkleśa*); and the determination of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) based upon the realization of phenomena (*dharma*). Therefore, immediately after the explanation of unreal imagination, he explains how emptiness is to be understood, starting with the detailed exposition: "The characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and then the synonyms (*paryāya*)," and so forth.

In this context, the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) consists in the nature of negating both existence and non-existence, because it pervades all the various divisions of emptiness. A synonym (*paryāya*) is another name.
The meaning of the synonym (*paryāyārtha*) is the ground for the application of that synonym, which accords with the synonym itself.

Although it is non-conceptual because its characteristic is undifferentiated like space, there is a distinction due to the difference between states of association with and dissociation from adventitious secondary afflictions;

furthermore, there is another sixteenfold distinction based on the differentiation of superimpositions regarding persons (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*). The means of proof (*sādhana*) is the reasoning (*yukti*) for demonstrating these various classifications of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Furthermore, what is the reason that emptiness must be understood through these modes? Because it is the object of purification, it should be understood by those seeking purification according to its characteristics (*lakṣaṇataḥ*).
The meaning of the synonyms is for the sake of non-confusion regarding the explanations of synonyms in other sūtras.
The meaning of the synonyms [is explained] because, through the realization of the meaning of the synonyms, emptiness is determined to be the object of purification.
When defilement has been eliminated, that [nature] is pure; thus, for the sake of generating effort toward the abandonment of that defilement, it should be understood through its differentiation.

Because one easily understands differentiation through the realization of the means of establishing that differentiation—even though there is no actual transformation—it should also be known by way of the means of establishing differentiation.

If there were separateness, it would not be tenable for the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) to be other than the phenomena themselves, just as [it is not tenable] in the case of impermanence and suffering.
If there were identity, there would be no knowledge that has purification as its object, nor would there be a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
By this, the characteristic that is free from both identity and difference is illuminated.

How is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) to be understood? Since the characteristic was indeed mentioned previously, that very thing was asked about first. It should be understood as follows: "The non-existence of duality is the existence of that non-existence; this is the characteristic of emptiness.

For duality—namely, the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*)—is non-existent in the form of a real entity (*vastu-rūpa*), because its nature is merely imagined (*parikalpita-ātmakatva*) within or by means of unreal imagination (*abhūta-parikalpa*).

And that which is the existence (*bhāva*) of this non-existence of duality (*dvayābhāva*) is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). For the sake of conforming to the verse (*kārikā*), the suffix indicating existence should be understood here as having been elided in the instruction. What is this "existence of non-existence"? It is the self-nature (*ātmatva*) or the existence (*astitva*) of non-existence.

Otherwise, there would be the very existence of duality; for that [duality] does not exist as a real entity (*bhāva*). Therefore, he said: "Thus, emptiness is shown to have the characteristic of having non-existence as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and not the characteristic of having the form of an existent entity."

Since the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*) denotes the negation of existence, this meaning is understood even in the absence of the word "existence" (*bhāva*); thus, the word "existence" here is redundant. [Response: It is not redundant. When it is stated merely that "the non-existence of duality is the characteristic of emptiness," the non-existence of duality would be understood here as an independent entity, like the non-existence of a rabbit's horn, rather than having the nature of a *dharmatā* (the true nature of phenomena) like suffering and so forth.
Therefore, it is said: "The non-existence of duality is emptiness.
Furthermore, the existence of that very non-existence within the unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is called "emptiness."
Because non-existence (*abhāva*) is grasped by the characteristic of existence (*bhāva-lakṣaṇa*), its nature as the true state of phenomena (*dharmatā-rūpatā*) is demonstrated.

Alternatively, since the word "non-existence" in the phrase "emptiness is the non-existence of duality" has a general meaning, it is not understood which kind of non-existence is intended here; therefore, in order to demonstrate absolute non-existence, it is said: "The existence of the non-existence of duality within the construction of the unreal (*abhūta-parikalpa*).
For indeed, prior non-existence (*prāg-abhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsa-abhāva*) are not fit to be designated apart from their own respective substrata.
Furthermore, it is not logical for mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) to have a single locus, because it depends on both [terms].
Therefore, since the characteristic of non-existence is derived from existence, it is demonstrated that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is precisely the absolute non-existence of the grasped and the grasper.

If emptiness is of the nature of non-existence, why is it called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)? Because it is the object of supreme knowledge (*paramajñāna*), like impermanence (*anityatā*), and not because it is a substantial entity (*vastu*).
Moreover, this is not of the nature of non-existence;
for that which is its nature of non-existence is neither existence nor non-existence.
How is it not existence? Because it is the absence of duality.
For if there were existence, there would not be the absolute non-existence of duality, nor would it be the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the imagination of the unreal.
Why is it not non-existence? Because there is the existence of the non-existence of duality;
for the non-existence of duality is not non-existent in its own nature as the non-existence of duality.

If that were non-existence, then the existence of the duality would follow, and there would not be the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the imagination of the unreal, just as [there is] the nature of permanence and suffering.

Because it consists in the absence of the nature of permanence and happiness—which have been superimposed upon the sentient being by way of perversion—it is said to be neither existence nor non-existence.
Furthermore, if emptiness is the true nature of the imagination of the unreal, should it be said to be different from it or non-different? To this he says: "And this is the definition of emptiness."
The very nature of non-existence is [the absence of duality],
or rather, existence itself consists in the negation of non-existence.
Therefore, it does not have the characteristic of being either different from or identical to the imagination of the unreal.
If there were separateness, it would not be tenable for the *dharmatā* (the true nature of phenomena) to be other than the *dharma* (phenomenon).
What, then, is the lack of tenability? Because it would have a characteristic distinct from the phenomenon, the *dharmatā* would become merely another phenomenon, just like any other phenomenon.

Furthermore, one phenomenon cannot be the *dharmatā* of another phenomenon, because that would necessitate searching for yet another phenomenon therein, leading to the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
"Just as impermanence is not other than impermanent things and suffering is not other than what is suffering, so too emptiness is not other than the empty.
If they were identical, there would be no object for purification, nor would there be a universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).

Purification (*viśuddhi*) is that by which one is purified; it is the path (*mārga*). Since it is not other than the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena, the object of the path would not exist, just like the specific characteristic of phenomena itself.
Consequently, a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is also untenable, because it is not other than the specific characteristic.
In that case as well, since there would be a mutual distinction between [the universal] and the nature of the dharma itself, its status as a universal would be lost.

Alternatively, because the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) would be distinct from it, there would be an absence of distinction [between them], just like the nature of an entity (*bhāvasvarūpa*).
Consequently, the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) would also be non-existent, because a universal characteristic depends upon distinction.

Alternatively, the object of focus for the sake of purification is the "object of purification" (*viśuddhyālambana*); it is not the case that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of an entity, when taken as an object, brings about purification, because that would entail the absurd consequence that all sentient beings are already purified. If [emptiness] is inexpressible as being either different or non-different [from an entity], how is it that the doctrine of the Nirgranthas is not being relied upon? For whoever explains an existing entity in terms of its identity with or difference from [its nature] relies upon the doctrine of the Nirgranthas. But since emptiness is not an entity, this fault does not apply.

By this, emptiness is elucidated as having the characteristic of existence, the characteristic of the nature of non-existence, the characteristic of non-duality, and the characteristic of being free from identity and difference.
The characteristic of emptiness has been explained.
Now the synonyms are stated: suchness, the limit of reality, the signless, the ultimate truth, and the realm of phenomena—these, in brief, are the synonyms for emptiness.

Thus, "synonym" (paryāya) refers to the communication of a single meaning through different words; it is called a synonym because it expresses the meaning of a synonym. Those designations are taught as emptiness itself in other sūtras.
And while these five synonyms have been stated in the verse according to their primary significance, other synonyms not mentioned here should likewise be understood from the scriptures (*pravacana*).
They are as follows: non-duality, the realm of non-conceptuality, the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), ineffability, non-cessation, the unconditioned, nirvāṇa, and so forth.

He shows how the meaning of these synonyms is to be understood: "These words are not figurative; rather, they are literal (anvartha) because they correspond respectively to non-alteration, non-perversion, cessation, the sphere of the noble ones, and the cause of the noble dharmas."
Thus, "tathatā" (suchness) is so called in the sense of being non-otherwise; that is to say, in the sense of being changeless.
To demonstrate this very point, he says: "because it is eternally just so."
The meaning is that because it is eternally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it does not undergo transformation.
It is the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*) in the sense of being non-erroneous; "reality" (*bhūta*) means truth, that which is non-perverted.

The "limit" (*koṭi*) is the boundary, because beyond it there is no other object of knowledge; therefore, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is called the ultimate limit of what is real (*bhūtaparyanta*).
How is suchness (*tathatā*) said to be an object of knowledge? Because it is the domain of the wisdom that purifies the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
It has the sense of being non-erroneous, in the sense of being free from both superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*).
Regarding this very point, he states the reason: "Because error has no real object.
For error is indeed conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); since it lacks a referent (*anālambana*), there is no real entity that constitutes the object of error.
"The signless (*animitta*) is so called in the sense of the cessation of signs (*nimittanirodha*).
Here, "signlessness" is said to be the cessation of signs.
To demonstrate this very point, he says: "because of the absence of all signs."
Emptiness is called "signless" because it is empty of all signs, whether conditioned or unconditioned.
It is signless because of the absence of all signs;
the signless itself is the signless.

Because it is the domain of noble gnosis (*āryajñāna*), it is called the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); for "ultimate" refers to supramundane gnosis (*lokottarajñāna*), and that which is its object is the ultimate reality.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "because it is the domain of supreme gnosis."
It is the *dharmadhātu* because it is the cause of the noble qualities (*āryadharma*).
Here, by the word "dharma," the noble qualities are meant, beginning with right view and ending with the knowledge of right liberation.
Because it is the cause of those, it is called a *dhātu*.
Elucidating this very point, he says: "Because the noble dharmas have that as their source (*ālambana-prabhava*).

He further states that this word *dhātu* is also used in the sense of maintaining its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*); however, in this context, the meaning of *dhātu* is the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
For example: gold-mine (*suvarṇadhātu*), copper-mine (*tāmradhātu*), silver-mine (*raupyadhātu*).
Other synonyms mentioned in other sūtras should also be explained according to their own meaning by this very same principle.

Since emptiness consists in the absence of the grasped and the grasper, one asks, not conceiving of any differentiation [within it]: "Alternatively, it was stated that differentiation is to be understood immediately after the meaning of the synonyms; therefore, following that explanation, one asks: how is the differentiation of emptiness to be understood?
For unreal imagination is defilement, and its abandonment is called purification.
And at the time of defilement and purification, there is nothing other than emptiness itself that becomes defiled or purified.

Therefore, in order to demonstrate that it is emptiness itself that becomes defiled and purified during the times of affliction and purification, he says: "It is both defiled and purified. This is its differentiation. Because of a lack of understanding as to when it is defiled and when it is stainless, he asks: "In what state is it defiled, and in what state is it purified? [The answer is: "It is with stain and without stain," and so forth in detail.
With reference to the non-transformation and transformation of the basis (*āśraya*), it is established as being both with stain and with stain removed.

For those ignorant ones whose mental continua are defiled by the afflictions such as passion and the like—due to their adherence to the grasped and the grasper—and for whom emptiness does not manifest because of the faults of non-comprehension and miscomprehension, it is established as being "with stain.
For those noble ones whose minds are non-erroneous due to the knowledge of reality, and for whom emptiness manifests continuously, stainless like space, it is said to be "with stain removed."
Thus, the defilement and purification of emptiness should be viewed as relative; it is not by way of having a stained intrinsic nature, because [emptiness] is luminous by nature.
As for the detailed explanation beginning with "if it were to become stained," a difference in states is never observed without some transformation.
Since transformation is permeated by arising and perishing, he asks: "How is it that [emptiness], having the nature of transformation, is not impermanent?
For there is no other transformation from the state of affliction to the state of the purity of emptiness.
The existence of reality, however, does not undergo any change in its intrinsic nature; rather, it is purified through the removal of adventitious defilements.
Since its purity is held to be like the purification of the water-element, gold, or space, it is therefore not impermanent.

For just as the elements of water, gold, and space— because they do not have that [impurity] as their intrinsic nature— are possessed of adventitious impurities even though they lack the nature of being impure,
and yet become pure upon the removal of those adventitious impurities without undergoing any change in their own nature;
so too emptiness is defiled by adventitious impurities, and it becomes pure upon their departure, despite its own essential nature remaining unaltered.

For one who establishes that very same entity as having the characteristic of defilement previously and the nature of purity subsequently, there can be no cessation of its quality of transformation, because it possesses the nature of transformation. However, this is not the case where both [defilement and purity] are adventitious;
therefore, such an entity does not touch upon the quality of transformation.
Since all the classifications of emptiness must be explained in the section concerning the exposition of classifications, he says: "This is another classification.

Emptiness is of sixteen kinds; thus, it becomes sixteenfold by way of the differentiation of entities (*vastu*), though there is no differentiation in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) which is the absence of duality.

This sixteenfold emptiness is taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, from internal emptiness up to the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence. This should be understood in brief as follows: the emptiness of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, their body, and the basis;
and so forth.

The general characteristic of emptiness is that all phenomena have a non-dual nature; otherwise, that multiplicity could not be demonstrated. Therefore, he demonstrates that multiplicity through the multiplicity of entities.
First of all, the enjoyer must be dissolved, for the sake of abandoning attachment and clinging to it.
For attachment and clinging to that [body] indeed constitute an obstacle to the attainment of the liberation of Buddhahood; following that is the food,
and following that is the body which is the basis for those two.

Immediately after that, the world as the receptacle for the support—that is, the body—should be contemplated, because it serves as an aid to the experiencer; this is for the purpose of turning away from the grasping at "mine" regarding affection for the self.
These four kinds of entities are called the emptiness of entities (*vastu-śūnyatā*).
Among them, the emptiness of the experiencer (*bhoktṛ-śūnyatā*) begins with the internal sense-bases (*ādhyātmikāny āyatanāni*).
And these [faculties], from the eye up to the mind, [are the experiencer] because there is no other experiencer apart from them.

Since the world observes the activity of the eye and the other faculties in the enjoyment of objects, there arises the conceit of being an experiencer with respect to the eye and the rest; therefore, the emptiness of the bases (āyatana) such as the eye is called the emptiness of the experiencer.
The emptiness of food refers to external things, from form (*rūpa*) up to and including mental phenomena (*dharma*).
These are called "food" because they are consumed by way of being objects; therefore, the emptiness of the external sense bases is called the "emptiness of food.

Because those two—the consumer and the food—exist within the body in a state of mutual inseparability, that body is called the "physical frame" (*śarīra*); thus, its emptiness is called "internal-external emptiness" (*adhyātmabahirdhāśūnyatā*).
The receptacle world is the "basis" (vastu) because it is known as the basis upon which sentient beings everywhere rest.
For this very reason, it is said: "Because of its vastness, the emptiness of that is called 'great emptiness' (mahāśūnyatā).
The word *vastu* is to be connected with each [term] individually.

When that yogic Bodhisattva attends with reasoned and systematic mental attention to the emptiness of the fourfold objects of knowledge, another grasping at signs arises: the conceptualization that "this very thing—the non-apprehension of subject and object—is here the ultimate mode of being, just as it was seen by that knowledge derived from hearing. This is the conceptual construction regarding the emptiness of the internal and external sense bases and so forth, which were perceived through that knowledge of emptiness.

For the purpose of eliminating that twofold conceptualization which is the cause of error regarding the stages of yoga, emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, and the ultimate emptiness have been taught respectively by means of the removal of the aspects of cognition.
Alternatively, that cognition is called "emptiness" because its object is emptiness.
Its emptiness of the nature of grasped and grasper is the "emptiness of emptiness."

The internal sense bases and so forth, as they are perceived by that knowledge of emptiness—that is the ultimate reality (paramārtha) here; thus, its emptiness in the form of the ultimate is "emptiness of the ultimate" (paramārtha-śūnyatā).
Why is this? Because the ultimate is empty of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).

This other apprehension of signs (*nimittagrāha*) is also an obstacle to the cultivation of emptiness (*śūnyatābhāvanā*): it superimposes the nature of an entity upon that very object for the sake of which the bodhisattva practices emptiness. To eliminate that [superimposition], the various forms of emptiness—beginning with the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtaśūnyatā*) and ending with the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnyatā*)—have been taught.
And for what purpose does one practice? One practices emptiness and cultivates emptiness for the sake of attaining the two kinds of merit, up to the purification of all the Buddha-qualities.
For the "two kinds of merit" are the conditioned and the unconditioned—the Path and Nirvana.
One is connected with these respectively as conditioned emptiness and unconditioned emptiness.
"And for the constant welfare of sentient beings":

"In every way and at all times, I must act for the welfare of sentient beings"—this is emptiness and absolute emptiness. "And for the sake of not abandoning cyclic existence": "For the sake of sentient beings, I must not abandon cyclic existence."
For if cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) were abandoned, one would fail to attain the enlightenment of a bodhisattva and would instead remain fixed in the enlightenment of a śrāvaka.
Its emptiness is the emptiness of that which is without beginning or end (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*).

Why, then, is its emptiness taught? To this he says: "Because if one did not see the emptiness of cyclic existence, which is without beginning or end, one would become weary and abandon cyclic existence."
And for the inexhaustibility of the wholesome.
Thus, he explains that one does not scatter [the roots of merit], meaning one does not relinquish them, thinking, "May my roots of merit not be exhausted even in the nirvana without remainder.
If this is so, how then is the nirvana-realm without remainder established? It is established because of the absence of a body that is the maturation of tainted dharmas (*sāsravadharma*).

However, the established tenet is that for the Buddha, the Blessed One, whose body is the untainted *dharmakāya*, there is no cessation even in the realm of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇadhātu*).
Therefore, its emptiness is called the "emptiness of non-rejection" (*anavakāraśūnyatā*).
And for the sake of purifying the lineage (*gotra*), its emptiness is "emptiness of intrinsic nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*).
He states the reason for this very point: "For the lineage is the intrinsic nature. Why is this so?
Therefore, he says: "Because it is intrinsic" (*svābhāvikatvāt*).
The meaning is that it is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), beginningless in time, and not adventitious.

Just as in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) some things are sentient and some are insentient, so too here, some of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) belong to the Buddha-lineage (*buddhagotra*) and some belong to the lineage of the Śrāvakas and others.
Nor is the lineage (gotra) accidental, because it has been transmitted through a beginningless succession, like the distinction between sentient and insentient beings.
Others hold that since all sentient beings possess the lineage of the Tathāgata, "lineage" here should be understood as suchness (tathātva).
[This is for the sake of attaining the primary and secondary marks.]
Therefore, the emptiness of the marks of a great person (mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa), together with their secondary characteristics (anuvyañjana), is called the "emptiness of marks" (lakṣaṇaśūnyatā).
Furthermore, the bodhisattva applies himself to this for the sake of purifying the qualities of a Buddha (buddhadharma).

Because of the statement "he enters into" (*prapadyate*), it should be understood that the bodhisattva enters everywhere for the sake of attaining the two kinds of merit, and that the bodhisattva always enters for the benefit of sentient beings.
To the question "Of which Buddha-qualities?", he says: "Of the powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities (*āveṇika*), and so forth."
One practices with the thought: "In brief, I must strive for the attainment of all the qualities of a Buddha.

Therefore, through the cultivation of emptiness, the emptiness of all phenomena is expressed. What kind of cultivation is this? It is the unimpeded engagement of knowledge toward the object of knowledge.
In this way, first of all, the systematic arrangement of the fourteen [emptinesses], beginning with internal emptiness and ending with the emptiness of all phenomena, should be understood.

Furthermore, what is emptiness (śūnyatā) regarding the enjoyer and so forth, and what is its essential nature? To this he says: "In this context, emptiness is indeed the non-existence of the person (pudgala) and of phenomena (dharma);
the existence of that non-existence within them is another emptiness."
Thus,
in this context, emptiness is the non-existence of the person and phenomena— such as the experiencer and so forth— as previously described;
and emptiness is also the actual existence of that non-existence.
In that regard, the non-existence and existence of both the person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*) is the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*).
The actual existence of that non-existence is the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
For what purpose, then, are these two kinds of emptiness established at the end? To this he says: "For the sake of making known the characteristic of emptiness."

For what purpose, then, is emptiness explained? To this he says: it is for the sake of avoiding, respectively, the superimposition of a person and of phenomena, as well as the denial of that emptiness.
He establishes the emptiness of non-existence for the sake of avoiding the superimposition of a person and of phenomena;
and he establishes the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence for the sake of avoiding the denial of that emptiness.
If the emptiness of non-existence were not taught, it would follow that the imagined natures of both phenomena and the person truly exist.
If the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence were not taught, it would follow that emptiness itself does not exist;
and due to its non-existence, the existence of the person and phenomena would persist as before.

In that regard, internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) is the non-existence of the imagined characteristics of the person who is the experiencer and of the eyes and so forth, which are considered by the ignorant to be the experiencer—these being the internal sense bases (*āyatana*) whose nature is the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*)—and the actual existence of that very non-existence.

External emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*) is the non-existence of the imagined characteristics of the objects of experience belonging to the self and of forms and so forth, which are considered by the ignorant to be the objects of experience—these being the external sense bases whose nature is the appearance of the representations of form and so forth—and the actual existence of that very non-existence.

The non-existence of the enjoyer-person (*bhoktṛ-pudgala*) within that body—the physical frame—and of form (*rūpa*) and so forth as imagined by foolish people, as well as the existence of that non-existence, is internal-external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*).

The non-existence of the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) within the receptacle-world (*bhājana-loka*), the non-existence of its imagined intrinsic nature, and the actual existence of that non-existence, is great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*).

In the case of the knowledge of emptiness and the aspect of the ultimate, there is the emptiness of the imagined characteristic of the knower—the person who grasps the aspect—and the non-existence of that [grasping]; furthermore, the existence of that very non-existence is, respectively, the emptiness of emptiness and the emptiness of the ultimate.

Regarding that purpose for which a bodhisattva practices—namely, those things to be practiced by a bodhisattva beginning with the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and ending with all the qualities of a Buddha—the non-existence of a person (*pudgala*) and of phenomena characterized by conceptual construction (*parikalpitalakṣaṇa*), as well as the actual existence of that non-existence, are respectively the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*) up to the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*).
For instance, there is no person who is the owner or the agent of the conditioned, nor does the conditioned exist by way of the self (*ātman*) imagined by foolish people.

In brief, these sixteen emptinesses, which are not shared by the Śrāvakas, have been taught for the sake of counteracting all grasping at conceptual constructions and for the sake of explaining the underlying intentions (*abhisandhi*) of all the Sūtras.
Herein, the Blessed One has demonstrated the objective domain of emptiness, the intrinsic nature of emptiness, and the purpose of the cultivation of emptiness.
Among these, the objective domain of emptiness consists of the referents beginning with the "enjoyer" and extending up to the qualities of a Buddha.
Furthermore, that demonstration is for the purpose of making known that emptiness pervades all phenomena.
The nature of emptiness is the nature of non-existence and the nature of the existence of non-existence.

Moreover, the demonstration of the nature of emptiness is for the purpose of making known that its essence consists in the transcendence of all views by way of being the antidote to superimposition and denial.
The purpose of the cultivation of emptiness begins with "for the sake of attaining the two kinds of merit" and extends up to "for the attainment of the qualities of a Buddha.

Furthermore, this demonstration is for the purpose of showing that the excellence of the perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)—both for oneself and others—is attained solely through the cultivation of emptiness.

Thus, the divisions of emptiness should be understood as follows: it is "defiled" in its stained state and "pure" in its stainless state. One should know the sixteenfold division just mentioned, beginning with internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*).
Since the proof for that [distinction] was indicated immediately after the enumeration of the distinction, he asks immediately following that explanation: "How is the proof to be understood?

What is established here? It is the state of being afflicted by adventitious secondary defilements and the state of natural purity. With regard to the proof concerning affliction, he says: "If this were not afflicted, all embodied beings would be liberated."
Thus:
liberation is the abandonment of the afflictions (saṃkleśa),
and that abandonment of the afflictions results from the cultivation of the path.

In this regard, if the emptiness of phenomena were not defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions even when the antidote has not arisen—the word "even" implying as if it had arisen—then, in that case, because there would be an absence of affliction, all sentient beings would be liberated without effort. "Without effort" means precisely without the antidote. However, since there is no liberation for living beings without the antidote, one must necessarily admit that during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), suchness (*tathatā*) is defiled by adventitious stains.

Thus, the classification of emptiness as being defiled has been established. Now, establishing the classification of its purification, he says: "If this [emptiness] were not pure, effort would be fruitless."
The term "of embodied beings" (*dehinām*) is to be connected [with the preceding].

Now, even if the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*) has arisen, because of the word "even" (*api*), it would not be pure as if it had not arisen; this being the case, the undertaking for the sake of liberation would be fruitless, since that impurity would not be removed even by the cultivation of the counteragent, and because liberation is impossible for one who possesses impurity.
However, it is not accepted that the undertaking for the sake of liberation is fruitless.
Therefore, it must be accepted that the purification of emptiness results from the removal of adventitious secondary afflictions through the practice of their antidotes.
In this way, the classification of the purification of emptiness is established.
Here, defilement arises from the appropriation of defiled phenomena, while purification arises from the grasping of purified phenomena.
But defilement or purification is not held to belong directly to emptiness, because the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is dependent upon the phenomena themselves.
For this very reason, it has been said: "Otherwise, all embodied beings would be liberated [without effort]."
Therefore, by saying "of embodied beings," it is precisely that [the body] which is stated to be the basis [of emptiness].

Otherwise, if defilement or purification were to belong directly to emptiness itself, what connection would there be with embodied beings, such that the purification of emptiness is called the purification of embodied beings, and the defilement of emptiness is called their defilement?

And since emptiness is defiled during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and pure during the stage of a noble one (*ārya*), for this very reason it is established that: "It is neither defiled nor non-defiled; it is neither pure nor impure.
How is it neither defiled nor impure?
It is pure precisely because it is purified of duality, as it makes manifest its own nature.
Regarding this very point, he cites scripture: "Because the mind is luminous by its very nature.
And here, it is the *dharmatā* (essential nature) of the mind that is expressed by the word "mind," since such is the characteristic of the mind itself.

How is it that [the mind] is neither non-afflicted nor pure? Rather, by means of two negations, he demonstrates that it is indeed afflicted; he shows that it is afflicted due to the adventitious nature of the afflictions, but not by its very nature.
And there is also scriptural authority for the statement that "it is defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions.

When the distinction was previously stated to be twofold—by way of being afflicted and purified—for what purpose is the distinction now stated to be fourfold? One [teacher] says: it is for the sake of distinguishing it from both the mundane and supramundane paths. For the mundane path is afflicted by the stains belonging to its own level, but not by those of lower levels, because it serves as their antidote.

However, the supramundane path is impure due to its distinctions of weak, medium, and so forth, yet it is pure because it is untainted (*anāsrava*); emptiness is not like that. Having stated that it is "not afflicted" (*akliṣṭa*), it is further said to be "not impure" (*aśuddha*) for the sake of distinguishing it from the eye and other faculties. Others explain that the eye and other faculties are not afflicted because they are unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), and yet they are called "impure" because their natural purity is not present due to their lack of essence (*asāravat*).

Thus, it is not said that this [dharmatā] is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), nor is it called pure (*śuddha*); these terms are used for the purpose of distinguishing it from the wholesome-with-outflows (*kuśala-sāsrava*).
For the wholesome-with-outflows, being included within *saṃsāra*, is not unafflicted;
and because its maturation (*vipāka*) is desirable, it is pure, but it is certainly not the *dharmatā*.
For that [emptiness] is indeed impure during its afflicted state;
thus, the distinction of emptiness regarding defilement and purification as previously indicated is established.

{The Summary Meaning of Emptiness} The summary meaning of emptiness should be understood in terms of its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and its formal establishment (*vyavasthāna*). Regarding that, in terms of its characteristic, it is both the characteristic of non-existence and the characteristic of existence. It is the characteristic of non-existence because of the statement, "Indeed, there is the non-existence of duality"; and it is the characteristic of existence because of the statement, "And the existence of that non-existence. Furthermore, it is the characteristic of existence because of the statement, "It is neither existence nor non-existence."
It is characterized by being free from existence and non-existence, and it is characterized by being free from identity and difference;
this is the characteristic of emptiness.
Therefore, because of the statement that it does not have the characteristic of being either distinct from or identical to the imagination of the unreal (*abhūtaparikalpa*).

Thus is the summary of the meaning according to its characteristics. How is the summary of the meaning to be understood according to its systematic arrangement? To this he says: "Furthermore, the systematic arrangement is to be understood through the arrangement of synonyms and so forth.
This means: [the presentation of] the synonyms, their meaning, their non-differentiation, and their proof.

By this fourfold teaching, which serves as the antidote to four types of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), there is revealed the characteristic of self-nature (*svalakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of activity (*karmalakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of defilement and purification (*saṃkleśavyavadānalakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of reasoning (*yuktilakṣaṇa*).

Among these, the characteristic of self-nature is taught as the antidote to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), for the latter consists in grasping at existence, non-existence, both, difference, and identity.
The characteristic of activity is taught as the antidote to the fear of those who lack conviction regarding the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

The non-erroneous suchness has the activity of karma, the activity of non-perversion, the activity of abandoning all signs, the activity of abiding as the object of all supramundane knowledge, and the activity of being the causal basis for the attainment of the noble dharmas.
Thus, the characteristic of differentiation is for the purpose of dispelling the indolence of those who are indolent and who grasp at what they have attained by hearing about the nature of emptiness.
The characteristic of reasoning is for the purpose of removing the doubts of those who doubt how it becomes both defilement and purification.
The commentary on the first chapter, "On Characteristics," of the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*.

The second chapter: The Determination of Obstructions. In this regard, the pervasive obstruction of afflictions and the known (*kleśajñeyāvaraṇa*) belongs to those of the bodhisattva lineage because it is universal.
The limited obstruction of afflictions belongs to those of the lineage of the śrāvakas and others.
The intensified [obstruction] belongs to those very same individuals who are dominated by conduct such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth.

For those whose conduct is characterized by equal proportions [of the afflictions], there is the obscuration of grasping at and abandoning cyclic existence; this is the cause for the lineage of the bodhisattvas because it is an obscuration to non-abiding nirvana.
Thus, these obscurations have been explained as they apply to both: those belonging to the lineage of bodhisattvas and those belonging to the lineages of śrāvakas and others.

Immediately after the explanation of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is now the occasion for the explanation of the obscurations (*āvaraṇa*), because they were mentioned immediately following that. Thus he says, with reference to the obscurations:
"Pervasive, limited, excessive, and the abandonment of what has been undertaken;

these are declared to be the two obscurations—the obscuration of the two. This refers to the obscuration of those belonging to the lineage of the Bodhisattvas and the obscuration of those belonging to the lineages of the Śrāvakas and others.
This verse is commenced in order to demonstrate the differentiation of the obscurations according to the differentiation of the objects to be obscured.
In that regard, the pervasive obscuration of afflictions and the knowable belongs to those of the Bodhisattva lineage.
It is called "pervasive" (*vyāpi*) because it pervades; that is, because it obscures all objects.
For "all objects" refers to both one's own welfare and the welfare of others.

Alternatively, it is called "pervasive" (*vyāpin*) by way of metaphorical designation because it pervades the two kinds of obscurations—the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*)—of the bodhisattva.

Since the afflictions themselves are the obscurations, due to the similarity (*sārūpya*) between the obscuration and the nature of the afflictions, secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are also included here under the term "affliction."

Otherwise, in the statement "the characteristic of the afflictions is ninefold," envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) would not be included, because they are secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Since it is an obscuration precisely with respect to the knowable, it is called the "obscuration of the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Because cognition is thus obscured by the knowable, there is no object for that cognition at all;

or rather, there is an obscuration of the knowable within cognition, since the knowable acts as an impediment to the arising of cognition. Thus, in the term "obscuration of the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one should understand it as a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopa*), like the expression "oil-vessel" (*tailapātra*).
Furthermore, that [obscuration] is undefiled ignorance.

For those belonging to the bodhisattva lineage who practice the accumulations of merit and wisdom in every way and everywhere in order to attain buddhahood—the attainment of the excellence of the fulfillment of their own and others' welfare—that twofold [obscuration] acts as an impediment.
Therefore, it is established as an obscuration for those of the bodhisattva lineage.
In this context, "pervasive" (*vyāpin*) means that which encompasses all objects in their entirety and in every way.

If it is asked how it is known that it encompasses everything in its entirety, it is because of the statement of the reason: "it is called pervasive because it encompasses the obscurations in their entirety.
Alternatively, the mention of "entirety" and so forth is for the purpose of demonstrating that the word "pervasive" signifies "without remainder."

The "partial" (*prādeśika*) afflictive obscuration belongs to those belonging to the lineage of the *śrāvakas* and so forth; it is designated as "partial" because it is metaphorically so called due to its being an obscuration only to one's own welfare and because it is not all-pervasive.

Is it that *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* have no non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*), such that only the afflictive obscuration is established for them? Let it be so; however, that [non-afflicted ignorance] is not an obscuration for them, because even while it exists, they attain the enlightenment of a *śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*. Indeed, for *śrāvakas* and others, ignorance consists precisely in being an obstacle to the arising of knowledge regarding the objects of the truths, such as suffering.
Consequently, they too would possess both types of obstructions;
therefore, one should not say that the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) belongs only to those of the lineage of the Śrāvakas and so forth.

This is not so; for it is established that only that ignorance which is afflicted, which serves as the antidote to knowledge, and which is the root of saṃsāra, is the obstruction of afflictions, and not the obstruction to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), just like doubt.
Just as doubt (*vicikitsā*) regarding the truths of suffering and so forth is called both a state of uncertainty and a defilement (*kleśa*), but not so regarding other objects;

for regarding other objects there is merely doubt, neither a defilement nor uncertainty— so too, ignorance (*ajñāna*) regarding the truths of suffering and so forth is called both nescience (*avidyā*) and a defilement, but not so regarding other objects.
In other objects, however, there is merely ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is neither nescience (*avidyā*) nor an affliction (*kleśa*).

Therefore, because it acts as an obscuration only with respect to the engagement in the knowledge of the knowable, it is called the "obscuration of the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); for it does not [act as an obscuration] even toward afflictions, karma, and birth, since these indeed arise from nescience alone.
If this were the case, then an obscuration would not be established for Bodhisattvas.
This is not so; for since Bodhisattvas are characterized by the accumulation of learning (*śruta-sambhāra*), their obscuration is the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
As it has been said: "Even an Arhat would never become omniscient without undertaking the five fields of knowledge (*vidyāpada*);
therefore, one should apply effort therein for the sake of refuting others, for the sake of assisting others, or for the sake of one's own knowledge."

Thus, even a mild object of passion and so forth, when it occurs excessively and repeatedly among those of the bodhisattva lineage as well as those of the śrāvaka lineage and so forth, becomes an obscuration for those whose conduct is dominated by passion and the like.
Those for whom any one of the passions, such as desire, operates intensely and repeatedly even toward a mild object are said to be "those whose conduct is dominated by passion."
Furthermore, the obscuration for those of the bodhisattva lineage and for those of the śrāvaka and other lineages is equal.
This is because there is no distinction between the two types [of persons].

Regarding the phrase "the obscuration of those whose conduct is of equal parts" (*samabhāgacarita*): those for whom afflictions arise when in proximity to or in the presence of sense objects, but not constantly, are those whose conduct is of equal parts.
"The obscuration regarding the taking up and abandoning of cyclic existence," and so forth.
For a bodhisattva, by the predominance of compassion, takes up cyclic existence; and by the predominance of wisdom, having seen the faults of cyclic existence as they truly are, abandons it.

Thus, even in the absence of afflictions, because of the lack of anything belonging to a self, there is the undertaking of birth, which is non-abiding nirvana, due to not abiding in either of the two—cyclic existence or nirvana.

The obscuration to that, however, consists in taking up cyclic existence because one is overcome by afflictions, and in abandoning it through a lack of compassion due to not seeing its faults as they truly are.
