Others say that ignorance is called the obscuration here because it acts as an impediment to both compassion and wisdom.
Alternatively, as it is said in the *Mahāratnakūṭa*: "He abides in nirvāṇa through his intention (*āśaya*), and he abides in cyclic existence through his application (*prayoga*)."
For this is the non-abiding nirvāṇa of the bodhisattvas.

In that state, by turning one's back on nirvāṇa through both intention and application, one takes up cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), like a sentient being who does not abide in a spiritual lineage (*agotra*).

Likewise, by turning one's back on cyclic existence through intention and application directed toward nirvāṇa, one abandons cyclic existence, like those belonging to the lineage of the śrāvakas and others.

Thus, the grasping at cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and the abandoning of it constitute an obstacle to non-abiding nirvāṇa for those belonging to the lineage of the bodhisattvas, because they involve falling into one-sidedness regarding either cyclic existence or nirvāṇa.

However, when bodhisattvas attain the state of a Tathāgata, due to the abandonment of the obscurations of afflictions and the known (*kleśajñeyāvaraṇa*), they do not remain in cyclic existence; yet, because of the continuity of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), they do not remain in a nirvāṇa without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*) like the śrāvakas and others.
Therefore, they do not abide in either of the two: cyclic existence or nirvāṇa.

In this context, these five kinds of obscurations are explained because they act as hindrances to the path of the bodhisattva and that of the śrāvakas and others, to their respective applications, to their fruits, and to non-abiding nirvāṇa.
The phrase "according to what is appropriate" means according to what is possible;
therein, the first and the last are obscurations for those belonging to the lineage of the bodhisattvas.
The first [obscuration] is the obscuration of those belonging to the lineages of the śrāvakas and so forth;
the other two, moreover, are declared to be the obscurations for both.
And among those, the obscuration of the knowable is said to be the obscuration of the bodhisattvas.
And that is non-afflicted ignorance.
The nine fetters are the obscuration of afflictions.
Of what are they an obscuration?
The fetter of attachment is an obscuration to spiritual urgency.
The fetter of aversion is an obstacle to equanimity; for because of it, one is unable to remain equanimous even toward an object that is disagreeable.
The remaining [fetters] are obstacles to the vision of reality.
How so?
For these, respectively, serve as obscurations to the full comprehension of the afflictions.

Indeed, the fetter of pride is a great obstacle to the full comprehension of the view of a self-identity; for at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), it is not abandoned because of the intermittent and continuous manifestation of the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*).

The fetter of ignorance [is an obstacle] to the full comprehension of the basis for the view of a self-identity, because through it there is a lack of full comprehension of the aggregates of clinging.

The fetter of views [is an obstacle] to the full comprehension of the truth of cessation, because one is terrified of it by means of the view of a self-identity and the view of grasping at extremes, and because one denies it by means of false view.
The fetter of adherence [is an obstacle] to the full comprehension of the truth of the path, because one adheres to other [methods] as being purification when they are not.
The fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) [is an obstacle] regarding the thorough knowledge of the Three Jewels, because of the lack of faith in their qualities.
The fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) [is an obstacle] regarding the thorough knowledge of gain and honor, because of not seeing the faults therein.

The fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) [is an obstacle] regarding the thorough knowledge of austerity (*saṃlekha*), because of attachment to requisites. [These are further classified] according to the distinctions of pride (*māna*) and so forth.

The thorough comprehension of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is that vision which is distinguished by the absence of [the notions of] self and what belongs to self, as well as grasper and grasped, and by the absence of the intrinsic nature of phenomena as imagined by foolish people.
Its mental fetter (*mānasaṃyojana*) constitutes an obscuration because it acts as a hindrance to its arising.

To the question "Where and how? he says: "Because at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), it is not abandoned due to the influence of the intermittent and continuous activity of the conceit 'I am' (*asmimāna*)."
At the time of the realization of the truths, during the stage conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),
there is the "interrupted" (*sāntara*), which is separated by the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*), and the "uninterrupted" (*vyantara*), which is not separated by the counteragent.
This should be understood to apply to both the superior and the mild counteragents.
As long as one continues to engage with the conceit "I am" (asmimāna), whether in its manifest or latent form, there is no abandonment of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi);
for the conceit "I am" proceeds precisely through the power of the view of a self-identity.
It is connected thus: the fetter of ignorance (avidyāsaṃyojana) is an obstruction to the full comprehension of the objective basis of the view of a self-identity.
The basis for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), by virtue of taking them as its object.

As it is said in the Sūtra: "Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas perceive a self, perceiving 'self, self,' and becoming attached, becoming attached, they do so only by clinging to these very five aggregates of clinging.
What, then, is that thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*)?

The vision of the emptiness of self within the self, and the vision of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of phenomena as imagined by foolish people within the aggregates—whether viewed as impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, or from the perspective of origination and so forth—that is their thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*).
Regarding this very point, he states the reason: "Because of the lack of thorough knowledge of the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) by means of that [ignorance].

For, since there is an absence of such thorough knowledge regarding the aggregates when they are obscured by modes such as permanence through ignorance, ignorance is the obscuration to the thorough knowledge of the aggregates.
The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*) is an obstruction to the full comprehension of the truth of cessation; this is understood from the context.
For the fetter of views consists of three views: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Among these, the view of a self-identity is the vision [of things] as a self or as belonging to a self with respect to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is indeed the view of either eternalism or nihilism regarding that very entity imagined to be a self.
That view by which one denies cause, fruit, activity, or an existing thing, or falsely conceptualizes them, is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The full comprehension of the truth of cessation is [to know it] through its aspects such as peace (*śānta*).

But how is that an obscuration for him? To this he says: "Because of fear of cessation due to the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and because of denial due to false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).

In this context, through the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes, one fears cessation, thinking, "I shall not exist there"; and through false view, one denies it, thinking, "Cessation does not exist at all.

Therein, by means of the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes, one does not fully understand [cessation] as peaceful, sublime, and an escape; and by means of false view, one does not fully understand it as cessation.
Thus, the fetter of views is an obstruction to the full comprehension of cessation;
the fetter of grasping is an obstruction to the full comprehension of the truth of the path.
Therein, the fetter of grasping consists of the grasping of views and the grasping of rules and observances.

In this context, *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (clinging to views) is the vision that regards a view, or the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) which are the basis for views, as being superior and so forth.

*Śīlavrataparāmarśa* (clinging to precepts and observances) is the vision of one who regards precepts, observances, both of these together, or the five aggregates of clinging which are their basis, as being purity, liberation, or leading to deliverance;
furthermore, the thorough knowledge of the path is by way of its aspects such as leading to deliverance.
Furthermore, why is the fetter of clinging (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) an obstruction to the full comprehension of the path? To this he says: "Because of clinging to purification in another way.

This refers to clinging to purification through mere rules and observances (*śīla-vrata-mātra*), or through dwelling in the pleasure of sensual desires (*kāma-sukhālaya*), or through difficult ascetic practices (*duṣkara-caryā*), or through the knowledge of the Sāṃkhya and other systems.
However, by means of clinging to views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*), one clings to that very thing by which one believes purification is attained as being supreme.
Thus, by means of the fetter of adherence (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*), one abandons the path and adheres to purification in another way.
The fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) functions as an obscuration to the thorough knowledge of the Three Jewels.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Because of a lack of faith in its qualities."
The fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) is indecision regarding the [Three] Jewels.
Full comprehension of the Jewel of the Buddha consists in understanding him as the ultimate refuge for one who has completely eliminated all virtues and defects through excellence.

Full comprehension of the Jewel of the Dharma consists in understanding it as that which enables the crossing of the ocean of saṃsāra, as that whose nature is the absolute separation from all suffering together with its causes, and as that which provides the means for such attainment.
Through abiding in the fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) and being an unsurpassed field of merit (*dakṣiṇīyakṣetra*), there is full comprehension (*parijñāna*) of the Sangha-jewel.

Because one has abandoned doubt through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) and has attained verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*), one places deep faith in the qualities of the Three Jewels; it is not the case that one has not abandoned doubt.
Therefore, the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) is said to be an obscuration to the full comprehension of the Three Jewels.
The fetter of envy is an obstruction to the full comprehension of gain and honor.
Regarding this very point, he states the reason: "because of not seeing its faults.
For the fetter of envy is a mental resentment—a portion of hostility toward the prosperity of others—in one who is attached to gain and honor.
The thorough understanding of gain and honor (*lābhasatkāra*) consists in realizing that they are the basis of all misfortune.

However, because of envy (*īrṣyā*), one does not thoroughly understand gain and honor as being opposed to all virtues and as the root of various forms of misfortune; therefore, envy as a fetter (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) is an obscuration to the thorough understanding of gain and honor.
Avarice as a fetter (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) is an obscuration to the thorough understanding of austerity (*saṃlekha*).

To the question "How so?", he says: "Because of attachment to requisites. Avarice (*mātsarya*) is an attachment to requisites, a part of passion (*rāga*), which consists of a grasping for the instruments of the mind. *Saṃlekha* is the separation from requisites.

The thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*) of that [object] consists in realizing it as the basis for all virtuous qualities; it does not mean knowing it as the basis for all virtuous qualities by way of being attached to requisites out of stinginess (*mātsarya*). Therefore, in the context of the thorough knowledge of austerity (*saṃlekha*), stinginess is said to be an obscuration.
In that regard, the fetters of attachment (*anunaya*) and aversion (*pratigha*) are obscurations to the application of the realization of reality (*tattva-adhigama-prayoga*).
The remaining [afflictions], however, are obscurations to the realization of reality that has already been applied; therefore, their sequence is as follows:
first of all, those seeking liberation must necessarily cause the mind to feel revulsion toward cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*);
thereafter, one must cultivate equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward everything.
Therefore, because it is the root of all misfortune, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is to be fully understood.
Immediately thereafter, its objective basis is to be fully understood as being of the nature of suffering and its origin.
Following that, its cessation is to be known.
Immediately following that, the path of attainment is to be understood.
Then, through the vision of the truths and the realization of the qualities of the Three Jewels, one attains verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*).

By the power of the vision of the truths alone, one comes to perceive the faults and virtues of gain, honor, and austerity; thus, by way of this sequence of factors to be obscured, the sequence of their obscuration is to be known.
[Objection: Since everything can indeed function as an obscuration in every respect, it is not logical to specify obscurations according to a fixed correspondence with specific objects.
[Response: No fixed correspondence with specific objects is being made here; rather, this specification is made on the basis of proximity and predominance.
Regarding the "obstruction of the bodhisattvas": what is this obstruction?
This [obstruction] is common to bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and others; however, [the following] is the specific obstruction for bodhisattvas.
There is another tenfold obscuration regarding the wholesome and so forth;
however, it is not known what the "wholesome and so forth" are.

Therefore, he says: "Non-application, [application] to what is not a proper sphere, and that which is practiced incorrectly"—such is the initial obscuration. Furthermore, there are those beginning with the wholesome (*śubha*).
The ten topics are: virtue, enlightenment, undertaking [the vows], and so forth.
Among these, "virtue" refers to all roots of merit that serve as the cause of enlightenment; "enlightenment," however, is the fruit thereof.

In this context, although "the auspicious" has been mentioned in general terms, its specific divisions and its intrinsic nature are not yet understood; therefore, it is undertaken for the purpose of explaining that: "The undertaking, wisdom, non-delusion, non-obstruction, lack of fear elsewhere, lack of stinginess, and mastery—this is the auspicious. Furthermore, since "enlightenment" (bodhi) is not understood by its mere mention in terms of its intrinsic nature, he demonstrates its sovereign power (vibhutva).

Some maintain that because the obstructions to the "auspicious" (*śubha*) and to "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) are taught independently—just as [the obstructions] to "undertaking" (*samādāna*) and so forth are taught independently—independence alone is understood here, and not a relationship of locus and located. For the obstruction to arising is established in relation to the auspicious, and that is common to the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) and so forth, since that [thought] is produced from the auspicious. However, the obstruction to maintenance and so forth is the obstruction to undertaking and so forth, due to the distinction in meaning between the functions of "undertaking" and so on. Furthermore, since enlightenment is both singular and something to be attained, the obstruction to its persistence and the obstruction to its attainment are established for it.
Therefore, there is no consequence of independence here.
Furthermore, their sequence is as follows: in brief, enlightenment is to be attained after having fully accomplished the roots of virtue without exception;
in detail, however, one must first generate the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), because it serves as the foundation for the accomplishment of the welfare of both oneself and others.
Then, there follows the practice of giving and so forth, in accordance with the generation of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), by which one receives the designation "Bodhisattva.

Thereafter, for one who practices for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeyakalpa*), the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)—which consists of non-delusion as the antidote to the delusions regarding persons and phenomena—must be generated for the sake of purifying the intention (*āśaya*) through the accumulation of the equipment of merit and knowledge (*puṇyajñānasambhāra*).
Following that, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), characterized by the removal of obscurations, must be brought to its culmination for the sake of attaining a distinguished purity.

Then, through the practice of transcending the stage of the śrāvakas and others, all these mundane and supramundane roots of virtue, as they have been accumulated, should be dedicated toward enlightenment.
Consequently, having reached that state and possessing the aspiration for great enlightenment, one is not terrified by the profound and sublime teachings of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Thereafter, endowed with extensive learning and correct practice, one teaches the sublime Dharma for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
Then, when those to be trained have reached maturity, one attains mastery—namely, Buddhahood—for the sake of their liberation.

For here, thirty obscurations have been mentioned, as well as the ten objects to be obscured, beginning with the wholesome; therefore, he asks: "Of these [objects], beginning with the wholesome, how many obscurations should be known for each? To this, he says: "Three and three indeed are to be known as the obscurations of these."
Thus,
there are three obstacles to the wholesome:
non-application and non-undertaking.

What is the obstruction here? It is that affliction by which one does not apply oneself—whether through negligence (*pramāda*) or laziness (*kausīdya*)—or that particular state accompanied by the seeds of affliction, whether neutral (*avyākṛta*) or defiled (*kliṣṭa*), in which one does not apply oneself.

One does not apply oneself either because of constant [engagement] or because of lack of respect, or because of insignificance; thus it is called "non-application" (*aprayoga*), but not because of a total absence of application, for in that case an obstruction would be impossible.

Non-application to the basis (*anāyatanaprayoga*) refers to that which is other than the basis (*āyatana*); the basis for enlightenment and the roots of virtue that bring about enlightenment is the teaching (*pravacana*) which is the gateway to their arising, and anything other than that is the non-basis.
In that regard, "application" refers to application toward what is not a proper basis (anāyatana), that is, toward external objects.

What is the obscuration therein? That very ignorance or affliction of views by which one applies oneself to what is not a proper basis is itself the obscuration; it is called "improper application" (ayoniśaḥ prayoga).
The source (*yoni*) is the means (*upāya*). To apply a practice in a manner other than its corresponding means is improper application (*ayoniśaḥ prayoga*).

It is recited in this very teaching: namely, that the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-bhāvanā*) is not the means for abandoning passion (*rāga*), whereas the cultivation of the foul (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is the means for abandoning aversion (*pratigha*).
Here too, improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*) or the application (*prayoga*) caused by it is an obscuration. Regarding awakening (*bodhi*), there are three [obscuring factors]:
awakening is the realization of reality as it is (*yathārtham avabodha*).
"The non-arising of the wholesome" is exactly as previously stated.
How is non-arising an obscuration? Since enlightenment would not exist if the wholesome were absent, the non-arising of the wholesome is an obscuration to enlightenment.
Alternatively, whatever affliction or specific state constitutes an obscuration to the arising of the wholesome is itself an obscuration to enlightenment as well.
For whatever is a certain obstruction to the equipment (*sambhāra*) is also an obstruction to its fruit.

"Non-attention" (*amanasikāra*) toward that which has already arisen means non-cultivation (*abhāvanā*) and lack of regard; the meaning is that by whichever affliction such as laziness (*kausīdya*), in whichever particular state, one does not repeatedly attend to the wholesome even though it has arisen—that is the obstruction here.

And "incompleteness of the accumulations" means that the accumulation of merit and wisdom by which awakening is attained is incomplete; as before, this refers to the state of affliction or a deficiency in the accumulations.

However, another [teacher] says: even though the statement is made without distinction, what is intended here is the non-arising specifically of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), and not of others.

Even for those [distractions] that have already arisen, non-attention to them is called an obscuration for one who is attending [to other things], provided that the accumulations have not been gathered.
"Formal undertaking" refers to the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

This formal undertaking—the generation of the thought of awakening—is defined by the intention: "By means of this, I shall establish all sentient beings without exception, as well as the accumulations of merit and wisdom and their fruit, which is Buddhahood, in the unsurpassed realm of nirvana without remainder. This is the generation of the thought of awakening.
Furthermore, that intention to act for the benefit of oneself and others consists of volition accompanied by aspiration.
Its three obstructions are:
being devoid of the spiritual lineage (*agotra*), or belonging to the lineage of the *śrāvakas* and so forth.
Lack of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra-vaidhurya*):

even when the lineage (*gotra*) exists, there is no association with those who would encourage one to generate the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), or by relying upon whom awakening would not turn back and wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*) would increase;

or, even when there is association with spiritual friends, there is a state of mental exhaustion due to the suffering of *saṃsāra*, and for beings who have fallen into wrong conduct, a mind of agitation and the desire for a swift *parinirvāṇa*.
What is the obstruction here? It is the deficiency of causes, the deficiency of conditions, a lack of compassion toward sentient beings, or laziness.
For one who lacks compassion becomes weary of working for the sake of sentient beings, as does one who is lazy.
"Possession of intelligence" refers to being a bodhisattva.

Because they possess sharp faculties by nature compared to those belonging to the lineages of the *śrāvaka*s and others, because they are qualified to investigate all objects of knowledge in every way, and because of their resolute faith in the profound and vast Dharma, only the wise *bodhisattva*—and no other—is [the subject of this discussion]. Bodhisattvahood is practice directed toward the welfare of others that is free from error.
Deficiency in practice is non-engagement in the perfections (*pāramitā*) and so forth.
For a bodhisattva is to be known as one whose conduct consists of practice.

"Wicked people" means foolish people, that is to say, people who lack discernment; for wicked people do not recognize even one who is comparable to a bodhisattva, despite that person being endowed with practice.
The wicked person is one who is hostile toward the Bodhisattva.
Because they are intent upon finding faults, they do not perceive the Bodhisattva’s actual virtues.
Due to their perception of non-existent defects, or due to a mind fierce with resentment, they conceal his real virtues and, having superimposed them, proclaim non-existent faults.
What is the obscuration here? It is ignorance and aversion, which are the opposites of the perfection of generosity and the other perfections.
Regarding non-delusion, there are three [points]:
delusion arises from superimposition and denial; its antidote, however, is the absence of delusion, which is the path of seeing.
Some say that the depravity of perversion (*viparyāsadauṣṭhulya*) is the nourishment of the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) for the adherence to the grasped and the grasper.

Others say it is the nourishment of the seeds residing in the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) of all proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by insight, or of the non-afflicted ignorance that obstructs the awakening to the all-pervading realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Still others maintain that perversion is indeed the conceptualization of a self and so forth where no self and so forth exist.
It means that one of the three obstructions, beginning with the afflictions (*kleśa*), remains.

Among these, the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) refers to those afflictions such as attachment (*rāga*) that manifest intensely and for a long duration; it is an obstruction to non-delusion because there is no opportunity for the application of their antidotes.
The obstruction of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*) refers to actions such as the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) which determine rebirth in the miserable states (*apāya*).
The obstruction of maturation consists of the miserable realms and so forth; for one born therein, there is no possibility for the arising of the noble dharmas.
Among those [three categories of] afflictions, karma, and birth, even a single one constitutes an undifferentiated obstruction, and not necessarily all of them together.
Furthermore, it includes the immaturity of the wisdom that brings liberation to fruition.

Some say that it is the unserviceability (*akarmaṇyatā*) of the wisdom that brings about liberation, because the stage conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) has not yet been attained. Others, however, say:
"In this context, non-conceptual wisdom is that which ripens liberation, while the second is that which is preparatory (*prayogika*) to it."
The immaturity of those two consists, respectively, in their unfitness for the realization of reality and their unfitness for the state that is its proximate cause, due to their being incomplete.

What is the obscuration here? It is the remaining presence of any one of the obscurations such as the nourished latencies of the afflictions of the defilements to be abandoned by vision, the ignorance that acts as a hindrance to the maturation of wisdom, and the incompleteness of the accumulations.
The removal of these obscurations is "non-obscuration."
That by which obscuration is abandoned is the "non-abandonment of obscuration"; the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is non-obscuration because it is the antidote to obscuration.
It has three [aspects]:
innate dysfunction (dauṣṭhulya), the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation, and [the result thereof].

It is either the innate seed, deposited in the *ālayavijñāna* and fully nourished, of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, as well as of the non-afflicted ignorance that obstructs the penetration of the *dharmadhātu*, contact, objects, and so on;
or it is laziness (*kausīdya*), which is the lack of mental enthusiasm arising from indolence that is a part of delusion (*moha*);
and negligence (*pramāda*), which is attachment to sense objects and a lack of heedfulness regarding what is wholesome.
Some say that negligence here consists in relishing meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
because of that corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*), one does not cultivate the path;
and due to negligence, one does not guard the mind from unwholesome states.
What is the obscuration here? It is precisely these three.
Regarding dedication, there are three [obscurations] by which one directs the mind elsewhere.
In that context, dedication (*pariṇati*) is the mental determination of arisen roots of virtue toward Buddhahood alone.
It has three obscurations.

What are the three? Those by which, other than toward Buddhahood, one directs the mind toward cyclic existence or the enlightenment of the śrāvakas and so forth, rather than toward unsurpassed perfect awakening. They are, moreover: attachment to existence, attachment to enjoyments, and a dejected state of mind.

Existence (*bhava*) refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*). Objects of enjoyment (*bhoga*) are the sense objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, because they are enjoyed. Attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*) to these two is clinging (*sakti*).
A depressed mind and a narrow mind—thinking, "Where is Buddhahood, and where is someone like me?"—constitute self-doubt.

In that regard, through attachment to existence and attachment to enjoyments, one directs the mind toward a happy rebirth; through a depressed mind, one directs it toward the vehicle of the Śrāvakas and so forth. What is the obscuration here? It is craving for existence and enjoyments, laziness, and lack of compassion.
Regarding fearlessness, there are three [obscuring factors].
What is this "fearlessness"? It is confidence and fearlessness regarding emptiness and the profound and sublime qualities of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

"Lack of conviction" refers to the mistaken understanding and speech of a person who contemplates the Mahāyāna method, or a lack of trust in their qualities such as ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
"Lack of faith" refers to a lack of conviction that the teachings which set forth the profound and sublime method are indeed the word of the Buddha and possess unerring meaning.
Regarding the investigation of the meaning according to the literal expression:
one understands the meaning of "unproduced," "unceasing," "primordially peaceful," and so forth, exactly as it is expressed in words, yet does not comprehend the reality of the intended meaning.
Therefore, there is a lack of conviction regarding the meaning of being unproduced and so forth.

What is the obscuration here? It is doubt, wisdom that is the opposite of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), knowledge that is the opposite of investigating the intended meaning of the teachings, and [wisdom] that is the opposite of analytical investigation.
There are three [obscuration]s regarding non-avarice:
non-avarice is that from which the teaching of the Dharma proceeds for the sake of the endurance of the true Dharma or for the purpose of benefiting others.
Lack of respect for the true Dharma means not holding it in high esteem;
because of that, one does not cause the true Dharma to endure for a long time by failing to transmit it to the mental continuums of others.
Respect for gain, honor, and worship means holding them in high esteem; regarding respect for the true Dharma, there is the apprehension: "Lest another person become equal to me or even superior."
Therefore, one does not teach the Dharma out of fear that there will be an interruption by gain and the like;
nor does one teach it due to a lack of compassion for sentient beings, even when attachment to gain and honor is absent,
because one who lacks compassion is not moved by the suffering of sentient beings.
What is the obscuration here? It is lack of respect, attachment to gain and honor, and lack of compassion;
this means there are three obscurations to mastery (*vaśitva*).
For mastery is indeed the attainment of all forms of mental mastery, which is Buddhahood.
Since his three obscurations are not yet known, he says: "those by which one does not attain mastery.
Because they obstruct the mastery of the mind, he states that those very things by which one does not attain mastery are the obscurations to mastery.
Furthermore, mastery is the perfection of knowledge (*jñāna*), abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and power (*prabhāva*).
Alternatively, because it is taught as a synonym for mastery (*vaśitva*), the phrase "by whom mastery is not obtained" means that they do not obtain seniority (*vṛddhatva*).
"Calamity of learning" (*śrutavyasana*) is the absolute separation from hearing the true Dharma (*saddharma*). "Calamity of kinsmen" (*bandhuvyasana*) is the absolute separation from one's relatives.
Furthermore, that misfortune regarding learning arises from the production of karma conducive to the disappearance of the true Dharma.

Because they remain fixed in their adherence to their own views or because they rely on unwholesome friends, those who, being free from remorse, reject the Mahāyāna sūtras—saying, "This was spoken by Māra, it is a cause for rebirth in the miserable states, and it was not spoken by the Buddha"—and furthermore cause others to be alienated from them; and by means of such acts as erasing what has been written, burning it, or casting it into water, they generate karma conducive to the ruin of the True Dharma, through the nourishment of a physical existence deprived of hearing the True Dharma.
In the absence of the calamity of [lack of] learning, having little learning—that is, the non-completion of the equipment for knowledge—is the obscuration; this is the subject at hand.
One who has little learning is unable to discern the dharmas.
Furthermore, the lack of preparation for meditative concentration (*samādhi*), even in one who is much-learned, is also an obscuration; such is the connection.

Due to the absence of any one of the factors beginning with zeal (*chanda*), concentration is unprepared because of its incompleteness; or, due to the absence of any one of the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) during cultivation, concentration is unprepared.
Alternatively, it is the non-perfection or lack of preparation regarding the diamond-like and other meditative absorptions of a Buddha.

What is the obscuration here? It is karma conducive to the ruin of the Dharma, limited learning, poor wisdom, and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as lethargy and restlessness that are antagonistic to concentration.
{The ten causes} Furthermore, this obscuration— beginning with lack of application and ending with lack of mastery—
pertains to ten kinds of objects, starting from the wholesome and ending with mastery.

Regarding those objects for which there are ten causes, beginning with arising and ending with attainment, there exist ten causes that are the opposites of those obscurations, beginning with application and ending with the state of being prepared for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

And here, because there is no distinction in their being causes for arising and so forth, even though they are distinct, they are designated as non-different individually. "By way of the purpose" means by way of the predominance of the purposes of arising and so forth. For when the obstruction of the causes of arising and so forth of those [factors] such as the wholesome exists, it is called an "obscuration to arising and so forth. Just as a wall or the like, by obscuring light, is called an obscuration to its effect, namely visual consciousness;
having established this, one should understand that for these ten factors, there are thirty causes corresponding to the reversal of the thirty obscurations.
In that regard, the causes for the arising of the wholesome are threefold: application, application to the bases, and appropriate application.
For example, the eye and so forth serve as the illustration in this very context;
the eye and so forth are the causes for the arising of consciousness, but not the causes for its duration and so on.
In this context, non-application and the other factors, while acting as direct obstacles to application and the rest, are also indirect impediments to the arising of the wholesome.

Thus, one should understand that the "obscuration to arising" pertains to the wholesome; he says, "because it is to be produced," thereby showing that since stability and so forth are impossible in the absence of the wholesome, this is indeed an obscuration to arising.
As for the cause of stability, it is awakening (*bodhi*).
Awakening is the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), and the basis is stainless suchness (*nirmala-tathatā*).
Regarding this, he states the reason: "because of its immovability" (*akopyatvāt*).
It is immovable because it remains as long as the world exists; it does not become otherwise, nor does it turn back.
However, the awakening of the śrāvakas and others ceases within their own mental continuum because they have achieved their purpose.

For bodhisattvas, who engage in the accumulations with the resolute intention for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings, it is said that they remain as long as there are sentient beings, because awakening has the characteristic of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*); this is not, however, due to a mere state of non-arising as it is with the śrāvakas and others.
Since stability arises from cultivation even without [further] arising, arising also occurs here.
Therefore, only the cause for the persistence of awakening is stated, not the cause for its arising;
nor is there any other cause for its persistence apart from that. For this reason, it is said that awakening is either pure suchness (*viśuddhatathatā*) or [the cause thereof].

Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of suchness (*tathatā*) is pure, there is no arising; rather, it is due to the removal of adventitious stains that its abiding is spoken of through these causes, and not its arising.
Furthermore, the causes for the abiding of awakening (*bodhi*) are the production of the wholesome, mental attention (*manasikāra*), and the complete equipment (*sambhāra*).

In this context, the non-arising of the wholesome and so forth—which exist as obstacles to the production of the wholesome and so forth—bring about the abiding of awakening; thus, they are called "obstructions to abiding."
For example, the four kinds of nutriment for sentient beings serve as an illustration of this very point:
indeed, new sentient beings are not produced by means of nutriments such as edible food (kavaḍākāra) and so forth; rather, those already produced are merely maintained.
Thus, it is the cause of sustenance (dhṛti).
Fortitude is the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), because it serves as the support for all wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*).
An illustration of this very point is that whatever serves as the support for something else, there is fortitude regarding it; for it is by means of this [support] that [the supported] is held.
For example, the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) is the support for the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*).
The causes for that are the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), the possession of virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and the absence of mental weariness.
In this context, because it is opposed to the cause of steadfastness (*dhṛti*), the deficiency of the lineage and so forth are also described as obscurations to steadfastness.

This very point is stated: "The obscuration to steadfastness is an obscuration to the formal undertaking (*samādāna*), because [the undertaking] serves as the support for the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*)."

The cause of manifestation regarding intelligence is that which must be revealed for a bodhisattva; this consists of the perfection of practice, dwelling among virtuous people, and not dwelling among wicked people. In this context, regarding intelligence, those things which result from a deficiency in practice are called obscurations to its manifestation.
For this very reason, he says: "The obscuration is of manifestation, because [the object] is to be manifested by the intellect.
An illustration of this is as follows: light is [the cause of manifestation] for form.
For light is indeed the cause of the manifestation of form alone, not the cause of its production and so forth.

"Transformation in the absence of error" means that because it consists in the overturning of the errors of superimposition and denial, the path of seeing— which is itself non-error— is called the "transformation of non-error," just as ashes and so forth are the transformations of wood and so forth.

It has three causes: the destruction of the corruption of cognitive distortions (*viparyāsa-dauṣṭhulya*), the absence of the three obscurations such as the afflictions (*kleśādy-āvaraṇa*), and the state of full maturation of the wisdom that brings liberation to maturity.
This is just as fire and so forth [are the causes] for things to be cooked and so on;
for what is to be cooked, such as rice porridge, is distinct from the raw rice and the like, yet it is included within their continuum.
And the cause of that [separation] is fire and so forth.
The "cause of separation" (*viśleṣakāraṇa*) refers to non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa*).
Since the remaining obscuration—other than that which is to be abandoned by the path of seeing—is abandoned by this, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is called "non-obstruction."
It has three causes: the destruction of innate dysfunction (*sahajadauṣṭhulya*), vigor, and heedfulness.
Because these serve as the remedies that counteract the causes of disjunction, it is for this very reason that he says: "The obscuration of disjunction [is the obstacle] to non-obscuration."
This [obscuration] is also an obscuration precisely by way of being the opposite of the cause of disjunction.
Regarding this very point, he states the reason: "because it is the dissociation from that obscuration. Disjunction (*viśleṣa*) is that by which one is dissociated (*visaṃyujyate*).
The cause of transformation lies in humility,
because it is characterized by the application of roots of merit toward great enlightenment;
that, moreover, consists of turning away from existence and enjoyments, as well as the absence of a dejected mind.
And therefore, the obscuration to transformation (pariṇatyāvaraṇa) is to be understood as an impediment to the cause of transformation.
Why? Because the inclination toward great enlightenment has the characteristic of the transformation of the mind.
The cause for conviction [is found] in fearlessness.
And that consists of: esteem for the person, conviction in the Dharma, and the realization of the intended meaning.
Through these qualities, confidence arises; therefore, because it obstructs the causes of confidence, there is an "obscuration of confidence" regarding fearlessness.
Regarding this very point, he states the reason: "because one fears due to a lack of confidence."
For one trembles at the Dharma due to a lack of conviction;
the means for producing conviction is non-avarice.
This, moreover, consists of reverence for the true Dharma, indifference toward gain, honor, and worship, and compassion for sentient beings.
Furthermore, because it is the opposite of the cause for producing conviction, the obscuration of making others believe is established as being contrary to non-avarice (*amatsaritva*).
Regarding this very point, he states the reason: "Because one brings about conviction in others through non-avarice regarding the Dharma.
Due to a lack of respect for the true Dharma and so forth, one practices avarice toward the Dharma.

Furthermore, due to stinginess regarding the Dharma, one does not teach the Dharma to others; therefore, non-stinginess is the removal of the obstacle to inspiring confidence. There are three causes for mastery: the absence of karma that leads to the ruin of the Dharma, extensive learning, and being refined through meditative concentration.
Furthermore, because it is contrary to that [mastery], the addiction to alcohol and so forth is established as an obscuration to mastery.
Regarding this very point, he states the reason: "Because that mastery has the characteristic of attaining sovereign power (*vibhutva*).
However, some state the reason for the sequence of the virtuous factors and so forth as follows:
Enlightenment is to be attained by a mental continuum supported by wholesome dharmas;
therefore, the auspicious was taught first,
and immediately after that, enlightenment was taught.

And by resorting to the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one becomes capable of accomplishing both [the welfare of oneself and others] until enlightenment, because the thought of awakening is the foundation for all wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*); therefore, immediately after that, the thought of awakening is mentioned.
For one who has generated the thought of awakening, there is application to the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and avoidance of both base persons and wicked persons.
In this way, his state of being a bodhisattva becomes manifest.
Therefore, immediately after the undertaking [of the vows], wisdom (*dhīmatva*) is mentioned;
for one who applies himself in this manner abandons error and generates non-erroneous knowledge.
Consequently, immediately after wisdom, non-delusion (*abhrānti*) is mentioned, which is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Because one abandons the obscurations through that practice, immediately following that, the "unobscured" (anāvaraṇa), which is the abandonment of obscurations, is mentioned.
Since one who is free from obscurations lacks attachment to existence and enjoyments, they dedicate their mind solely toward Buddhahood and not elsewhere;
therefore, immediately following that, "reverence" (nati) is mentioned.
For one who has become thus, even regarding the most profound Buddha-qualities, joy arises and there is no fear; therefore, immediately after that, fearlessness is taught.

Seeing through the direct perception of the Dharma whatever means by which the training of sentient beings is to be accomplished, he resorts to that very means; how then could he have any stinginess? Therefore, immediately after fearlessness, non-stinginess is taught.
Thus, having abandoned all obscurations and being perfected in pure qualities, the Bodhisattva proceeds with mastery over the mind; therefore, immediately after that, mastery is taught.
This is the sequence:
since this chapter concerns the topic of obscurations (*āvaraṇa*), the causes for the arising of virtue and so forth are presented as aphorisms alongside the obscurations.
A summary of those topics introduced in this context is now provided by means of an intermediate verse.
The cause is tenfold: in arising, in persistence, in support, in manifestation, in transformation, in separation, in cognition, in attainment, in departure, and in acquisition.
This second intermediate verse is for the purpose of summarizing the examples: "The eye, food, the earth, a lamp, fire, and so forth are its illustrations;
others are the sickle, craftsmanship, smoke, the cause, the path, and so on."
Thus it is said.

{The obscurations regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment, the perfections, and the stages} Previously, virtue and its obscuration were taught without distinction; now, however, he teaches virtue through the distinctions of "factors" and so forth, and through the distinctions of common and uncommon,
as well as the obscuration of the factors and so forth through the distinctions of "lack of skill in the entities," "laziness," and so on.

In this context, the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*) are common to both Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas without distinction, because they do not differ therein. However, the perfections (*pāramitā*) and the stages (*bhūmi*) are uncommon [to them], for they are the domain of Bodhisattvas alone, due to the Bodhisattvas' sovereignty over them. Furthermore, while previously the obscuration to the fruit was explained by way of the obscuration to the causes such as virtue, here the obscuration to the fruit itself is addressed directly; thus, it is stated as something distinct from what preceded.
Alternatively, since lack of skill regarding the objective (*vastvakauśalya*) and so forth are indeed distinct from non-application (*aprayoga*) and the rest, they are stated as something else.

Or rather, in the passage "the auspicious and awakening," non-application and so forth were described as the obscurations to the conduct and its fruit of a bodhisattva alone when accompanied by skillful means; however, here it should be understood that lack of skill regarding the objective and so forth—which pertain specifically to the auspicious [nature]—whether common or uncommon, categorized by the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika*) and so on, are obscurations distinct from non-application and the rest.

In that regard, there are three types of enlightenment according to the distinctions of the *śrāvaka* and others; corresponding to these, the factors from the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the path are called the "aids to enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*). There are ten perfections (*pāramitā*) and ten stages (*bhūmi*), as described in the sūtras. Regarding the applications of mindfulness, lack of skill with respect to the objective bases (*vastu*) is the obscuration. These, moreover, are the four applications of mindfulness: the application of mindfulness to the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena.
Furthermore, their objective basis (*vastu*) consists of the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena, because these are their objects.
Among these, the body is the objective basis for the attachment to a support;
feelings are the objective basis for the attachment to the enjoyment of a self.
The mind is the basis for the adherence to a self;
phenomena (dharmas) are the basis for the adherence to the defilement and purification of a self.
That which is the lack of understanding regarding the specific and general characteristics of the body and so forth is non-skillfulness with respect to them.
In that regard, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the body is its nature of being comprised of many impure substances;
that of sensation (*vedanā*) is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as pleasure and so forth;
and that of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the discernment of objects.

The general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena (*dharmas*), according to their respective possibilities, consists of the aspects of permanence, suffering, emptiness, selflessness, and so forth.

Alternatively, the lack of proficiency regarding the object refers to either the non-comprehension of the body and so on through the aspects of impurity, suffering, impermanence, and selflessness, or the conceptualization [of them] through the aspects of purity, pleasure, permanence, and self; for such ignorance or false vision constitutes an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) to the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthānas*).

If the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) have wisdom (*prajñā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) as their intrinsic nature, why is it said that only "lack of skill regarding the object" (*vastvakauśalya*) is the obscuration, and not also "non-recollection of the object"? Because their activity is dependent upon wisdom.

For, since wisdom consists in the nature of vision, mindfulness and the other factors operate with respect to the focal object by following in the wake of wisdom (*prajñāpṛṣṭhalabdha*), and not independently like wisdom itself.
Therefore, mere non-recollection is not stated here to be the obscuration.
Regarding the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), what is the obstacle? It is, as the context implies, "laziness" (*kauśīdya*).

For it is vigor (*vīrya*)—when it functions for the abandonment of arisen adverse factors and the non-arising of those not yet arisen, and for the further increase and production of arisen antidotes—that receives the designation of "right abandonment."
Furthermore, although there is no difference in their essential nature, they are established as fourfold due to the difference in their results; such is the traditional teaching (*smṛti*).
Therefore, because the right abandonments (*samyak-prahāṇa*) consist essentially of vigor (*vīrya*), laziness is said to be their obscuration.
Regarding the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the obscuration is the twofold deficiency of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
That by which one is made to succeed is *ṛddhi*.
And that consists of the concentrations of desire (*chanda*), energy (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*mīmāṃsā*).

These very [concentrations] are the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*), because they serve as the foundation for supernormal powers such as traveling through the air and the manifestation of emanations.

"Going" (*gamana*) refers to supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), meaning the excellence of traveling through space and so forth; its "bases" (*pāda*) are the bases of supernatural power (*ṛddhipāda*) because they serve as its support. This very [power] is the fourfold concentration (*samādhi*), consisting of the concentration of desire (*chanda*) and the others.
In that regard, within the concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*), desire is predominant because concentration is attained by means of it;

however, it is not that energy (*vīrya*) and the other factors are absent there. Rather, because they are auxiliaries to desire, they are subordinate therein and thus were not explicitly mentioned. The same should be said for the concentrations of energy, mind, and investigation.

The obscuration consisting in the twofold deficiency of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) has been mentioned, but it is not yet understood; therefore, he says: "Due to non-fulfillment—because of the deficiency of any one among desire, energy, mind, and investigation—and due to the deficiency in cultivation because of the deficiency of any one of the formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*).

In this context, "deficiency in fulfillment" means that because there is an absence of meditative concentration which is governed by any one of those [factors]—desire, energy, mind, or investigation—the cultivation [of concentration] is deficient; thus, there is a deficiency of any one of the eight formative forces of abandonment.
Furthermore, these consist of faith, aspiration, vigor, pliancy, mindfulness, clear comprehension, volition, and equanimity.

For it is through the cultivation of these formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) that mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is attained, and not otherwise; therefore, due to their deficiency, there is a lack of cultivation, and mastery over concentration is not attained.

What is the obscuration here? It is the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) which are the opposites of aspiration and the other [factors], and the opposites of the formative forces of abandonment—namely, laziness, forgetfulness of the object, lethargy and excitement, non-application, and application.

Regarding "the non-planting of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) in the faculties (*indriya*)": one who is terrified of *saṃsāra* cultivates roots of merit with liberation as their objective. Because of that, there is a certainty of attaining liberation; therefore, it is called "conducive to liberation. When these [roots] have been planted, faith and the other [faculties] acquire the name of "faculties," and not otherwise. For this reason, the non-planting of the factors conducive to liberation is said to be an obscuration to the faculties. What is the obscuration here? It is that secondary affliction (*upakleśa*) by which the factors conducive to liberation are not made to grow.
Furthermore, that attachment to existence and fear of nirvāṇa refer to the weakness of those very faculties among the powers;
"obscuration" is the term under discussion.
Furthermore, as to how there is weakness of the faculties, it is said: "due to being interspersed with opposing factors.
This means that they are overcome by opposing factors consisting of lack of faith, laziness, forgetfulness, distraction, and impaired wisdom.
For the faculties are brought forth by the stages of *ūṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*.
And both of these types of aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are weak because they are overcome by their opposites, such as lack of faith;
for this very reason, falling away from them is possible.

However, because their opposites have been conquered, faith and the other [faculties] receive the name "powers" (*bala*) at the stages of patience (*kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*).

Therefore, that weakness of those very same factors—faith and the rest—which occurs in the stages of "Heat" (uṣmagata) and "Summits" (mūrdhan) due to being overcome by their opposites, is the obscuration of the powers (*bala*).
Since the state of the powers is impossible when that [weakness] exists, what is the obscuration here? It is precisely that opposite, beginning with lack of faith (*aśraddhya*) and so forth.

Regarding the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), the fault of [wrong] view is the obscuration; this is the subject under discussion. For here, "enlightenment" (bodhi) is intended to mean the path of seeing (darśanamārga).

At the time of abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), those seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)—consisting of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, vigor, joy, pliancy, concentration, and equanimity—arise; thus they are called "factors.

However, if they were called "factors" merely because they are conducive to enlightenment (*bodhi*), then it would follow that the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth would also possess the status of factors of enlightenment.

To the question, "How is it that the fault of views (*dṛṣṭi-doṣa*) is an obscuration among the factors of enlightenment? he says: "Because they are produced by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)," which means because they are established by the path of seeing.

What, then, is the fault of other views? They are the five imagined views, doubt, ignorance, and the afflictions and secondary afflictions such as attachment, along with their associated mental factors, which take those [views] as their objects.
But is it not the case that doubt and the others are also obscurations here?
Let them be obscurations.
In this context, however, because the primary intention is to explain the faults of the views, it is not contradictory that those [other factors] are not explicitly mentioned.

Furthermore, it is precisely the seeds of those views and so forth, as they reside within the *ālayavijñāna*, that are called "obstructions," since they are to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Regarding the limbs of the path—namely, right view, intention, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, and concentration—it was introduced that the fault of *dauṣṭhulya* is the obstruction.
Regarding this very point, he states the reason: "Because those path-factors are brought forth by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)," meaning they are established by the path of cultivation.

What is that fault of corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*)? In detail, it consists of the innate views of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) along with their associated mental factors; the afflictions and secondary afflictions such as attachment (*rāga*) and so forth, together with their associated factors, which take those [views] as their objects or take sense-objects as their objects;
and the seeds of these [afflictions] deposited within the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). That is corruption.
In brief, however, that which is other than the [afflictions] to be abandoned by vision—namely, the contaminated potentiality residing within the *ālayavijñāna*—is *dauṣṭhulya*.
And because it is to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is established as an obscuration to the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
Thus has been explained the obscuration regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
{The Obstructions to the Perfections} Immediately following that, the obstructions to the perfections (*pāramitā*) must be explained; therefore, he says:
"The obstruction to sovereignty, to a happy rebirth, and to not abandoning sentient beings," and so forth in detail.

In this context, regarding the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), the obscuration of whichever perfection is defined by the obscuration of its respective fruit is thereby revealed. What is the reason here that avarice (*mātsarya*) and so forth—which in reality function as obstacles to giving (*dāna*) and the other perfections—are described as obscurations to their fruits rather than as obscurations to the perfections themselves? It is because everyone engages in giving and the rest for the sake of those fruits. Therefore, in order to generate diligence toward the abandonment of avarice and the like, they are called "obscurations to the fruit" rather than "obscurations to the perfection."

Alternatively, the obscuration consisting of stinginess and so forth—which is the opposite of sovereignty and the like, and which produces results such as poverty—is called an "obscuration" because it obstructs the results such as sovereignty.
What, then, is their result? In that regard, the primary result of the perfection of generosity is sovereignty and dominion;
the result of the perfection of ethical discipline is a happy rebirth.
The perfection of patience consists in not abandoning sentient beings;
the perfection of vigor consists in the elimination of faults and the increase of virtues;
the perfection of meditation consists in introducing sentient beings into the teaching.
The perfection of wisdom consists in the liberation from heavy burdens;
the perfection of skillful means consists in the inexhaustibility of virtue through its dedication toward awakening;
and the perfection of aspiration consists in the uninterrupted continuity of the auspicious.
The perfection of power consists in the stabilization of wholesome qualities;
the perfection of knowledge consists in the enjoyment of the Dharma and the maturation of sentient beings; and the perfection of sovereignty consists in the removal of obscurations.
In this context, *aiśvarya* (sovereignty) is the abundance of wealth and requisites;
*ādhipatya* (lordship) is the mastery over their enjoyment.
The obscuration of both of these is the obscuration of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), because they are its fruit.
What, then, is that? It is stinginess (*mātsarya*).
Regarding the phrase "an obstruction to a happy rebirth" (*sugatyāvaraṇa*): a happy rebirth (*sugati*) is an auspicious state of existence, namely, as a human or a deity.
Its obscuration is the obscuration of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), because that [obscuration] is its result.
Furthermore, that immorality (*dauśīlya*) is contemptible bodily and vocal action;
[the perfection of patience consists in] not abandoning sentient beings.
One should embrace harmful beings just as one embraces those who are helpful;
this is the fruit of patience, while its obscuration is anger.
Thus, there is the loss of faults and the increase of virtues.
The abandonment of faults already arisen and the non-arising of those not yet arisen among those engaged in harming oneself or others is "diminution.
The further increase of those already arisen and the arising of those not yet arisen among those engaged in benefiting oneself or others is "growth.
What, then, is the obscuration here? It is laziness (*kausīdya*).
Regarding the "obstruction of introducing those to be trained":

this refers to the introduction of those to be trained into the teaching, because it is accepted as the cause for attaining heaven and liberation. When reverence arises through tranquility, sentient beings enter the teaching effortlessly by means of conversation and supernatural power.
And here, distraction is an obscuration;
it is called the obscuration to liberation.
Liberation is the abandonment of the afflictions.
And that [liberation] occurs through instruction; since instruction is wisdom and nothing else, liberation is the fruit of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Its obscuration is afflicted wisdom, delusion, or poor wisdom.
This is the obscuration to the inexhaustibility of generosity and the other perfections.
That which is an obscuration to the inexhaustibility of generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth, is the obscuration to the perfection of skillful means (*upāyapāramitā*).
Furthermore, as to how that inexhaustibility of generosity and the rest comes about, it is said: "Because of its inexhaustibility through dedication to awakening (*bodhipariṇāmanā*).
Roots of virtue such as generosity, when dedicated toward great awakening (*mahābodhi*), do not perish, just like Buddhahood itself.

Some say that the obscuration to this is the lack of knowledge regarding skillful means, characterized by the failure to dedicate [merit] toward great enlightenment. Others say that the obscuration is the grasping at the three spheres, which constitutes a lack of skill in means.
Still others say it is the obscuration to the uninterrupted engagement in wholesome deeds throughout all births.
The uninterrupted continuity of wholesome states occurs daily or even moment by moment;
and that is the fruit of the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā).
How so? To this he says: "Because, through the power of aspiration, one takes up rebirths favorable to that [wholesome state]."
For by the power of aspiration, one secures a rebirth conducive to the uninterrupted practice of generosity and the other perfections.
Its obscuration is the lack of aspiration for a rebirth favorable to generosity and so forth;
it is the obscuration to the stabilization of that very same wholesome state.
"Daily" or "moment by moment," *niyatīkaraṇa* means making certain.
He states the reason for this very point: "Because the opposing factors are not overcome by the powers of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
In this context, the power of analytical discernment is wisdom (*prajñā*) accompanied by steadfastness (*dhairya*).
Furthermore, fortitude (*dhairya*) is a designated phenomenon (*prajñaptidharma*),
because it consists in the analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) of the three— energy, concentration, and wisdom— which are innate.

The power of cultivation (*bhāvanābala*) is the engagement in giving and so forth without effort, accompanied by repeated practice, because one is not overcome by their opposites, such as stinginess and the like.
What is the obscuration here? It is the weakness of non-analytical discernment (*apratisaṃkhyāna*) and of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
It is the obscuration to the enjoyment of the Dharma and the ripening of oneself and others.

The fruit consists of being established within the assembly circle (*parṣanmaṇḍala*) of the Enjoyment Body (*sambhogika*), the enjoyment of the profound and vast Mahāyāna Dharma, and the ripening of sentient beings through various forms of emanation-activity and the teaching of the Abhidharma.
Furthermore, the obscuration to that consists in the failure to investigate the meaning of what has been heard as it truly is, and dullness of wisdom; this is the obscuration.
And herein, while there are six perfections in substance, they are ten by name, because the [latter] four perfections are characterized by the perfection of wisdom.
In this context, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is supramundane non-conceptual knowledge (*lokottara-nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
By means of that knowledge, there is the gradual abandonment of all obscurations.

Furthermore, the perfections of skillful means, aspiration, power, and knowledge are comprised within the knowledge obtained subsequent to the supramundane path (*lokottara-mārga-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

If the perfection of wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*) is preeminent, why is it not non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*)? For the perfection of wisdom is the knowledge obtained subsequent to non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpajñānapṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Having discerned that which is realized through that knowledge, it itself experiences the enjoyment of the Dharma (*dharmasambhoga*) and brings others to maturity.
Since both of these [experiencing and maturing others] do not exist within non-conceptual [knowledge], the perfection of wisdom is therefore not non-conceptual.
The obscuration of the perfections has been explained.

Regarding the obscurations on the stages (*bhūmi*): there are ten kinds of obscurations which, in their respective order, are the opposites (*vipakṣa*) of those [stages], because they are the opposites of the stages. For the stages consist essentially of specific opportunities for supramundane meditative concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth;
thus, non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) is the opposite, as it acts as an obstruction to their arising.

Furthermore, it is not only non-afflicted ignorance that constitutes an obscuration here; rather, other afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) do as well. For instance, on the stage of *pramuditā*, all [afflictions] to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) constitute an obscuration. This is because, through the path of seeing—which brings about the realization of the meaning of all [truths]—all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of erroneous views regarding the truths are abandoned. However, those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are abandoned by the remaining stages.
However, even though they have not been abandoned, these [afflictions] do not cause defilement for Bodhisattvas, as if they were already abandoned.
With reference to this very point, it was said in verse: "Affliction has become a limb of enlightenment through the application of delusion as a skillful means;
even cyclic existence is itself pacified, and therefore the Tathāgata is inconceivable."

Since it is stated that "in the ten stages, the ten perfections become increasingly more excellent in their respective order," it is understood that there is also a corresponding abandonment of their opposites, such as stinginess and so forth.
If other afflictions were also obstructions, why was it said that on the stages only non-afflicted ignorance is the obstruction? Because it is unique [to Bodhisattvas].
For this indeed functions as an impediment to the attainment of nirvana for Bodhisattvas alone, and not for Śrāvakas and others.
For indeed, while the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are liberated upon that very [attainment], the bodhisattvas are not; therefore, this is an uncommon [obscuration].
This has been described as an obscuration regarding the stages (*bhūmi*), but it is not intended to mean that this alone is the obscuration regarding the stages.

Since afflictions (*kleśa*) are common to both bodhisattvas and others such as the śrāvakas, there is neither a prescription nor a prohibition regarding them as an obscuration within the bodhisattva stages. Thus, even if they are not explicitly mentioned, the obscuration [of affliction] does not cease.

Another says: Non-afflicted ignorance is common to both Śrāvakas and others as well as Bodhisattvas; therefore, it is specifically called an "obstruction" (āvaraṇa) of the stages (bhūmi). However, afflictions (kleśa) are not mentioned [as such], because they are merely incidental (ānuṣangika).
For if afflictions were also common to Bodhisattvas as they are to Śrāvakas and others, they would not be considered merely incidental.

Others, however, say that the ignorance regarding the stages (*bhūmi*) which constitutes an obscuration is the non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) of the Śrāvakas and others; even though it exists, it does not act as an impediment to liberation, because the Śrāvakas attain liberation while that ignorance regarding the stages still persists.
For Bodhisattvas, however, it is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), because it serves as a cause for obstructing the attainment of Nirvāṇa.
Others say this is not so, [stating]: "The non-afflicted [obscuration] is a tenfold obscuration.
For, by means of the first stage, one penetrates the all-pervading nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
Therein, the first is supramundane wisdom together with its retinue, comprised within the path of seeing.

It is the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), emptiness. Because it is omnipresent—since it is the same everywhere as it is in one place by virtue of its universal characteristic—it is called "omnipresent" (*sarvatraga*).
Because no phenomenon exists that is separate from the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
This statement indicates that the *dharmadhātu* is omnipresent.
"Penetrates" (*pratividhyati*) means to realize directly (*sākṣātkaroti*).
By means of this penetration, one attains the equality of self and others.

Thinking, "I am that which is the other, or that which is the other is I," he perceives the non-difference of emptiness in both the other and himself; thus, he considers there to be no difference between self and other.
For this very reason, on this stage, the perfection of generosity becomes most preeminent.
Consequently, in this state, the bodhisattva engages in the welfare of others just as he does in his own welfare.
Thus, penetration, the counteragent, and the fruit of the counteragent have been set forth.
These three should also be understood to exist in the other stages;
by means of the second [stage], the supreme meaning is attained.
"It penetrates the *dharmadhātu*" is how it is connected [in the text].

Because of seeing that [the *dharmadhātu*] is luminous by nature, he shows the scriptural authority (āgama) by means of which this occurs for him: "Therefore, since the realization is equal for all, we must apply ourselves (*yoga*) exclusively to the realization of purification in every aspect."

For it is said in the Sūtra: "Because the ten paths of wholesome action, when contemplated through the aspect of wisdom, lead as far as the Śrāvaka vehicle; further purified, they lead as far as the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; and further purified, they lead to the purification of the Bodhisattva stages, the purification of the perfections, and the vastness of conduct."
Thereafter, because they become increasingly more purified, they lead up to the attainment of the power of the ten powers (*daśabala*).
Therefore, it is said in detail: "Thus, we should have an equal accomplishment," and so forth.
This is because this very [thought] occurs for him on the second stage; hence the words "therefore" (*tasmāt tarhi*), and so on.
Therefore, it is understood that one penetrates the supreme object by means of the second [insight].
"Actualization" (abhinirhāra) means effort or activity.
"Purification in all aspects" refers to the removal of both afflicted and unafflicted delusion regarding the dharmadhātu.

Therefore, on that stage, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) becomes even more predominant, because by seeking a distinguished goal, one makes oneself even more completely subject to it. By the third [perfection], one penetrates the meaning of its supreme outflow (*niṣyanda*); this is what is being discussed.
Because the word of the Buddha is characterized by the penetration of the *dharmadhātu*;

for the teaching-dharma consisting of the sūtras and so forth—which is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the *dharmadhātu*—is manifested by the power of the *dharmadhātu*, which is designated as the *dharmakāya* purified in all its aspects.
This is because of the preeminence of the *dharmadhātu*, because of the preeminence of the teaching-dharma that is its outflow, and because it is the cause for the purification of the *dharmadhātu*.
"By him, having understood the preeminence of what has been heard, which is the outflow of the *dharmadhātu*," and so forth.

"By him" means by one who has realized the *dharmadhātu*. "Of what has been heard" refers to the teachings such as the *sūtras* that have been heard. "Having understood their preeminence" means having known them thus within oneself through non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
"For that purpose" means for the sake of hearing the Buddha's word;
it means one should cast oneself even into a mass of fire as vast as the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system.

For it is said in the Sūtra: "If someone were to say this to you: 'I shall cause you to hear this verse of Dharma brought forth by the Perfectly Awakened One, which purifies the conduct of a Bodhisattva; provided that you would throw yourself into a great pit of fire, blazing and become a single mass of flame, and undergo a great onset of painful sensations with your own body.'"

It occurs to him: "I am able, for the sake of even a single word of Dharma brought forth by the Perfectly Enlightened One which purifies the conduct of a bodhisattva, to cast myself from the Brahma-world into a great trichiliocosm world-system filled with fire;

how much more so into an ordinary pit of fire? Furthermore, we must seek all the qualities of a Buddha even through dwelling in all the sufferings of the hells and the states of woe, let alone through dwelling in the sufferings of human beings."

For this very reason, on this ground, the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) becomes even more predominant, because it is unbreakable even by the endurance of all afflictions for the sake of what has been heard.
Regarding the fourth [ground], it is under discussion that one penetrates the meaning of the non-appropriation of the *dharmadhātu*.
On the fourth ground, due to its equality, one penetrates the lack of "mine-ness" (*anātmīyatva*) of the *dharmadhātu*, because there is no equality of the *dharmadhātu* belonging to anyone at all.
Alternatively, because it is not an object for any cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*), there is no appropriation by anyone;
because it is itself not an object, there is no appropriation here whatsoever.
For this reason, there is a scriptural statement that even craving for phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) is turned away.

Thus, in the Radiant stage (*arciṣmatī*), through the realization of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) by means of non-conceptual knowledge (*niṣprapañca-jñāna*), there is the attainment of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Even that craving for the Dharma—such as the sūtras and so forth—which the bodhisattva previously possessed, is also turned away.
Others maintain that "craving for the Dharma" refers to the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*).
Therefore, on that stage, the perfection of vigor becomes even more preeminent,
