because one constantly dwells in the factors conducive to awakening that have transcended the discursive speech of body and mind;
and on the fifth [stage], for the sake of the non-differentiation of the mental continuum.
It is understood that he penetrates the *dharmadhātu*.
He perceives the non-difference of his own continuum from the continua of all the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as well as from those of the Bodhisattvas, through their succession.
By means of the ten equalities of purity of mental intention, he demonstrates the scriptural tradition (*āgama*).

And by the equality of the pure intention regarding the qualities of the past Buddhas, and by the equality of the pure intention regarding the qualities of the future Buddhas, and by the equality of the pure intention regarding the qualities of the present Buddhas; and by the equality of the pure intention regarding the purity of ethical discipline, and by the equality of the pure intention regarding the purity of the mind, and by the equality of the pure intention regarding the purity that removes views, doubt, uncertainty, and hesitation; and by the equality of the pure intention regarding the purity of the knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path, and by the equality of the pure intention regarding the purity of the knowledge of practice and abandonment; and by the equality of the pure intention regarding the purity of the progressive cultivation of all the factors conducive to enlightenment, and by the equality of the pure intention regarding the maturation of all sentient beings.

Through these equalities, one penetrates the non-differentiation of the mental continuums of all Buddhas, because the Dharma-body—characterized by the revolution of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)—is undivided.

Therefore, on that stage, the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*) becomes preeminent, because there is an abundance of cultivation of the aspects of truth from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).
This is for the sake of the sixth [stage], which concerns the meaning of being neither afflicted nor purified.
It is connected with the phrase "one penetrates the dharmadhātu.
Defilement, which has dependent origination as its characteristic, does not become defiled by nature within that [dharmadhātu] because it is adventitious;
nor does it become purified because of its natural purity.
Thus, he shows the scriptural authority for the point that one penetrates the *dharmadhātu* by means of non-conceptual knowledge (*jñāna*) in the form of self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedya*).
This is because of the penetration [realized] that within dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there is no dharma whatsoever that is either afflicted or purified;
it is on the sixth stage (*bhūmi*) that the bodhisattva penetrates dependent origination.

In that regard, one does not perceive the defilement or purification of any dharma whatsoever, because the *dharmadhātu* is luminous by nature and because the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are merely defilement. Furthermore, there exists no other self (*ātman*) or anything belonging to a self (*ātmīya*) apart from those [factors], in which either defilement or purification could be conceived.

Therefore, on this stage, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) becomes even more preeminent, in the sense of being free from defilement and pure, due to the realization of the profundity of dependent origination. On the seventh stage, there is the state of non-differentiation (*anānārthatva*).
It is understood that [the Bodhisattva] penetrates the *dharmadhātu*.

On that stage (*bhūmi*), the Bodhisattva overcomes [all conceptualizations] because of the absence of the manifestation of all signs (*nimitta*), and because the manifestation of diversity (*nānātva*) occurs through the door of the manifestation of signs.
Therefore, due to the absence of the manifestation of signs, it is said that on the seventh [stage], one penetrates the *dharmadhātu* in the sense of non-diversity (*anānātva*).
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "By way of being signless (*nirnimittatā*), because of the non-occurrence of the diversity of signs of phenomena such as the *sūtras*.

Those signs of phenomena such as the *sūtras* by which one enters the *dharmadhātu* forcibly manifest in their diversity during both that entry and the subsequently attained state (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) up until the sixth stage (*bhūmi*).
However, on the seventh stage, through a cognition that has the single flavor of all signs, one penetrates the signlessness of the *dharmadhātu*; thus, those various signs do not occur.

Therefore, on that stage, the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) becomes preeminent, because one penetrates all signs (*nimitta*) as being signless (*animitta*), yet does not contradict the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) produced by signs.
And through that penetration, one attains mastery (*vaśitva*) on that very same stage.
This is for the purpose of the eighth [stage], which is characterized by neither deficiency nor excess.
It is connected with the phrase "he penetrates the dharmadhātu.
Because the dharmadhātu is pure by nature, there is no distinction between its stained and stainless states;
therefore, because it is eternally just so, it is called "tathatā" (suchness).
In the absence of signs, there is no inferiority whatsoever;
in the presence of signs, there is no superiority whatsoever.
For indeed, the sign itself is the signless; the reason for this is precisely the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

On the eighth stage, because of the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the bodhisattva penetrates the fact that there is neither increase nor decrease in the *dharmadhātu*.

This is because one perceives no diminution or growth of any phenomenon whatsoever in terms of either affliction (*saṃkleśa*) or purification (*vyavadāna*), since no previously non-existent phenomenon arises.

There are four masteries: mastery over non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa-vaśitā*), mastery over the purification of the field (*kṣetra-pariśuddhi-vaśitā*), mastery over knowledge (*jñāna-vaśitā*), and mastery over action (*karma-vaśitā*).

In this regard, it should be understood that the dharmadhātu is the basis for mastery over non-conceptuality because, through effortlessness (*anābhoga*), there is an absence of the manifestation of all signs (*nimitta*).
While the absence of the manifestation of signs is also possible on the seventh stage through deliberate application (*abhisaṃskāra*),
the distinction here is that it occurs without deliberate application.
It is the subject at hand that one penetrates the eighth [stage] as the basis for mastery over the purification of the field (*kṣetrapariśuddhivaśitāśrayatva*).

This basis for mastery over the purification of the field arises from the attainment of the power to manifest Buddha-fields and the circles of assemblies (*parṣanmaṇḍala*) according to one’s wish within the *dharmadhātu*.

Therefore, on that stage, the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhānapāramitā*) becomes even more predominant, because through the attainment of non-conceptual mastery over the field, there is uninterrupted application toward what is wholesome.

The state of being the basis for mastery over knowledge is [attained] through the ninth [ground]. It is the subject under discussion that one penetrates the *dharmadhātu*. How is it to be understood that one penetrates the state of being the basis for mastery over knowledge through the ninth ground? To this he says: "Because of the attainment of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*)."
For on this stage, one attains the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of phenomena, meaning, etymological derivation, and eloquence, which are unsurpassed by others;
therefore, it is understood that here the dharmadhātu is penetrated as the basis for mastery over knowledge (*jñānavaśitā*).
Consequently, on that stage, the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*) becomes even more predominant due to its association with the specific excellence of the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*).
It is connected [to the statement] that one penetrates the state of being the basis for mastery over karma on the tenth stage.
How is this understood? To this he says: "Because of performing the welfare of sentient beings through emanations according to one's wish.
By this certainty, on the tenth stage, one penetrates the state of the dharmadhātu as the basis for mastery over karma; thereby, one attains sovereign mastery over the activities of a Tathāgata.

For it is thus: by virtue of being a Sugata, he performs for sentient beings dwelling in the infinite world-systems of the ten directions whatever must be done for whomever, in whatever manner, and at whatever time, by means of emanation bodies according to his will.
Therefore, on this stage, the perfection of gnosis (*jñāna-pāramitā*) becomes even more preeminent, due to its connection with the excellence of enjoying the Dharma and maturing sentient beings.

Thus, for these aforementioned bodhisattva stages, there exists an undefiled ignorance that acts as an obstacle to the penetration of the tenfold dharmadhātu and to its purification in all its aspects; this constitutes an obscuration for each individual stage. The ten bodhisattva stages are established as the antidotes to that. The distinction between the ninth and tenth stages is illustrated by their fruit, rather than by a difference in the types of obscurations or a distinction in penetration, because the state of those two abodes has reached an indescribable condition.
The purpose of penetrating the meaning of the all-pervading [dharmas] and so forth is the progressive attainment of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) across the ten stages (*bhūmi*) respectively.
Therefore, it is said that this very [obstruction] is the "obstruction to the stages," which is the obstruction to the progressive attainment of the perfections.

Alternatively, the result—consisting of the various forms and diverse culminations such as meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and attainments (*samāpatti*) mentioned in the Sūtras, each distinguished according to the successive stages—is the purpose of penetrating the meaning of the all-pervading [dharmas] and so forth.

{The Summary of Obscurations} In order to demonstrate that all the various types of obscurations previously mentioned are included within two obscurations, it is said: "In brief, moreover, the obscuration of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa) and the obscuration of the knowable (jñeyāvaraṇa) alone are declared.
How is this understood? That in summary there are only these two and not even a third.
Therefore, it says: "All obscurations here [are included]."
The phrase "included herein" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
It is understood that all obscurations are included within the two obscurations; there is no third [obscuration] other than these.

And because all obscurations are included precisely within this, liberation from all obscurations is intended through the destruction of this very pair—the obscuration of afflictions and the obscuration to the knowable—which comprises all obscurations. The meaning is the abandonment of all obscurations.

If the obscuration of the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*) has not been mentioned, how can it be included within this very [category of obscurations]? For inclusion does not occur through verbal expression; rather, it occurs by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, because the all-pervading obscuration (*vyāpyāvaraṇa*) has been stated, that too is indeed already expressed. Otherwise, it would merely be an obscuration of a limited portion (*pradeśāvaraṇa*).
Alternatively, in order to include the obscuration to the stage of Buddhahood, it is said: "All obscurations here [are included] because liberation is held to occur through their destruction;
since there is no liberation as long as the obscuration to Buddhahood is not destroyed, it is thereby established that this too is an obscuration, just like the remaining ones."

However, non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) in its state of extreme subtlety, as well as the latent predispositions of the afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*), are said to be the obscuration of the stage of a Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*).
Therefore, because of that extreme subtlety, it cannot be perceived otherwise; such is the explanation.
{The summarized meaning of the obscurations:} The great obscuration is that which is pervasive—the obscuration of afflictions and the knowable belonging to those of the bodhisattva lineage.
The slight obscuration is the partial obscuration of afflictions alone, belonging to those of the śrāvaka and other lineages.

The obscuration to application is that which is excessive; it belongs to those very same individuals whose conduct is dominated by passion and so forth, because they fail to attain application due to those [afflictions].
The obscuration to attainment is that which is called "equal," belonging to those whose conduct is characterized by equal parts; for it functions as a hindrance to attainment.

The obscuration to the distinction of attainment is that which pertains to "taking up and abandoning," because it is an obscuration to the distinction of realization for those of the Bodhisattva lineage.
Non-abiding nirvana is the distinction of realization.
And this very distinction of results should be understood:

that which is the obstruction to correct application (*samyak-prayoga*) consists of the ninefold characteristics of the afflictions (*kleśa*), because of the statement that "the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) are the obstruction.
These constitute the obstruction to correct application, as has been explained accordingly.
The obscuration regarding the cause is that which pertains to the tenfold causes of virtue and so forth;
for since it constitutes an obscuration by way of obstructing the causes of virtue and so forth, it is called the "obscuration regarding the cause.
The obscuration regarding the entry into reality is that which pertains to the factors conducive to awakening.
For by means of those [perfections], one enters into reality.
That which is an obscuration to supreme excellence regarding the perfections is so called because there is no excellence beyond them;

that which is an obscuration to the attainment of distinction regarding the stages (*bhūmi*) is so called because it is precisely the perfections themselves, when they have become the basis for supramundane distinction, that are called "stages."

The summary of the obstructions is that, in brief, they are of two kinds: the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstruction to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), because by these all obstructions are subsumed.
This statement of the summarized meaning is for the sake of easy grasping and retention;
for what is condensed is easily grasped and retained.
The second chapter, on Obscurations, in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-ṭīkā* following the tradition of the scriptures, explained by the venerable master Sthiramati, is completed.

The Third Chapter: The Determination of Reality. Immediately after the exposition of the obscurations (*āvaraṇa*), it is now the occasion for the exposition of reality (*tattva*), because it was listed immediately following them. Therefore, he says "with reference to reality" (*tattvam adhikṛtyāha*). Furthermore, reality is manifold;

thus, if its divisions are not understood, the essential nature of reality is difficult to comprehend. Consequently, demonstrating first the classifications of reality itself, he says: "The reality of the root, the reality of characteristics," and so forth, [detailing] the ten kinds of reality.

In that regard, the statement concerning the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*) is for the purpose of demonstrating how the other realities are subsumed within it. The statement concerning the characteristic reality (*lakṣaṇatattva*) is for the purpose of abandoning defects associated with the thorough knowledge, abandonment, and realization of the fundamental reality.
The statement concerning the reality of non-perversion (*aviparyāsatattva*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the means for becoming weary of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
The statement regarding the reality of cause and fruit is for the purpose of demonstrating the departure by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle for one who is agitated;
for the Śrāvaka departs through the penetration and cultivation of the four noble truths.
The statement regarding gross reality is for the purpose of demonstrating the means for practicing the knowledge of all aspects.
The statement regarding subtle reality (*sūkṣmatattva*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the means for abandoning all obscurations;

the statement regarding well-known reality (*prasiddhatattva*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the means for teaching the well-established Dharma and for demonstrating the means for refuting all opposing disputants.

Although the *dharmadhātu* is uniform, its nature is said to be threefold as the "fundamental reality" (*mūlatattva*) by way of its causes; demonstrating this, he says: "Because therein other realities are established."
The meaning here is that other realities, such as the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, are included therein.

For what purpose is the threefold nature (*svabhāva*) to be understood? Some say it is for the purpose of demonstrating conventional reality (*vyavahāra*), ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), and their basis.
Others say it is for the purpose of demonstrating error (*viparyāsa*), its cause, and the objective support (*ālambana*) for its antidote.
Others say it is for the purpose of demonstrating the objects of abandonment, thorough knowledge, and realization so that Bodhisattvas may be dissociated from their obscurations.
Others say it is for the purpose of achieving non-erroneous practice regarding the nature of the *prajñāpāramitā*, which is profound by its very nature, by means of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
For it is thus stated in the two verses of the *Abhidharmasūtra*: "The teaching of illusion and so forth concerns the perfected nature; there is no teaching of the imagined [nature] in reality."
However, the teaching on the perfected nature concerns the fourfold purity.
Purity is natural and the absence of defilement; likewise, it does not have the path as its objective support.
For the apprehension of purified phenomena is considered to be fourfold.

Thus, others say that the three natures are mentioned according to their possibility in order to demonstrate that they are the objects of mundane knowledge, supramundane knowledge, and the knowledge subsequently attained therefrom.
One might ask: "Among these three natures, which one is intended here as reality (*tattva*)?"
The meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*) is indeed the non-erroneous meaning.
The intention of the question here is: "What is the non-erroneousness in these three natures (*svabhāva*), since reality is asserted within the three natures? [The answer is:
"The nature is threefold: non-existent, eternal," and so forth, in detail.

The imagined characteristic (*parikalpitalakṣaṇa*) is eternally non-existent; for it is therein that the attachment of the ignorant to the grasped and the grasper, and to the signified and the signifier, proceeds like a dream.
And because it lacks its own intrinsic nature, the imagined nature (*kalpitasvabhāva*) is non-existent.
Therefore, due to its being of the nature of non-existence and because it is not an error, the imagined characteristic is non-being.

This very non-existence within the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is called reality (tattva), because it is non-erroneous; thus he shows that here the meaning of "reality" (tattvārtha) is the sense of being non-erroneous.
As for the dependent characteristic (paratantra-lakṣaṇa), it exists but does not exist from the standpoint of reality.
It exists because it serves as the basis for conventional designations such as the grasped and the grasper;
yet, because it lacks the nature of the grasped and the grasper, it does not exist in that way in reality.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "because it is mere illusion."
This is what is meant: that which appears exists as its material cause is illusion (*māyopādāna*);
however, it does not exist in the manner in which it appears—namely, in the form of the grasped and the grasper—just like an illusory person (*māyāpuruṣa*) and so forth.
Therefore, it is an error (*bhrānti*).

This is the reality within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); otherwise, it would be the manifestation of that which exists [in itself] through a form that does not exist in its own essence.
Here too, the phrase "because of being non-erroneous" is connected [to this], as it is the subject under discussion.
The perfected characteristic (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*) is reality in terms of both existence and non-existence.
Reality is both existent and non-existent, having the characteristic of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).
It is existence because its essence consists in the absence of duality;
it is non-existence because its essence consists in the absence of that duality.
It is reality because it is the object of purification;
this is reality within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). It is connected with the phrase "because it is non-erroneous."

The reality of characteristics (*lakṣaṇatattva*) refers to the reality of the three natures (*svabhāvatraya*), which has been explained; however, it has not yet been explained as a definition (*lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, he asks [the question].

Alternatively, since the reality of characteristics was mentioned immediately after the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*), and that [definition] is not well-known, he asks: "What is the reality of characteristics? To this, he says:
"In this context, regarding phenomena (*dharma*) and the person (*pudgala*), there is superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*)."
Thus is the detailed explanation.

That knowledge through which the views of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*) regarding the person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*) do not arise is the characteristic of reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) within the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Furthermore, the adherence to the view that phenomena such as the self and form exist in an ultimate sense as objects of perception, distinct from the consciousness in which they appear, is the view of superimposition.

Others say that the view of negation (*apavādadarśana*) is the realization that even things existing for the sake of conventional usage do not exist; they further state that the view of negation is the abandonment of consciousness appearing as persons (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*). This should be reflected upon as the rejection of grasping (*grāha-apakṣepa*).

The characteristic of reality within the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is to be understood as being free from superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*). It is that characteristic through the discernment of which the view of superimposition and denial regarding the person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*) does not arise.

Furthermore, that is reality by way of conventional designation (*vyavahāra*), but not by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); for, through the realization of the imagined nature, the view of superimposition and denial regarding phenomena and the person does not arise—that is to say, it is not produced.
"The view of superimposition and denial regarding the grasped and the grasper," and so forth.

That error which appears as the grasped and the grasper and is apprehended as either a phenomenon (*dharma*) or a person (*pudgala*), if one adheres to it as existing in reality, that is the superimposition of the grasped and the grasper.
On the other hand, if one adheres to the non-existence of the grasper just as much as the grasped, that is the denial of the grasped and the grasper.

That characteristic of reality within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), through the knowledge of which the views of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*) regarding the grasped and the grasper no longer arise, should be understood as being free from superimposition and denial.
Furthermore, it is non-existent in its imagined form as the nature of grasped and grasper, yet existent as the basis for conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).
For by understanding it in this way, the views of superimposition and denial do not arise with respect to the dependent nature.
"The view of superimposition and denial regarding existence and non-existence," and so forth.
Some say: "If one perceives emptiness as being indeed an existent entity, then there is the view of superimposing existence;
if, however, one perceives it as being indeed a non-existent entity, then there is the view of [denying] existence."
Both of these views—existence and non-existence—are views of existence and non-existence.
That characteristic through the knowledge of which those views of existence and non-existence do not arise is the characteristic of reality within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
And that has a nature liberated from both existence and non-existence.
Some say that because of that knowledge, the demonstration of existence and non-existence does not occur with respect to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Others, however, say: "Emptiness is the very nature of the non-existence of duality"—this is the extreme of superimposing non-existence (*abhāva-samāropānta*), because one superimposes the nature of existence upon that which is essentially free from both existence and non-existence.

"This [emptiness] does not exist" as a nature free from existence and non-existence, which is the object of non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)—this is the extreme of deprecating non-existence (*abhāvāpavādānta*).
Another [teacher] says: "This twofold explanation is to be considered because each of existence and non-existence is connected with the views of superimposition and denial.
Here, 'existence' refers to the existence of the non-existence of duality;
if one grasps that as being merely existence, then existence becomes superimposed."
If one grasps it as non-existence alone, it is thus negated.

If one grasps existence—which is established as the absence of duality—as being subject to annihilation, then existence is superimposed as absolute non-existence. Furthermore, if one grasps it as precisely duality, it is thus negated, because this [existence] is characterized by the absence of duality.
Alternatively, if one perceives it as having the nature of both existence and non-existence, it becomes thus superimposed;
or if one perceives it as merely non-existence, then both affliction and purification are negated.
This avoidance of these two extremes is the characteristic of reality within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpannatva*).
But was not the characteristic of the three natures already stated previously? It was taught [as follows]: "From the object, from unreal imagination, and from the absence of duality."

Thus, in that context, "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), whereas here it refers to a sign (*cihna*); therefore, there is no redundancy. For that by knowing which one would not engage [with phenomena] is indeed the defining characteristic of reality (*tattva*).

Thus, that which does not arise through knowledge as the view of superimposition or denial regarding the person (*pudgala*) and so forth is the characteristic of the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*).

{The Reality of Non-perversion} Immediately after the reality of characteristics (*lakṣaṇatattva*), the reality of non-perversion (*aviparyāsatattva*) must be explained, because it was listed immediately thereafter; hence he says, "the reality of non-perversion," and so forth.

For it is called the reality of non-perversion because it is the antidote to the perversions of permanence, pleasure, purity, and self—namely, [the view of things] as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
Since it was previously asserted that the other realities are included within the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*), he asks: "How [are they included] in the fundamental reality? and so forth.
Regarding the term "impermanence and so forth" (*anityāditā*):
those which are impermanent and so forth—namely, the modes of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self—are "impermanence and so forth. The state of being that is "impermanence and so forth."
In order to demonstrate the inclusion of the reality of non-perversion within the fundamental reality, he says: "For the meaning of impermanence is the meaning of non-existence," and so forth.
For the meaning of impermanence is threefold: the meaning of non-existence, the meaning of arising and ceasing, and the meaning of being with stain and without stain.
That which exists eternally in such a manner is permanent (*nitya*).
The opposite of that is impermanent (*anitya*). Regarding these [three natures], respectively:
therein, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is impermanent in the sense of being eternally non-existent.
Others maintain that it should be understood through the method of etymological derivation (*nirukti*) as "the non-existent is impermanent" (*asannityam anityam*).
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is impermanent in the sense of impermanence characterized by arising and ceasing at every moment;
for it arises from conditions and its destruction is without cause.

The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), although its characteristic is non-change, is impermanent by virtue of the adventitious meaning of impermanence, which is characterized by being both stained and stainless.
"Suffering is called appropriation and characteristic," and so forth;
suffering is also threefold: the suffering of appropriation (*upādāna-duḥkha*), the suffering of characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-duḥkha*), and the suffering of connection (*sambandha-duḥkha*).
In this context, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is suffering by way of appropriation (*upādāna*).
It is called "suffering" because, when not fully understood, suffering is appropriated either in this world or in the next.

Demonstrating how suffering is appropriated through that lack of full understanding, he says: "Like the intrinsic nature of a rabbit’s horn and so forth, there is no mode whatsoever by which its existence could be grasped through delusion; thus, its emptiness is simply its non-existence."
The emptiness of the absence of that [nature] belongs to the dependent nature (*paratantra*).
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "The characteristic of the dependent nature does not exist in the way it is imagined by the foolish as having a dual nature;
yet it is not non-existent in every respect. And in the way that it does exist, it is realized through pure mundane knowledge (*śuddhalaukikajñāna*)."
The absence of that [duality] in it is emptiness;
this is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) pertaining to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*).
For this very reason, it is said: "The characteristic of the perfected nature has emptiness as its very essence, because its intrinsic nature is the non-existence of duality."
Therefore, its very nature (prakṛti), its very essence (svabhāva), is emptiness;
it is the absence of characteristics (alakṣaṇa) and selflessness (nairātmya)—such is the detailed explanation.

Selflessness is threefold: the selflessness of being without characteristics (alakṣaṇa-nairātmya), the selflessness of having different characteristics (vilakṣaṇa-nairātmya), and the selflessness of specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa-nairātmya).
In that regard, because the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) lacks any defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), its selflessness (*nairātmya*) is precisely the absence of characteristics.
For this very reason, he says: "The imagined nature has no characteristic at all; thus its selflessness is the absence of characteristics, and not in any other way.

This demonstrates that [the selflessness of] the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is a selflessness characterized by difference (*vilakṣaṇa-nairātmya*), because the dependent nature possesses a characteristic in the form of a real entity (*vastu-rūpa*).
But it is not as it is conceptualized by the foolish as a duality;
it is "of a different characteristic," meaning it is dissimilar to the imagined characteristic.
That dependent characteristic is selflessness.
Thus, by means of the imagined self, its lack of self (nairātmya) is demonstrated.
The lack of self as its own characteristic belongs to the perfected nature;

because the perfected nature, being of the form of the absence of grasped and grasper, is itself the lack of self, it shows that the lack of self is its own characteristic—thereby demonstrating that the perfected phenomenon has the lack of self as its intrinsic nature.

What, then, is the distinction between these two—emptiness and selflessness? Some say that the distinction between them is this: when something is not present in a certain place, that [place] is empty of it; whereas when something does not have a self or intrinsic nature (svabhāva), it is selfless in that respect. However, in terms of actual meaning there is no distinction at all; the difference exists only through a difference in formal definition.

Because that which does not exist in a certain place is, by virtue of its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), "selflessness" (*nairātmya*); whereas for the other [that which exists there], by virtue of its unestablished intrinsic nature, it is "emptiness" (*śūnyatva*).

Within the threefold fundamental reality, the three kinds of impermanence are elucidated respectively as the antidotes to the two extremes of superimposition and denial, and by way of demonstrating adventitious stains:
namely, impermanence as non-existence, impermanence as arising and ceasing, and impermanence as being stained and stainless.
Thus, up to the threefold selflessness, what has been described is the reality free from error.

{The reality of cause and fruit}: immediately following that, the reality of cause and fruit must be explained; therefore, he says: "The reality consisting of cause and fruit is the fundamental reality," and so forth.

In that regard, with reference to the side of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) is the reality of the fruit, and the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*) is the reality of the cause. On the side of purification (*vyavadāna*) as well, the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is the reality of the fruit, and the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) is the reality of the cause.
Thus, the four truths beginning with suffering constitute the reality of cause and fruit.
It has been stated that within the fundamental reality (mūlatattva) lie the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

However, since it is not understood how the fundamental reality has the nature of the truths of suffering and so forth, he asks: "In what way is the threefold fundamental reality the truth of suffering and so on? To this, he says: "Because it possesses the characteristics of impermanence and so forth, it is considered the truth of suffering."
Thus,

because impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness constitute the characteristics of the truth of suffering, and because all of these exist individually within the imagined [nature] and the others, it has been explained in detail that the imagined nature and the rest are each intended to be the truth of suffering.
The fundamental reality of origination is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) by way of a threefold meaning of origination, respectively.

Since that very origination is not understood, he says: "The threefold meaning of origination consists of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), as well as emergence (*samutthāna*), and non-separation (*avisaṃyoga*)."
Thus,

the threefold origination consists of the origination of latent impressions (*vāsanā-samudaya*), the origination of manifestation (*samutthāna-samudaya*), and the origination of non-separation (*avisaṃyoga-samudaya*).
Among these, the origination of latent impressions should be understood as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Therefore, he says: "the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) for adherence to the imagined nature.

For, based on the adherence that the imagined nature exists, worldly phenomena establish the latent predispositions of conceptualization and affliction; however, supramundane phenomena do not [so establish them] because they are free from such adherence.
Consequently, the imagined nature is said to be the origination of latent predispositions.
The dependent nature (*paratantra*) is the origination by way of arising (*samutthānasamudaya*).

"Arising" (*samutthāna*) means the acquisition of self-existence (*ātmalābha*). That from which this occurs is the "origination by way of arising," because it is that from which [the phenomenon] originates (*samudeti*).
Furthermore, as to what its essential nature is, he says: "karma and afflictions.
And because they have the nature of real entities, they are the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Regarding the phrase "the state of being situated in the origin that is non-separation":
To the question "How so?", he says: "Because of non-separation from the obscurations.
This is what is meant: as long as suchness (*tathatā*) is not separated from the obscurations, so long does suffering arise.
Or, suchness that is not separated from the obscurations is the nature of origination (*samudaya-dharmatā*), and thus it receives the name "origination" (*samudaya*).
The fundamental reality is the truth of cessation by way of three kinds of cessation;
since that is not understood, he says: "Threefold cessation is considered to be the non-arising of the two natures and the twofold pacification of stains."

In this context, the non-arising of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) refers to the imagined (*parikalpita*), for because it lacks intrinsic nature, its non-arising is absolute, like that of the son of a barren woman.
The non-arising of the grasped and the grasper refers to the dependent (*paratantra*);
since that too is absolutely devoid of the essential forms of the grasped and the grasper, its non-arising consists in its being of the nature of a delusion regarding duality.
The two types of cessation of defilements (*malaśānti*) are the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*).
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of conjunction.
Since that [perfected nature] is not yet understood, he says: "namely, what is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and suchness (*tathatā*)."
Defilement is twofold: the obscuration of passion and so forth, and the imagined [nature].

Therein, when the seed has been extracted from the basis by means of non-conceptual knowledge, the peace consisting in the absolute non-arising of the defilements such as passion is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Likewise, the peace consisting in the non-arising of the imagined defilement through non-dual knowledge whose sphere is suchness (*tathatā*) is suchness itself.
For this pair is indeed the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
This threefold cessation is to be understood as corresponding respectively to the imagined (*kalpita*) and the other [natures] within the fundamental reality (*mūla-tattva*).

Others, however, maintain that through the penetration of suchness (*tathatā*), there is the pacification of the two stains—afflictions and the imagined; thus, the "pacification of stains" is called suchness because of the statement: "the cessation of duality and the cessation of intrinsic nature."
"Nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to suchness (*tathatā*), because the mind is luminous by nature.
Therefore, that cessation which has suchness as its object is called "cessation by nature.
Simple cessation (*niruddhamātra*) is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
Others maintain that "cessation" (nirodha) refers to suchness (tathatā), because [phenomena] are ceased within it.
Furthermore, since cessation has the nature of non-arising, all aspects such as the non-arising of intrinsic nature are subsumed under the term "the truth of cessation.
Thus, the inclusion of the truth of cessation within the fundamental reality has been explained.

Immediately following that, the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) must be included; therefore, he asks: "How is the truth of the path established within the threefold fundamental reality? To this, he says: "In thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) and in abandonment (*prahāṇa*)," and so forth.
Regarding "thorough knowledge of the imagined (*parikalpita*)," because the imagined is absolutely non-existent, there is only its thorough knowledge, not its abandonment.
For the abandonment of that which is non-existent is not logical,
whether in the case of the dependent nature (*paratantra*) through thorough knowledge or through abandonment.
Indeed, the dependent nature should be understood as being non-existent in the manner that it appears, but not as being non-existent in its entirety like the imagined nature (*parikalpita*).
Because karma and afflictions have the nature of being existent entities, they are to be abandoned;
and because the perfected nature is to be fully understood through wisdom and realized as an attainment,

the perfected nature— since its characteristic is being free from both existence and non-existence— is to be thoroughly known, and [it is to be realized] through the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).

Emptiness is to be thoroughly understood as the transformation of the underlying disposition (*āśaya-parāvṛtti*), which is to be realized as the liberated *dharmakāya*. Cessation (*nirodha*) is to be realized through the realization of attainment.
Others, however, maintain that both [emptiness and cessation] are both [to be understood and realized].
For thorough knowledge is twofold: thorough knowledge as cognition and thorough knowledge as abandonment.
Among these, the first and the third are to be thoroughly known through thorough knowledge as cognition;
the second, however, is to be thoroughly known through both.
Direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) is also twofold: direct realization through knowledge (*jñāna-sākṣātkriyā*) and direct realization through attainment (*prāpti-sākṣātkriyā*).
Among these, all three [truths] are to be directly realized by means of direct realization through knowledge;
however, by means of direct realization through attainment, only the third [truth] is so realized.

Thus, in this context of the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*), the establishment of the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) should be understood in terms of full comprehension, abandonment, and realization; it is not, however, because [the path] is included within that [reality].
Furthermore, by means of these four truths, that which is affliction (*saṃkleśa*), from what it arises, and the purification (*viśuddhi*) of those two, and from what it arises, are fully elucidated.
Their sequence, moreover, is according to the order of realization (*abhisamaya*).

The reality of the coarse and the subtle: this refers to the reality of the coarse and the reality of the subtle. The reality of the coarse is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), while the reality of the subtle is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Since one first ripens sentient beings through the coarse and subsequently liberates those who have been ripened through the subtle, the coarse comes first and the subtle follows.
The statement is expressed in reverse order for the sake of conforming to the *kārikā*.
In that context, because it is the object of non-concentrated knowledge, conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) is the coarse reality;
because it is the object of concentrated knowledge, ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is the subtle reality.
Alternatively, it is coarse because it is an object of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and subtle because it is an object of knowledge (*jñāna*).

Since it has been asserted that all realities are included within the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*), he asks: "How is that to be understood within the fundamental reality? To this, he replies: "By way of designation and realization."

"Likewise, the manifestation is the gross [reality]" means that designation (*prajñapti*), practice (*pratipatti*), and manifestation (*udbhāvanā*) are to be understood as the gross reality within the fundamental reality.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "For conventional reality is threefold," and so forth.
The establishment of the form of a non-existent object as "a pot" or "a cloth" is conventional designation (*prajñapti-saṃvṛti*).
Others maintain that conventional designation is the verbal expression of names according to the specific intrinsic natures of form, sensation, perception, and so forth.
Some hold that whatever is conventionally expressed in dependence upon verbal expression—such as "form" or "sensation"—is conventional designation.
And this very [nature] is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) because of its non-existence.

Regarding the conventional of practice (*pratipatti-saṃvṛti*): that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) by which form (*rūpa*) and so forth, as well as jars (*ghaṭa*) and so forth—which, though not existing externally to the manifestation of consciousness, appear as if they were external—are adhered to as real entities according to their established arrangement, that conceptual construction is the conventional of practice.
There is also the conventional of manifestation (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛti*).
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction.

Even for the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*), which transcends conceptual construction and verbal expression, its manifestation through such synonyms as "emptiness," "suchness," "with stains," and "stainless" is conventional disclosure (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛti*).
Through these three types of conventionality, the status of being conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satyatva*) in the fundamental reality (*mūla-tattva*) should be understood respectively.
Conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is worldly discourse (*vyavahāra*).
Designation (*prajñapti*) is a verbal expression. When there is no actual object, discourse by means of mere verbal expression is "conventional reality as designation" (*prajñaptisaṃvṛti*).
Precisely because of the non-existence of objects, that which is imagined through the convention of designation is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
Adherence to an object when no object exists is "apprehension" (*pratipatti*); the linguistic usage based upon that is "conventional apprehension" (*pratipattisaṃvṛti*).
Furthermore, this is the conceptual construction of adherence (*abhiniveśavikalpa*).
Therefore, by way of the conventionality of practice, the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).

That which indicates the ineffable realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) through terms such as "suchness" (*tathatā*) is its manifestation (*udbhāvanā*). The linguistic usage regarding the realm of phenomena by means of that [manifestation] is the conventionality of manifestation (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛti*).
Therefore, by way of the conventionality of manifestation (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛti*), the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) is conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

In this regard, it should be understood that the establishment of the inclusion and application of designation and the conventionality of manifestation occurs through occasion (*avasara*), and not by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus has conventional truth been explained.
Now, the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) must be explained; therefore, he says: "But the ultimate is from one [perspective].
This means that the imagined (parikalpita) and the dependent (paratantra) do not exist ultimately.
Furthermore, truth is to be understood as arising solely from the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

For what reason, then, is that perfected nature called the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)? To this he says: "The ultimate reality is considered to be threefold, according to object, attainment, and cognition."

For the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is threefold: the ultimate truth as object (*arthaparamārtha*), the ultimate truth as attainment (*prāptiparamārtha*), and the ultimate truth as practice (*pratipattiparamārtha*). Among these, the ultimate truth as object is suchness (*tathatā*).

Because supramundane knowledge (*lokottarajñāna*) is supreme and suchness is its object (*artha* or *viṣaya*), suchness is called the "ultimate truth," just as one speaks of the objects of the senses (*indriyārtha*).

Demonstrating that very point, he says: "considering it to be the object of supreme knowledge. The meaning is: because it is established as an objective support (*ālambana*), yet at that time the objective support does not exist as something separate from knowledge, just like the appearance of mere-cognition (*vijñaptimātra*).
For example, for those who accept that there is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), there are no appearances of form and so forth apart from the mere representation of form and so forth.
Nirvana is the ultimate attainment; its characteristic is the fundamental transformation (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) of the basis, which is the absolute, stainless suchness (*tathatā*).
Why is it the ultimate? To this he says: because it is the supreme object (*paramo 'rthaḥ*).
It is called "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*) because it is both supreme (*parama*) and an object (*artha*).
In this context, it is "supreme" because it is the foremost among all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, and it is an "object" because it is the purpose of the path;
for the path has the attainment of nirvāṇa as its purpose.
Nirvana, however, is the ultimate object (*artha*), because it is free from all faults that cause harm;
for that which is accompanied by faults is called "non-object" (*anartha*).
The path is the ultimate reality of practice (*pratipatti-paramārtha*).
What is the reason? Because its object (*artha*) is supreme. "Object" means either the objective domain (*viṣaya*) or the purpose (*prayojana*).
The objective domain is suchness (*tathatā*), and the purpose is nirvāṇa.
If the ultimate is being described by way of its objects, how could there not be mutual dependence? And if there is mutual dependence, what is the fault? It is the absence of certainty.
This will not be so, because of their mutual dependence, like the lion and the forest.

How can that which is unconditioned and called *nirvāṇa*, and that which is conditioned and called the "path," both be said to be the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)? For it is taught that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the perfected nature.
However, it is not logical for the path to be the perfected nature,
because it lacks the distinction between prior and posterior parts.
Therefore, the path is not the ultimate truth, nor is there an inclusion within the ultimate truth of that which is unperfected.
Therefore, he says: "The two [are established] through the perfection of being changeless and non-erroneous."
Thus it is said.
Alternatively, how is it that the unconditioned, called *nirvāṇa*, and the conditioned, called the "path," are both termed the "perfected nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)?
For the perfected nature is indeed suchness (*tathatā*).

And since this [emptiness] is the absence of the two characteristics in the dependent nature (*paratantra*), it is not tenable that the path and nirvāṇa possess the nature of the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*).
This is inexpressible because, in that case, the non-existence of the two is itself the perfected;
however, it is not the case that the perfected is merely the non-existence of the two, for that would be a negation of something else.
Therefore, that and the other are both perfected through the perfection of being changeless and non-erroneous; thus, both are connected as "perfected," namely the unconditioned nirvāṇa and suchness.
The unconditioned is perfected by way of the perfection of being changeless because it does not undergo alteration.
The conditioned is comprised within the Path and not otherwise;
it is "perfected" by way of the perfection of non-perversion—this is how it is connected.
To the question "How so?", he said: "Furthermore, because of the absence of perversion regarding the objects of knowledge."

Since one no longer falls into error regarding the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), the path (*mārga*) is also not [exclusively] perfected; therefore, there is no contradiction, as both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) possess the quality of being perfected (*pariniṣpannatva*) from different perspectives.

Regarding "the well-known reality" (*prasiddhatattva*): therein, that which is well-known in the world arises from one [cause], namely, from the imagined (*parikalpita*) alone, because it is impossible for it to exist otherwise than according to its designation. However, since its intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is not known, he says: "in whatever object," and so forth.
"Convention" (*saṃketa*) is the knowledge of the relationship between the name and the named.
"Familiarity" is the repeated observation of its application;
it is by means of an intellect that has entered into that [object]. But what is this entry of the intellect into the familiarity with conventions? It is through the recollection of that.

This is what is meant: by means of an intellect that follows upon the recollection of conventional familiarity, for all worldly people—whether they know the treatises or not—there is, in the state of verbal expression, a similarity to the perception of bamboo and so forth [in a rope], such as "this is indeed earth" and so on. This is the reality established by the world (*lokaprasiddha-tattva*);
it is accepted as being exactly so because it is established by worldly consensus.
"It is established by reasoning from the three [natures]," because reasoning is indeed applied with reference to all three types of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, the establishment of [the three natures] as being proven by reasoning is set forth through the three intrinsic natures (*svabhāvatraya*).
Since that is not understood, he says—showing it—"That which [is accepted] by the wise who are experts in the meaning of reasoning," and so forth.
In this context, "the wise" refers to those who are experts in the meaning of reasoning.
Those who are logicians and Mīmāṃsakas;
this is a subsequent statement explaining the intention of what preceded. Alternatively, "the virtuous" refers to seekers of what is wholesome.

Those skilled in the meaning of reason (*yuktārthapaṇḍita*) are those who possess expertise in what is produced through the fourfold reasoning that is not contradictory with the meaning of the four principles: dependence (*apekṣā*), causal efficiency (*kāryakāraṇa*), logical proof (*upapatti*), and the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
Logicians (*tārkika*), however, are those capable of affirmation and negation (*utthāpana-apohana*) who, relying on the teachings of the Tathāgata, compose treatises that are not erroneous.
Mīmāṃsakas are those learned in their own and others' treatises who examine excellence and defects.
Some do not read "Mīmāṃsakas. They say this: when it is said "of the wise" (satām), who then are the wise? To this he replies, "those learned in the meaning of reasoning" (yuktārthapaṇḍitāḥ).
And they are of two kinds, because they are established on the level of logic (tarka-bhūmi) and on the level of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā-bhūmi).

Therefore, they are called "logicians" (tārkika). Among them, some follow what is commonly established in the world; hence he says, "relying on the three means of valid cognition," meaning in accordance with the non-contradiction of the three means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, the three means of valid cognition are direct perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), and scripture (āgama).

In that regard, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) consists of that which arises from the five sense faculties and mental [perception], which is the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth. Inference (*anumāna*) is the knowledge of an object to be inferred by means of a logical mark (*liṅga*) possessing three characteristics. Scripture (*āgama*) is the word of a reliable person (*āpta*).
Furthermore, "authoritative persons" (āpta) are those who are free from the causes of falsehood.

Alternatively, it means "relying on the three means of valid cognition" because one establishes for another a probandum that is already established by means of a reason and an example well-known through perception, inference, and scripture;
thus, it is a "thing established by the reasoning that proves through logical possibility."
Logical proof (*upapatti*) is the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpa-liṅga*), because it is the means for establishing what is to be proven (*sādhya*).
The "proof of logical proof" (*upapatti-sādhana*) is the statement of the three-featured mark, since that [proof] is established by means of it.
Reasoning (*yukti*) is the method, which is the rule of formal application by which the three-featured nature of the mark is stated.
Alternatively, *upapatti* is that which cannot be otherwise;
*sādhanayukti* is the connection between the members [of a syllogism]. The analysis of the compound is: "the means of proof (*sādhana*) for the demonstration (*upapatti*)."
Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is: "the reasoning of logical proof (*upapatti*) itself is the method of demonstration (*sādhana-yukti*).
The inclusion of the term "logical proof" is for the purpose of distinguishing it from other methods of demonstration.

Thus, whatever object is established by means of the reasoning of logical proof, relying upon the three valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*), and which is one of the three natures—that is called "established by reasoning" (*yuktiprasiddha*).
The well-known reality has been explained.

Regarding the reality of the domain of purification (*viśuddhigocaratattva*): immediately after that, the object of purification must be explained; therefore, he says, "The reality of the domain of purification is twofold.

Demonstrating how it is twofold, he says: "The domain of the knowledge that purifies the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the domain of the knowledge that purifies the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The purification of the obscuration of afflictions is the abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions.

The term *kleśāvaraṇaviśuddhijñāna* means knowledge for the sake of purifying the obscuration of afflictions, or knowledge regarding the purification of the obscuration of afflictions; the meaning is that its purpose is the purification of the obscuration of afflictions, or that it has that as its cause. "The range (*gocara*) of that knowledge which purifies the obscuration of afflictions" means its object (*viṣaya*).
In the same way, the object of the knowledge that purifies the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna*) must also be explained.

In this regard, the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) consists of all the primary and secondary afflictions to be abandoned by the paths of seeing and meditation; therefore, that reality which is called the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—the object of the knowledge of seeing, meditation, and their preparatory stages belonging to Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—is the object of the knowledge that purifies the obscuration of afflictions.
It is to be known as the "knowable" (*jñeya*).
And that consists in its entirety of the five fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*).
These, moreover, are known as inner science (*adhyātma*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), logic (*hetu*), medicine (*cikitsā*), and all the fields of arts and crafts (*sarvaśilpakarmasthāna*).
Among these, non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*) which constitutes an obstruction to knowledge is the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

That purification consists of the knowledge comprised within the stage of practice through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) which accords with supramundane gnosis (*lokottara-jñāna*), as well as the subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Furthermore, that [knowledge] resides in the mental continua of Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas.

Since suchness (*tathatā*) is its object by way of its all-pervading nature and other meanings, suchness is the reality (*tattva*) of the sphere of the knowledge that purifies the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa-viśuddhi-jñāna-gocara*).

Since both types [of reality] within the sphere of purification have already been indicated by the statement of the reality of cause and fruit and by the statement of subtle reality, their further prescription would be redundant.
It is not redundant;
for that reality of cause and fruit and the subtle entity were stated according to their formal establishment (*vyavasthāna*).
In this context, it has been explained how obscuration is purified;
these two types of objects of purification are proclaimed to arise solely from the one perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Regarding this very point, he states the reason: for no other nature can be the object of the knowledge of purification.
What is the reason? Because the unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is defiled by the two stains of *dauṣṭhulya*, and because that which is imagined (*parikalpita*) does not exist.

However, since the reality of the object of purification (*viśuddhiviṣayatattva*)—which is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of the object of the two kinds of knowledge—is established solely on the basis of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*), the reality of the sphere of purification has been explained.

{The Reality of Compendium} Immediately following that, the reality of compendium (*saṃgrahatattva*) must be explained; therefore, he asks: "How is the reality of compendium to be understood within the threefold fundamental reality?

Demonstrating that the reality of compendium is subsumed within the threefold fundamental reality, he says: "The compendium of the two [consists of] the sign (*nimitta*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and the name (*nāman*)," and so forth in detail.
The inclusion [of all phenomena] occurs within the two—the dependent and the imagined.
Regarding that, the reality of inclusion consists of five entities; therefore, it says, "starting from the five entities as appropriate.
It should be understood that the five entities are included within the fundamental reality as appropriate, but not according to their sequential order.
Furthermore, there are five entities: the sign (*nimitta*), name (*nāma*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), suchness (*tathatā*), and right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Because all that is knowable is subsumed within these five kinds of entities, these five are called the "reality of inclusion" (*saṃgrahatattva*).
Among them, the sign consists of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), and the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
The sign (*nimitta*) consists in being the mutual cause of one another.
The name (*nāman*) is the designation that indicates that very sign—even though it is inexpressible—just as the winking of an eye does.

Conceptualization (*vikalpa*) refers to the minds and mental factors associated with the three realms, which involve the conceptual differentiation of the specific characteristics of the nature of the aforementioned signs.
Emptiness is suchness;
it is supramundane right knowledge that has suchness as its object.
Furthermore, the sequence of these is as follows: first is the sign, because it is the basis for the designation of defilement.

Because it is the designation of affliction (*saṃkleśa-prajñapti*), "name" follows immediately after; and because it is the conceptualization of the object that is the basis for the designation of affliction, "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) follows immediately after it. Furthermore, since that affliction is ceased by means of suchness and correct knowledge, some maintain that "suchness" and "correct knowledge" follow immediately after that.
The cause of error is the corruption of error; that is its cause.
Therefore, error has that as its cause, while knowledge therein is primordial peace.
According to others, the meaning of these five kinds of entities is expressed by this verse.

In that regard, the cause of the error comprised within internal consciousnesses such as the eye-consciousness is the external and internal objects, such as forms and the eye, which are themselves comprised within error. The cause of that external and internal error is *dauṣṭhulya* (corruption).
That, moreover, is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
The cause (*nimitta*) of that impression is precisely that same error regarding the external and internal;
therefore, verbal expression (*abhilāpa*) proceeds therein.
And by the power of verbal expression, the latent predisposition (vāsanā) persists within the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
"Quiescence by nature" refers to suchness (tathatā),
because the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is afflicted by its very nature.
And therein, "knowledge" refers to that knowledge which has suchness as its object and is comprised within the path.
Among those, signs and conceptual constructions are included within the dependent nature because they are produced by causes and conditions;
whereas name is included within the imagined nature.

Just as, because the object does not exist according to its name, the name is included within the imagined [nature], so too, regarding what was stated—that the inclusion by way of function (*adhikārasaṅgraha*) of the name is by means of the imagined [nature], but there is no inclusion of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—this does not contradict the statement that the imagined nature is not included among the five things beginning with the "sign" (*nimitta*), because it is established as being without intrinsic nature; for in that context, what is intended is inclusion by way of intrinsic nature.
[This refers to] "the reality of correct knowledge."

That which is always excellent is the reality (*satattva*), namely suchness (*tathatā*) and the non-dual gnosis that has emptiness as its object, as well as the pure mundane right gnosis subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-śuddha-laukika-jñāna*).

Because suchness and right gnosis are perfected respectively through the perfection of being changeless and the perfection of being non-erroneous, they are subsumed under the single perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Thus, the reality of inclusion (*saṃgraha-tattva*) has been explained.

Regarding the *prabhedatattva* (the reality of differentiation): now, since it is not understood how many kinds of *prabhedatattva* there are and how they are subsumed within the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*), he asks: "How is the *prabhedatattva* to be understood within the fundamental reality? To this he replies: "The *prabhedatattva* is sevenfold. As to how [it is so], he says: "The reality of manifestation (*pravṛttitattva*), the reality of characteristics (*lakṣaṇatattva*), and so forth," and so on in detail.

Furthermore, that very sevenfold suchness which was taught in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, from "suchness of occurrence" (*pravṛtti-tathatā*) up to "suchness of correct practice" (*samyak-pratipatti-tathatā*), is here stated to be the sevenfold reality of differentiation (*prabheda-tattva*), namely: the reality of occurrence up to the reality of correct practice.

Among these, the reality of occurrence is the beginningless and endless nature of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); and this itself is the suchness of occurrence, because there is never any connection with a beginning for it.
The reality of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-tattva*) is the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-nairātmya*).
Because it is non-different [from the ultimate], it is the suchness characterized by the fourfold aspects.
The reality of representation (*vijñapti-tattva*) is the state of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) of all phenomena.
Others maintain that the reality of representation is non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), because it is the basis for representation.
Because the reality of representation (*vijñapti-tattva*) is non-alterable, it is called the suchness of representation (*vijñapti-tathatā*).
The reality of structural arrangement (*sanniveśa-tattva*) is the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are arranged as suffering;
and that very suchness is so called because it is eternally just so.
The reality of wrong practice is the truth of origination;
it is that engagement with those conditioned formations through the perception of them as possessing virtues.
The reality of purification is the purification of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable.
Furthermore,
others maintain that the truth of cessation is the very nature of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), which is itself the nature of cessation;
and the truth of the path is the reality of correct practice.
The reality of representation (*vijñaptitattva*) is correct application (*yoniśaḥ prayoga*).
Others maintain that the reality of right practice (*samyakpratipattitattva*) and the reality of representation are simply the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).
These three realities are also always thus; therefore, they are called "thusness" (*tathatā*).

In that regard, the reality of manifestation (*pravṛttitattva*) should be understood as having two kinds of fundamental realities (*mūlatattva*), characterized by the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the dependent (*paratantra*).
Therein, "manifestation" is the beginningless continuity of births;
and because that [continuity] does not exist [ultimately], it is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
However, for those for whom that continuum is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) because it is produced by causes,
it is thus indicated that whatever the process of occurrence (*pravṛtti*) is, that is the reality of occurrence (*pravṛtti-tattva*).
Alternatively, the beginningless arising of afflictions, karma, and birth is called the occurrence of *saṃsāra*.

And since that [delusion] arises from the influence of adherence to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), he says: "The reality of activity (*pravṛtti-tattva*) is twofold; it is called the fundamental reality (*mūla-tattva*). Likewise, there is the state of being wrongly established in its arrangement (*sanniveśa-kupannatā*)."
False practice is wrong course.

Likewise, the fundamental reality is twofold; because suffering and its origin are produced by causes and conditions and because they have the imagined as their object, the reality of arrangement and false practice is subsumed within the two [fundamental realities].
One is the correct course characterized by the purity of representation.

The reality of characteristics (*lakṣaṇatattva*), the reality of representation-only (*vijñaptitattva*), the reality of purity (*viśuddhitattva*), and the reality of correct practice (*samyakpratipattitattva*)—these four realities are in fact one single fundamental reality, namely, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpannasvabhāva*).
Among these, the perfected nature is so called because the reality of characteristics and the reality of purity are established as being non-otherwise (*ananyathā-pariniṣpanna*).
Furthermore, the reality of representation-only and the reality of correct practice are perfected through their establishment as being free from error (*aviparyāsa-pariniṣpatti*).
Here, the equality with sentient beings is shown by means of the three realities of activity, manifestation, and false practice;
the equality with phenomena (dharma) is shown by means of the two realities of characteristic and representation;
and the equality with enlightenment (bodhi) is shown by means of the reality of purification.
Thus, the equality of wisdom is demonstrated by means of the reality of correct practice.
And it is said: "The equality of sentient beings is proclaimed by three [factors], while the equality of phenomena is shown by two;
likewise, the equality of awakening and wisdom is demonstrated by each one individually."
Thus it is said.
{The Reality of Skillfulness} Immediately after the reality of differentiation, the reality of skillfulness (*kauśalyatattva*) was indicated.
It was stated that the reality of skillfulness serves as the antidote to [false] views.

However, it is not yet understood how there are ten kinds of views of a self (*ātmadarśana*) regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth; therefore, he asks: "How is there a tenfold view of a self in these aggregates and so forth? To this, he says: "Unity, causality, being an enjoyer, agency, and sovereignty..."
It is also [the basis] for sovereignty, for the meaning of permanence, and for both affliction and purification.
"Because the view of a self exists in these regarding their being bound or liberated";
here, "in the aggregates and so forth" is to be connected [to the preceding].
This tenfold grasping at a self (*asadgrāha*) is called "grasping at what is non-existent" because the self does not exist.

If the self does not exist, one might ask: how can a grasping that is dependent upon such grasping proceed without an object? It is not, however, without an object; it proceeds with respect to the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth. Therefore, as an antidote to those [forms of grasping], the tenfold skillfulness regarding the aggregates and so forth has been taught.

How, then, is it determined that this grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*) refers only to the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, and not to a self (*ātman*) [existing] as a separate entity? Because when a self distinct from the aggregates and so forth is examined through reasoning, it is not perceived. Furthermore, since all the essential characteristics of a self’s activity—such as its nature as a self and so on—occur only within the aggregates and so forth, it is understood that the aggregates and so forth alone are the basis for the grasping at a self. Through these ten types [of views], the adherence to a self, namely the grasping at a self, proceeds, and not by others; therefore, skill regarding the aggregates and so forth should be known as the antidote to all grasping at a self.
Namely, "grasping at unity" refers to grasping at a solid self within the five aggregates of clinging; as its antidote, there is skill in the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*).
"Grasping at causality" refers to grasping at a self as the cause because of the eyes and so forth acting as instruments; as its antidote, there is skill in the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*).
In this same way, the opposition and the antidote should be stated for the others as well.
Alternatively, the grasping at causality is the notion that "everything proceeds because of the self.
Or, the grasping at causality is the thought that "the self is the cause of that wholesome or unwholesome karma which results in desired or undesired fruits in this life.
The grasping at being an experiencer is the notion that "the self is the experiencer because it is conscious."
The manifest and the unmanifest are the "food," because they are insentient.

Alternatively, the grasping at being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva-grāha*) is the notion that he for whom auspicious and inauspicious [results] arise through his actions is himself the enjoyer of those fruits.

The grasping at being an agent (*kartṛtva-grāha*) is the notion that the self alone is the agent of well-done and ill-done deeds; or, the grasping at being an agent is the notion that the self is that which, endowed with instruments and so forth, performs various actions.

The "grasping at independence" (*svatantra-grāha*) refers to the grasping that that which possesses autonomous mastery (*vaśitva*) is the self, or that the presiding authority (*adhikāra*) is the self;
or it is the grasping that this [self] possesses mastery over the production of a result that corresponds exactly to its cause.
The "grasping at sovereignty" (*adhipatitva-grāha*) refers to the view that the sovereign, the master, the lord (*īśvara*), is the self.
Or, the practice that conforms precisely to the fruit is the self because of its sovereign power (*adhipatitva*); thus, there is the grasping at sovereign power.

Regarding the grasping at permanence: although the self is impure due to the fivefold entities such as causes and so forth, it is nonetheless permanent; otherwise, there would follow the arrival of what was not done and the destruction of what was done.
Furthermore, the absence of memory and recognition would result.

The "grasping at being defiled or purified" refers to [the self] being the basis for defilement and purification. The "grasping at being a yogin" means that yoga is the fixing of the mind upon the self, or the restraint of the vital breath and the mind;
yoga is a specific conjunction of the self with the minds, and one who possesses this is a yogin.
And the grasping at being unliberated or liberated refers to the conceptual construction that there is liberation of the self from bondage.
How is it that these ten kinds of skillful reality (*kauśalyatattva*) are included within the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*)?
For skillfulness is proficiency regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth;
how then is it included within the three natures (*svabhāva*)? This is a question posed by one who does not perceive the connection.

Since those aggregates and so forth are included within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), they are designated by the term "skillfulness" (*kauśalya*) because they are the objects of skillfulness; however, they do not constitute that very skillfulness itself. Therefore, it should be understood that even the reality of unskillfulness (*akuśalyatattva*) is included therein by way of its thematic context (*adhikāra*), but not by way of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). This is just as it was stated that the reality of cause and fruit (*phalahetutattva*) and the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) are included within the three [natures].

Even so, it is not yet understood how they are included; therefore, he asks, "In what way are they included? and for this reason he says: "By means of the object of the imagined, the conceptualized, and the true nature (dharmatā), they are [included] within those.
This refers to the fact that those aggregates and so forth are included within those three natures.
