In this regard, one must first clarify that the aggregates (skandhas) are included within the elements (dhātus) and so forth, because they were taught first; and among those, form (rūpa) was taught first.
Therefore, it says: "Form is threefold.
How? It is imagined form (parikalpita-rūpa), conceptualized form (vikalpita-rūpa), and the form of true nature (dharmatā-rūpa).
In that regard, what is imagined form? It is the imagined intrinsic nature of form.
And that which is the apprehension of an object elsewhere than by name—therein the intrinsic nature of the object is imagined; because it is absolutely non-existent, it is called "imagined."
The "imagined form" (*vikalpitaṃ rūpam*) is that which is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) of form; this means it is bound by causes and conditions.
For what purpose, then, is this called "imagined form"? To this he says: "For therein the conceptualization of form is performed.

This is because, in the consciousness appearing as form, those who have not seen reality perform an adherence to form due to their lack of thorough knowledge of the designation "form," just as one grasps at a self among the aggregates (*skandhas*).
Therefore, in the dependent nature (*paratantra*), there is what is called "imagined form" (*vikalpita-rūpa*);
and "dharma-nature form" (*dharmatā-rūpa*) is that which is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) of form.
That [perfected nature] is emptiness, whose essence is the absence of both imagined form and the form conceptualized by imagination.
Just as with "form," so it is.

Just as form is divided into three ways and included within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), so too should feeling and the other aggregates, as well as the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*), be applied accordingly. Thus, the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the elements and bases; the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); the bases and non-bases; the faculties; the three times; the four truths; the three vehicles; and the conditioned and unconditioned—all these, beginning with feeling and the elements, each divided into three according to the distinctions of the imagined (*parikalpita*), the conceptualized (*vikalpita*), and the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), are to be included within the three natures.

In that regard, among the appearances such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth, that which is absolutely non-existent—the state of grasped and grasper—is conceptually constructed just as the state of being a grasped object is imagined in the appearances of form; this is *parikalpita-vedanā*, up to and including *parikalpita-vijñāna*.
That in which the conceptual construction of grasped and grasper is performed is *vikalpita-vedanā*, up to and including *vikalpita-vijñāna*.
*Dharmatā-vedanā* is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) of sensation.
In this way, it should be understood up to the consciousness of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-vijñāna*).
Likewise, this should be explained in detail, as applicable, regarding the elements (*dhātu*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), and so forth.

Whatever entity is denotable by a name—ranging from form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*) up to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—that too should be understood as having the imagined (*parikalpita*), the dependent (*paratantra*), and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) natures.

How so? In that regard, it is the *parikalpita* (imagined) because it is designated as having the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form and so forth; it is the *paratantra* (dependent) because it exists as the basis for designation and because it is dependent upon conditions; and its absolute absence of the state of being form and so forth is the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected). [Objection: But surely it is the *paratantra* itself that is designated by names such as "human" and so on, not the *parikalpita*; therefore, the conceptualization of the *parikalpita* is entirely purposeless. [Response: It is not purposeless.

In that regard, because the intrinsic nature of humans and so forth is superimposed, it does not exist in the very same way that the name functions toward the object. However, the foolish become attached to that intrinsic nature; and that is a false determination, not [a determination] by way of the actual reality.
Why is this so? Because the relationship between signifier and signified is excluded whether there is similarity or dissimilarity between name and object.

If words such as "tree" and their objects were of an identical nature, then, because the form of the name would not be distinct from the form of its object, the word's status as a signifier would be excluded, just as the object [is not a signifier];
and likewise, because the object would not be distinct from the nature of the name, its status as the signified would be lost, due to the absence of any restrictive cause.

Alternatively, if the name were something other [than the object], it would follow that there must be a designator for the name and a designated object for that designator, leading to the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Furthermore, if a single object has many names, or if a single name has many objects, it follows that they would possess multiple forms;
however, it is not tenable for a single thing to have multiple natures.

Regarding words that express non-existence (*abhāva*) yet possess meaning, there is either the non-existence of the object because that object is of the nature of non-existence, or else the existence of that object because of the existence of the name itself. Even though there is a difference in form, there is no cognition of an object corresponding to the word; for in that case, it is the word alone that is the "tree," not the object.
The referent (artha), however, is neither a tree nor a non-tree.
Therefore, the referent of the word "tree" cannot be the object of the cognition of a tree, because that referent does not have the nature of a non-tree.
And such being the case, there is an exclusion of the relationship of signifier and signified between the word and its referent.

Furthermore, if there were a lack of correspondence [between word and object], there would be no fixed rule for the signifier and the signified, because of the absence of a cause for such a restriction.
Moreover, a name could either produce an object or manifest it;
in that regard, it does not produce it, because naming occurs only when the object has already arisen.
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that even what has already arisen must arise again and again, because the name is applied repeatedly.
Nor does it manifest [the object], because a name is created after one has grasped the object; and it is not logical for something to be a manifester of what has already been grasped.
For this very reason, another person who does not know it does not grasp that same object by means of that very name.
It is not logical that the very same thing should be both the manifestor and the non-manifestor of that very same object.

Manifestors such as lamps do not manifest the object to be manifested in dependence upon linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). Furthermore, no fixed rule regarding manifestors is observed among objects to be manifested, such as jars and cloths; therefore, every object would be manifested by every name.
Nor is there a lack of restriction regarding odors and so forth;
for it is accepted that axes, water, and the like are producers of odors and so forth, rather than mere manifesters.
Therefore, it is understood that the adherence to the denoted and the denoter is as unreal in its object as the adherence to the grasped and the grasper.

Thus, because the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are not included within the three natures (*svabhāva*), the tenfold reality of skillfulness (*kauśalyatattva*) should be understood as being contained within the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*) alone.
This skillfulness regarding the aggregates and so forth has been taught as the antidote to the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).

However, the meaning of the aggregates and so forth—in which sense skillfulness regarding the aggregates serves as the antidote to the opposing view of self—has not yet been stated; therefore, that is now explained.
{The meaning of the aggregates (skandha):} From the beginning, they have the sense of being manifold, of being a collection, and of being delimited.
"From the beginning" is connected with the phrase "is stated at the outset. First of all, the aggregates are stated.
And these [aggregates] are to be understood through three meanings.

First, by the meaning of multiplicity: whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—it is called a "skandha" because the word *skandha* denotes many substances, such as those of the past, future, and so forth, in their manifold aspects.
Second, by the meaning of "heaping together," since it is said that they are "summarized" (*abhisaṃkṣipya*), it is a "skandha" in the sense of a collection.
"Completely condensed" means having been unified.
And the word "skandha" is connected with the sense of "delimitation.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction, [uniting] both meanings: the sense of being many and the sense of complete condensation.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because the aggregates (*skandha*), characterized by form and so forth, are established as distinct from those characterized by feeling and so forth.
"Distinct" (*pṛthak*) and "separately defined" (*paricchinna*) are synonyms.

What is the reason here that the meaning of "aggregate" is established by these three factors? For the meaning of "aggregate" is the sense of a "heap" (*rāśi*); therefore, it is established in this way.
And thus, the meaning of "heap" (rāśi) is observed in the world:
that which is manifold, collected together, and delimited is called a heap.
Just as it is with the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), so too should the aggregates of feeling (vedanā) and the others be understood.

In this regard, as a counteragent to that grasping at a single self—such as [the view] that "all this, whether past or future, is indeed the Person" (puruṣa)—it has been explained how skillfulness regarding the meaning of the aggregates (skandha) should be practiced. How so? Because the aggregates such as form are designated by condensing into a unity those things such as form which have distinct natures, such as being past and so forth.
And this threefold establishment of the aggregates is a counteragent to three kinds of delusion.
Delusion is threefold: delusion regarding unity, delusion regarding conventional reality, and delusion regarding the confusion of characteristics.
{The Meaning of the Elements (dhātu):} Immediately after the meaning of the aggregates (skandha), the elements were listed.

Therefore, immediately after the meaning of the aggregates, he states the meaning of the elements: "Furthermore, it is considered to have the sense of the seeds of the grasper, the grasped, and the grasping thereof."
The word "other" (apara) here is connected specifically with the element (dhātu), because it was mentioned immediately after the aggregates (skandha).
For this very reason, the author of the Commentary (bhāṣyakāra) also says: "Which is the other? The element."
The meaning of "element" (*dhātu*) is the meaning of "seed" (*bīja*). For example, when gold exists, it is called the "gold element," which is understood to mean the "seed of gold.

And that [element] is divided into three types according to the distinction of its fruits: the apprehending element (*grāhakadhātu*), the apprehended element (*grāhyadhātu*), and the element of the apprehension thereof (*tadgrāhadhātu*).
Among these, the meaning of the seed of the apprehender consists of the eye-element and so forth.
Those beginning with the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) and ending with the mind-element (*manas*) are the "eye-element and so forth.
Because they serve as the basis for grasping objects such as visible form, they are "graspers" (*grāhaka*).
They are called "elements" (*dhātu*) because they act as the causes for their own subsequent homogeneous instances, such as the eyes and so on.
The meaning of "seeds of the graspable" refers to the elements beginning with the form-element (*rūpadhātu*) and ending with the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*).
They are called "graspable" because they are the objects of the visual consciousness and the other sensory consciousnesses.
Furthermore, these are called "elements" (*dhātu*) because they likewise serve as the causal basis for their corresponding homogeneous [phenomena], such as visible forms and so forth.
The eye-consciousness element and the others have the sense of being the seeds for grasping those [objects].
Because their intrinsic nature consists in the apprehension of form and so forth, the eye-consciousness and the others, up to mental consciousness, are the graspers of form and so forth.

Furthermore, because they serve as the causes for the corresponding (sabhāga) eye-consciousnesses and so on, they are called elements—the eye-consciousness element and the others, up to the mental-consciousness element.
Others, however, say: the *ālayavijñāna*, perfumed by the karma of attachment to the eye and so forth, is the seed of the eye and so forth respectively;
likewise, the *ālayavijñāna*, perfumed by the karma of attachment to form and so forth, is the seed of form and so forth respectively;
and likewise, the *ālayavijñāna* itself, perfumed by the karma of attachment to the visual consciousness and so forth, is the seed of the visual consciousness and so forth respectively.
Thus, it should be considered that it is the *ālayavijñāna* alone that is denoted by the term "element" (*dhātu*), and not the eye and so forth.
The "element" is established in its threefold sense as seed for the purpose of dispelling confusion regarding agent, action, and object.

In this context, the preceding eyes and so forth serve as causes only for subsequent eyes and so forth; there exists therein no other self or any other cause whatsoever. Thus, through skill in the elements, the grasping after a cause in a self is eliminated.
{The meaning of the bases (āyatana):} Immediately after the meaning of the elements (dhātu), the meaning of the bases must be stated.
Therefore, he says: "Furthermore, [the meaning of the bases is] by way of being the gate for the arrival of feeling, the discernment of objects, and enjoyment."

Since there are many other [categories] such as the *āyatanas*, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and so forth, and because the word "other" (*apara*) is general, the question is asked: "What is the other?
In order to indicate that—because it was mentioned immediately after the *dhātus*—this word "other" refers specifically to the *āyatanas* by implication, he says: "The *āyatana*.
In that context, the six internal *āyatanas* are so called in the sense of being the doors for the arising of the experience of feeling (*veditopabhoga*).

The six external [bases] are so called in the sense of being doors for the enjoyment of the discernment of objects; the meaning of "āyatana" is the meaning of a door of arrival (*āyadvāra*). "Arrival" (*āya*) means coming (*āgama*).
They are called *āyatanas* because they extend (*tanvanti*) the experience of feeling and the discernment of objects.
There is a distinction between internal and external based on the differentiation of the doors through which the experience of the perception of feeling occurs.
For "feeling" (*vedita*) consists of pleasure, pain, and that which is neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
That very thing which is enjoyed is "enjoyment" (upabhoga);
the meaning is that it is experienced.
The internal sense bases (āyatana) alone have been taught as the gateway for the arising of that enjoyment of feeling.

Even though the objects serve as the gateways for their [the sensations] arising, the eyes and other sense organs are the bases because they are the uncommon causes by virtue of being subject to benefit or injury and by virtue of their proficiency; thus, when the eye and so forth exist, there is no experience of sensation through them.
Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the discernment of an object, because its nature consists in the grasping of the signs of an object.
That very perception experiences the object because its nature consists in the comprehension of the object.

The external bases (*bāhyānyāyatanāni*) are described as such because they serve as the gateways for the arising [of consciousness], whereas the internal bases are not so described even though they also possess the nature of being gateways for that arising. This is because, even when the internal bases such as the eye exist, there is an absence of the experience of discerning objects in the absence of those objects; therefore, these [external] bases are to be understood as such because they serve as the gateways for the feeling and the discernment of objects, along with their associated mental factors. For the apprehension of the pair [of object and subject] is primary.
Furthermore, the predominance of the sense-faculties (*grahaṇa*) is due to the experience of the fruits of karma and because they consist in the discernment of objects.

Since the conceptualization of an experiencer (*bhoktṛ*) proceeds by way of the experiencer’s enjoyment of the discernment of objects, the establishment of the bases (*āyatana*) is made according to these two types of meaning.
Thus, skill regarding the bases consists in this: the internal bases are the experiencer, and the external bases are the objects of experience.
The grasping at the self as an experiencer—the notion that there is no other experiencer—is thereby overturned.
As for the claim that the conventional designation of "experiencer" applies only to the basis [of the self] due to the benefit or injury of the sense-bases such as the eye, that is incorrect;
because form is negated, the sense-bases such as the eye are also non-existent, just like the self. Thus, this is not a valid objection.
Because here it is only the imagined form (*parikalpita-rūpa*) that is negated, and not the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpita-rūpa*).

In this context, the internal sense-field (*ādhyātmika-āyatana*) is the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) which, having been perfumed by the proliferation of the eye and so forth and projected by karma, has attained a specific transformation.
The external sense-field (*bāhyāyatana*) is the appearance of forms and so forth within the active consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*), which has that [internal field] as its cause.

That which is the appearance of common objects (*sādhāraṇārtha*) of the *ālayavijñāna*, as well as the appearance of sentient beings (*sattvapratibhāsa*), is called an external sense-field (*bāhyam āyatanam*) because it serves as the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for the arising of the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) that appear as grasped object and grasping subject; it is not, however, [called so] because it is their objective domain (*viṣaya*).
[Objection: But if this were so, it would contradict the statement in the Sūtra that "visual consciousness and the others arise depending on two things.
For the appearance of form and so forth is distinct from the consciousness, and it is not logical that the very same thing should be the condition for its own arising.
Because [the object] exists in the state of having arisen and does not exist in the state of not yet having arisen, and because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself,
one must necessarily admit that form and the other [objects] are distinct from the manifestation of consciousness.
This objection, too, is not valid.

Since the consciousness appearing as form and so forth deposits a latent impression (*vāsanā*) within the causal consciousness (*pratyayavijñāna*) for the sake of producing a subsequent homogeneous consciousness, and since a further consciousness appearing as form and so forth arises from the transformation of that latent impression,

it is stated that the "condition of consciousness" (*vijñānapratyaya*) consists of the latent impression deposited by way of having the nature of a consciousness-appearing-as-form; thus, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra.

In this way, the status of being an object (*ālambana-artha*) for that which appears as form and so forth is also established, because consciousness, in its aspect of self-appearance, serves as the condition.

Alternatively, just as proponents of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*) establish a simultaneous objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) with consciousness—despite the absence of a causal relationship between producer and produced—by means of the presence and absence of the one corresponding to the presence and absence of the other; so too here, even though there is no relationship of producer and produced between consciousness and that which appears as form and so forth, the status of condition and conditioned is established because the presence and absence of the former do not deviate from the presence and absence of consciousness.

Because the appearance as form (*rūpa-nirbhāsa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are non-different, there is no primary dissimilarity with the example; this is not [the case] because of a metaphorical attribution of difference.

For instance, because it serves as the basis for the conceptual construction of the grasped and the grasper (*grāhya-grāhaka-vikalpa*), the consciousness of dreams, illusions, and cities of Gandharvas, though ultimately non-different, is established as if differentiated by way of the forms of the grasped and the grasper, in the sense of being the object and the subject. Thus, there is no contradiction in other cases either. Furthermore, the relationship of object and subject is everywhere merely metaphorical; it does not exist in a primary sense.
Neither consciousness that has arisen nor that which has not arisen can take an object as its support;
for, because it perishes immediately after arising, it does not persist at the time of the action, and thus lacks existence.
Furthermore, an object—whether arisen or unarisen—is in neither case suitable to serve as a support.
Because that which has arisen does not endure and that which has not yet arisen does not exist,
an act of apprehension without a basis is not tenable.

Even for one who holds that the relationship of object and subject is simply the relationship of cause and effect by virtue of mere existence, the object of a present consciousness would be purposeless, since it is already established as being of the same nature as that consciousness.
Even for that which is in the process of arising, [consciousness] would be purposeless because of its non-existence.
It is not purposeless for that which is in the process of arising, because when an object exists, consciousness acquires a self-nature that manifests as that [object].
If the manifestation of the object in consciousness were caused by an external entity, then consciousnesses of the past, the future, dreams, and so forth would be devoid of form.
Therefore, existence [of the effect] must be due to the absence of [external] objects;
for an effect is not produced by incomplete conditions, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*),
nor is it logical for that which is non-existent to possess the status of a condition.
Furthermore, an external object is not the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of consciousness, because consciousness occurs even in its absence;
therefore, it must be admitted that all consciousness is independent of an external object as its objective support, just as in the case of those suffering from ophthalmia.
{The Meaning of Dependent Origination} Immediately after the meaning of the sense-bases (*āyatana*), the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) must be explained; therefore, he says:
"The meaning of dependent origination is [to be understood] from the non-superimposition and non-denial of cause, fruit, and effort."
It is for the purpose of producing conditions that are effortless, impermanent, and efficacious.
As it is also stated in the Sūtra: "When this exists, that comes to be;
with the arising of this, that arises—namely, conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces," and so forth in detail.

Demonstrating that this dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is intended as the negation of superimposition and denial regarding causes, effects, and activities, he says: "The meaning of dependent origination is the meaning of not superimposing or denying causes, effects, and activities.
By the word *āyāsa* (exertion), activity is expressed.

Among these, the superimposition of a cause consists in imagining a person (*puruṣa*), a Lord (*īśvara*), an atom (*aṇu*), or primordial matter (*pradhāna*) to be the cause, while setting aside ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other [links of dependent origination].
Explaining this very point, he says: "Because of the conceptualization of a discordant cause for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth, ending with old age and death.
For the meaning is that a permanent cause, such as a *puruṣa* (primordial spirit), would be discordant—that is, dissimilar—to the impermanent formative forces and so forth.
Alternatively, a cause is observed to be something like a seed for sprouts and the like, which depends upon a transformation of its own nature.

Furthermore, since there is no modification of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of that which is eternal, the attribution of causality to what is not a cause constitutes the superimposition of causality (*hetusamāropa*).

The negation of causality (*hetvapavāda*) results from the conception of causelessness, because by accepting that formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth arise without a cause, the fact that ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth are the causes of formations and the rest is denied.
The superimposition of the effect (*phalasamāropa*) results from the conception that formations and so forth—which possess a self—proceed with ignorance and so forth as their conditions.

Some maintain that when a self exists, the fact that the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth proceed with ignorance (*avidyā*) and other conditions as their causal basis, yet [the self] does not exist, constitutes the superimposition (*samāropa*) of a self upon the fruits of the formative forces and so on.

Others hold that because the formative forces and so forth—possessing a self—are conceived as proceeding with ignorance and other conditions as their causal basis, either by way of inherence in the substance of a self (*ātmadravya-samavāyitva*) or by way of being the agents of its benefit and injury, this is a superimposition upon the fruit.

Still others hold that it is a negation of the fruit (*phalāpavāda*), based on the conception that the formative forces and so forth, which have ignorance and other conditions as their causal basis, do not exist at all.
For example, it is like those who deny good conduct, bad conduct, and the next world, claiming: "There is no good conduct, there is no bad conduct, and there is no next world.

This is the superimposition of action (*kriyāsamāropa*), because one imagines that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors have an active function in the production of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth.

If one were to imagine that ignorance and the others produce a real entity (*vasturūpa*) as something distinct from themselves in the production of the formative forces and so forth, such would indeed be the superimposition of action.
The denial of activity (*kriyāpavāda*) arises from the conceptualization of [factors] as being devoid of efficacy;

for it is a denial of activity because one conceptually constructs the factors of ignorance and so forth as being devoid of efficacy, even though they possess the capacity to produce the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) by their mere existence.
It should be understood that because of the absence of that [denial], there is neither superimposition nor denial.
Because there is an absence of superimposition and denial regarding its causes, fruits, and activities, it should be understood as being free from superimposition and denial.

Thus, this skill in dependent origination should be understood as the antidote to that grasping at agency which occurs either in a self or in something else apart from ignorance and the other factors.
For herein, there is no self or anything else, distinct from ignorance, that acts as the agent of wholesome and unwholesome karmas.
Apart from the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), there is no other agent of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Thus, it should be stated accordingly in all cases: that from ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors—which are effortless, impermanent, yet efficacious—the formative forces and so forth arise.

{The Meaning of the Possible and the Impossible} Since the meaning of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*) must be explained immediately after dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), he says: "Of the undesirable, the desirable, and purification," and so forth.
The possible and the impossible are to be understood by way of seven kinds of dependence (*pāratantrya*).
In this context, the possible (*sthāna*) is the cause (*hetu*), and the impossible (*asthāna*) is the non-cause (*ahetu*).
As it is said in a verse: "One should speak the truth, one should not become angry, and one should give even a little when asked;
by these three stations here, one shall go to the assembly of the gods."
It is understood that this refers to "by means of reasons.
Alternatively, "possibility" (sthāna) is occurrence, while "impossibility" (asthāna) is non-occurrence;
skill regarding these is skill in the possible and the impossible (sthānāsthānakauśalya).
The state of being dependent is *pāratantrya*;
it means reliance on another.
And although that is sevenfold, it is subsumed within the three types of dependence: dependence regarding karma, afflictions, and birth.

Regarding the phrase "therein, dependence upon others [leads to] the undesirable": the undesirable refers to the miserable destinies (*durgati*). Demonstrating that going there consists in the reality of misconduct and constitutes dependence upon others, he says: "because one goes to a miserable destiny even against one's will by means of misconduct—such as the taking of life—which is comprised within the actions of body, speech, and mind, along with its preliminary and subsequent stages."
The miserable destinies consist of the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals.
Because these are exclusively characterized by suffering, no one has a desire to go there.
Nevertheless, due to the power of karma and because [evil] conduct is the cause for the miserable destinies, one goes there solely through the force of karma, even against one's will.
Regarding "dependence on another in what is desired" because one goes to a happy destination through good conduct: "what is desired" refers to going to a happy destination;
a happy destination consists of gods and humans.

Good conduct consists of abstaining from the taking of life and so forth, along with their preliminary and concluding stages; it includes acts such as giving, honoring, and showing respect toward teachers, gurus, and those endowed with excellence; and it comprises specific virtues such as loving-kindness and compassion.
Dependence upon good conduct means that for those who seek [a higher rebirth] otherwise, there is no going to a happy destination in the absence of good conduct;
for birth in a happy destination is strictly contingent upon good conduct.
"Dependence regarding purification," and so forth. Purification is the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The five hindrances (*nivaraṇa*) are: sensual desire, ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt.

By combining *styāna* (sloth) and *middha* (torpor) into one, and likewise *auddhatya* (restlessness) and *kaukṛtya* (remorse), there are five [hindrances]. They are called "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*) because they obscure the side of wholesome qualities without distinction. Furthermore, when distinguished, they respectively conceal: delight in the life of a renunciant; physical and vocal actions appropriate thereto; correct practice when properly exhorted by fellow practitioners of the holy life; lack of dejection at the time of *śamatha*; non-distraction at the time of *pragraha* (exertion); and spontaneous flow at the time of both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Without having abandoned or relinquished these, and so on until one has not cultivated the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).

Because the instruction uses the term "up to" (*yāvad*), this includes the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), and the powers (*bala*).
Regarding the phrase "because of not making an end to suffering":
the end of suffering is that state where suffering does not exist, which is *nirvāṇa*; "not making" it means its non-attainment, the sense being that one does not attain *nirvāṇa*.

Alternatively, "the end of suffering" means that because from that suffering no other suffering is joined [to it], one does not produce such suffering; the meaning is that one does not produce suffering that is without reconnection (*apratisandhika*). Dependence on others regarding purification refers to being bound by the abandonment of the five hindrances (*pañca-nivaraṇa*). Dependence on others regarding simultaneous arising refers to two things that are neither prior nor posterior; the meaning is that they arise together.
Regarding the statement that two Tathāgatas and two wheel-turning kings do not arise simultaneously in a single world-system:

some maintain that for the two Tathāgatas, the intended world-system is the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*), whereas for the two wheel-turning kings, it is the four-continent world (*cāturdvīpaka*).
Others maintain that even for two Tathāgatas, it is only within a single four-continent world-system (*cātur-dvīpaka*).

For the Blessed Buddhas, by virtue of their sovereignty over the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), manifest both perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) and final nirvana (*parinirvāṇa*) through their emanation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) in each of the four-continent world-systems throughout the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*).
This is because the purpose of Bodhisattvas—descending from the Tuṣita heaven and taking birth among humans—is fulfilled within a single four-continent world-system.
This is the same for all other four-continent worlds as well.

Therefore, they believe that the Blessed One, having attained perfect enlightenment in Akaniṣṭha itself, displays through his emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) everything—such as rebirth in the Tuṣita heaven and the taking of birth among humans—in all the four-continent worlds contained within the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system.

Furthermore, regarding the simultaneous appearance of Buddhas and wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*), there is a dependence on others due to their being subject to karma that leads to a common destruction (*samasaṃvartanīyakarma*).

Regarding dependence in terms of sovereignty: because a woman cannot become a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) and so forth, since karma conducive to becoming a universal monarch has the capacity to yield its maturation (*vipāka*) only in a male body.
Indeed, a woman is not capable of enjoying the [seven] jewels, such as the jewel of the queen, and so on;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), being Śakra and other such states are included.
Regarding attainment, there is dependence because a woman does not realize the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha or the Unsurpassed [Buddha-enlightenment].
Attainment (*prāpti*) is the realization of the state of a Buddha or a Pratyekabuddha;
in this regard, such attainment belongs to a man, but not to a woman.

For, due to the absence of association with it, she is respectively incapable of being a master of the three levels [of existence] like a rhinoceros, because she lacks the capacity for realization without a teacher due to her small wisdom, and because she is accessible to all deceitful people.

Furthermore, regarding the state of dependence in active manifestation: this is because one endowed with right view does not manifest killing and so forth, whereas an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) does manifest them.
One who is endowed with right view is one who has seen the truth.
"Killing" refers to the taking of life;
by the word "etcetera," [the other precepts such as] taking what is not given and so forth are included.

Those [acts] such as killing, which have the nature of bodily and vocal actions, do not manifest for one endowed with right view, because through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the afflictions that give rise to misdeeds such as killing have been abandoned. They do manifest for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) because those [afflictions] have not been abandoned.
Furthermore, that non-abandonment is due to the fact that the path which serves as their antidote has not yet arisen.

Thus, skill in the "impossibility" (*asthānakauśalya*)—which follows the dependence on others regarding what is undesirable and so forth—is the antidote to the grasping at independence in [entities such as] a primal man (*puruṣa*) or a Lord (*īśvara*).
For if anyone were independent, they would not go to an evil rebirth because of misconduct;
the same should be said for other cases as well.

{The Meaning of the Faculties (Indriya)}: Immediately after the explanation of the meaning of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), the meaning of the faculties must be stated; therefore, he says: "The faculty is of twenty-two kinds," beginning with the eye-faculty and ending with the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Here, moreover, the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*) is in the sense of sovereignty (*ādhipatya*).
To the question, "What, then, exercises sovereignty over what? he says: "By way of the objects of grasping, abiding, connecting, enjoyment, and the two types of purification."
Thus [it is said].

And here, regarding the phrase "in the sense of the sovereignty of the two," it should be understood that the word *ādhipatya* (sovereignty) has been elided for the sake of conforming to the meter of the verse.
Therefore, the author of the Commentary says: "because of their sovereignty over those."

Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of apprehension": here the word *artha* signifies "purpose. This indicates that the sense-faculty (*indriya*) is the cause (*nimitta*) with the purpose of apprehension.
In the same way, this should be stated elsewhere as appropriate.
Regarding the phrase "in those," meaning in the apprehension of objects and so forth, "sovereignty" (*ādhipatya*) means superior power; thus, sovereignty means the state of being a cause.
From form (*rūpa*) up to mental phenomena (*dharma*), these are the objects such as form and the rest.
The apprehension of these [objects] is the consciousness of the eye and so forth.
In that regard, the six [faculties], beginning with the eye, possess sovereignty;
because the eye is the basis for the consciousness that discerns all varieties of form without exception, it has superior power over forms and so forth, and is thus called an "indriya" (faculty).
But a blue form does not become the objective support (*ālambana*) for the cognition of a yellow form and so forth.
In the same way, this should be stated in detail as appropriate for the ear and the other [senses] as well.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)," it refers to its proper locus.

Furthermore, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the capacity for reconnection in subsequent moments that are similar to each preceding moment within the continuum of maturation (*vipākasantāna*), provided there is no cause for its interruption—this being the nature of the latent impressions of karma (*karmavāsanā*).
Regarding the statement that the life-faculty has sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) over duration, he states the reason for this very point: "Because by its sovereignty there is non-death.
Non-death is the continued persistence of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*) projected by prior karma.

Even though food and the like are causes for the maintenance of sentient beings, they do not possess the status of a faculty (*indriya*), because even when they are present, the continued existence [of life] does not occur if the life-force (*āyus*) has perished;
furthermore, in the realms of form and formlessness, the continued existence [of life] occurs solely from the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), even in the absence of physical food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
Furthermore, it is not logical for contact (*sparśa*) and the other [mental factors] to exercise sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) in that regard,

because the continued existence of sentient beings is possible even in the absence of contact and the rest during the states of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), and among the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñika*). Therefore,
the sovereignty of the female and male faculties (*strīpuruṣendriya*) lies in the linking of the lineage (*kulasandhāna*).
Since the non-interruption of the lineage occurs upon the birth of a son, the birth of a son is the "continuation of the lineage.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "due to the predominance of procreation.
A certain portion of the body-faculty itself acquires the designation of the female or male faculty due to a specific kind of predominance.
Wherever the female faculty (*strīndriya*) and the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) exist, there is the establishment of a family (*kulavyavasthāna*);
by virtue of that, the family lineage does not cease.
Furthermore, even among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), the establishment of a family exists when the female and male faculties are present, and not when they are absent.

For gandharvas and the like do not possess sovereignty over that [rebirth], because even when a gandharva is present, there is an absence of the capacity to produce offspring among eunuchs and others due to the non-existence of the female and male faculties (*strīpuruṣendriya*). Furthermore, although food and so forth have sovereignty [over the body], they are not faculties because they are not enumerated among sentient beings. Regarding experience, the faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*) [are sovereign].
The term "sovereignty" (ādhipatya) is the subject under discussion.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Because of the experience of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma.
The five faculties of sensation (vedanendriya) are: pleasure, pain, mental joy, mental grief, and equanimity.
In that case, the fruit of wholesome and unwholesome karma is experienced because its nature is that of experience.
Name-and-form does not have sovereignty over that [experience], because it is merely the equipment for feeling;
and its status as equipment exists because maturation has feeling as its primary constituent.
Mundane purity is the abandonment of mundane afflictions.
In that regard, "of faith and so forth" refers to the five faculties—faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
The term "sovereignty" (ādhipatya) carries over [from the previous context].
Because they are produced by the mundane path as the antidotes to lack of faith and so forth;
others say it is because they are produced by the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).

Regarding the statement "non-knowledge in supramundane purification" in the case of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the others, the term "sovereignty" (*ādhipatya*) continues to apply.

The abandonment of the afflictions by means of the supramundane path is supramundane purity. In that regard, there is the predominance of the three faculties— the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known"—
because they are respectively subsumed within the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning.

In that regard, with respect to their occurrence based on the specific distinctions of the supports such as the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage] and so forth, these nine faculties— namely, faith and the others, along with mind, pleasure, mental joy, and equanimity— are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*) on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) on the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
For the Yogācāras, however, the arrangement is otherwise:
in the two faculties—the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*)—there are ten faculties.
By adding the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasya*) to the nine previously mentioned, they become ten.
The faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), however, consists of exactly nine.

In that regard, during the fifteen moments of the path of seeing—which constitute the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) consisting of the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)—there are the mental faculty (*manaindriya*), the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), and whichever among the faculties of pleasure, joy, displeasure, or equanimity is possible according to the specific basis such as the *anāgamya* stage. Furthermore, the faculty of displeasure (*daurmanasyendriya*) should be understood as being comprised of the longing for higher liberations following the levels conducive to penetration at the time of preparation. Thus, these are the ten types of faculties as they occur.
Because one has begun to know that which was previously unknown, it is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

That same tenfold faculty, from the first moment of the sixteen moments of the path of seeing up until the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), is called the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*) within the path of training (*śaikṣamārga*), because there is no longer any previously unknown object to be known.

On the path of no-more-training (*aśaikṣamārga*), the remaining faculties—excluding the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*)—acquire the designation of the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Regarding the "faculty of one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*), it is called the faculty of one who has already known;
thus, for one who is skillful in the faculties, the grasping at a supreme lord (*adhipati*) among Puruṣa, Nārāyaṇa, Īśvara, and so forth, is turned away.

{The Further Meaning} Since the three time periods must be explained immediately after the sense objects, he says: "And likewise another [meaning] by way of the utilization and non-utilization of fruit and cause."
Thus:
therein, the cause is the reason for birth;
the fruit is birth itself, not included [within the cause].
The utilization of the cause is the giving of the fruit;
the utilization of the fruit is the complete exhaustion of what has been experienced.
Since the cause and its fruit are of such a nature and have passed away, the "past time" is so called in the sense of the utilization of that fruit and its cause.
In that same manner, the future time-period is to be understood in the sense of the non-application of both fruit and cause;
whereas the present time-period is the present birth.

Since the cause has already yielded its fruit, it should be understood in the sense of the application of the cause, and because that fruit—the present birth—continues to persist, it should also be understood in the sense of the application of the fruit.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the establishment of the time-periods (adhvan) with respect to moments is based on the fact that entities exist as cause and effect at every moment.
In this context, the "utilization of the cause" consists in the production of its own fruit;
the "utilization of the fruit" consists in the destruction of the fruit immediately after its birth.

Thus, it is established that the past time is so called in the sense of having already employed the fruit and the cause, while the future time is so called in the sense of not yet having employed the fruit and the cause.
It should be understood that there is no employment of the fruit and the cause because the effect has not yet arisen, and for that which has not arisen, there is no destruction.
Regarding the phrase "in the sense of the employment of the cause and the non-employment of the fruit," the employment of the cause consists in the production of the effect.
Because the effect is not destroyed, there is no utility in the fruit [of action].
Thus, for one skilled in the [three] time-periods (*adhvan*), the grasping after a permanent self (*nityātman*) is overturned,
because nothing else is perceived apart from the time-periods.

{The Meaning of the Four Truths} Immediately after the meaning of the three times, the meaning of the four truths must be explained; therefore, he says: "By way of sensation, its cause, its object, and the practice toward that cause," and so forth.
In the world, it is commonly established that sensation has the meaning of suffering.

And because of the statement in the Śāstra, "Whatever is felt here is suffering," the author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakāra), demonstrating that within the establishment of the Truths, all contaminated (sāsrava) feelings—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-pleasant-nor-painful—along with their causes (sanimitta), constitute the meaning of the Truth of Suffering, says: "In that regard, the Truth of Suffering is [defined] by way of feeling together with its cause. From what [source] is it known that "all feeling is suffering"? To this he replies: "On the grounds of the statement, 'Whatever is felt here is suffering.'"

And that feeling is suffering according to its occurrence through the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*);
or it is suffering simply by way of the suffering of conditioned formations.
Furthermore, the causes of feeling (*vedanā-nimitta*) should be understood as those phenomena that serve as the basis for feeling (*vedanā-sthānīya-dharma*).
Phenomena to be experienced as pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant are the bases of feeling.
Thus, the five aggregates have been explained as the truth of suffering;
by way of the practice directed toward that [suffering], they constitute the truth of origination.
By the word "that," the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya) is connected.
The practice by which suffering is produced is the truth of origination (samudayasatya).
Furthermore, that [practice] consists in the nature of the agitation of body, speech, and mind, preceded by craving (tṛṣṇā) for feelings and for those phenomena that are the basis of feeling.
In brief, it is said that the truth of the origin of karma is that which gives rise to existence (*bhava*). By way of the cessation of those two, there is the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
"Of those two" refers to the truths of suffering and its origin.
"In the sense of pacification" means in the sense of non-arising.

Thus, cessation is said to be twofold because it is characterized by the non-arising of suffering together with its causes: as "with remainder" in the sense of the pacification of the origin (*samudaya*), and as "without remainder" in the sense of the pacification of suffering (*duḥkha*). The truth of the path is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering and its origin, in the sense of being the antidote to those two aforementioned factors, suffering and its origin. Consequently, for one who is skilled in the truths, since only defilement (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) are understood, the grasping at defilement and purification other than that [i.e., the four truths] is turned away, because of the absence of such [grasping].

{The Meaning of the Three Vehicles} Immediately after the meaning of the truths, the meaning of the three vehicles is explained; therefore, he says: "by means of knowledge [consisting of] qualities and defects and non-conceptual knowledge," and so forth.
The word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is connected with both:
namely, by means of the knowledge of qualities and defects, and by means of non-conceptual knowledge.
Alternatively, it should be understood that the word "vikalpa" (conceptualization) is elided in the middle [of the compound].
In that context, [it refers to] "by others and by oneself through the knowledge of virtues and faults"; for this very reason, he says in the commentary, "according to what is appropriate.
Therein, it means "through the knowledge of the virtues and faults of nirvāṇa and saṃsāra."
In this context, by the term "nirvāṇa," both the path and cessation are subsumed, just as they are by the term "tranquility.

Therein, regarding cessation, there is knowledge through aspects such as peace; regarding the path, there is knowledge through aspects such as leading to liberation; and regarding nirvāṇa, there is knowledge of its qualities.
Furthermore, cyclic existence (saṃsāra) is also characterized by the nature of suffering and its origin.

In that regard, knowledge through the aspects of impermanence, suffering, and so forth, as well as through the aspects of origin, conditions, and so forth, constitutes the knowledge of the defects of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
"Having heard from others" means having heard from Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others about the virtues of nirvāṇa and the aforementioned defects of cyclic existence.
"For the sake of departure" means for the sake of exiting cyclic existence.

Regarding the term "Śrāvaka-vehicle" (*śrāvakayāna*): it is called the Śrāvaka-vehicle because one goes forth by relying on the voice of another; this demonstrates its distinction from the Pratyekabuddha-vehicle.

"By that very [means]" refers to the knowledge of the virtues and faults of nirvāṇa and saṃsāra; the Pratyekabuddha-vehicle is for the purpose of going forth by oneself, without having heard it from others—namely, from Buddhas or Bodhisattvas.
The phrase "without having heard it by oneself" serves as a qualification distinguishing it from the Śrāvaka-vehicle.
"By non-conceptual knowledge" means that non-conceptual knowledge arises from the penetration of the ineffable nature of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
It is called the "Great Vehicle" (Mahāyāna) because it leads to deliverance by itself, without having heard it from another.
In this context, the phrase "by knowledge" constitutes its distinction from the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.

Others, however, say: the Śrāvaka vehicle is the departure [from saṃsāra] after hearing from another by means of non-conceptual knowledge that has the selflessness of persons as its object and is free from the conceptualization of virtues and faults;
the Pratyekabuddha vehicle is the departure by oneself, independent of hearing [the teachings];

and the Mahāyāna is said to be the departure by oneself by means of non-conceptual knowledge that has the selflessness of phenomena as its object and which brings about the attainment of non-abiding nirvāṇa.
This explanation contradicts the Bhāṣya;
for one who is thus skilled in the three vehicles, the grasping at the self as a "yogi" is turned away through the vision of mere yoga.

The latter [of the two types of objects] is said to be comprised of enjoyment (*bhoga*). These two are "enjoyment" because the remaining consciousnesses experience them as objects of dominance (*adhipati-vastu*);
or alternatively, they are "enjoyment" because objects such as food and drink are enjoyed.
That consciousness appearing as such is comprised within experience.

This—along with its designation, its cause, its objective image (*nimitta*), and its associated mental factors (*samprayoga*)—should be understood as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because it is comprised within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
And the "associated factors" are the mental concomitants (*caitta*).
He shows that the conditioned is not merely that [form] alone.

For what, then, is its cause? It is the cause of the sets of names and so forth (*nāmakāya* etc.), because they indicate the essential nature and specific qualities of those [phenomena]. Furthermore, it is the cause of the mind and mental factors—designated as mind (*manas*), apprehension (*udgraha*), and conceptualization (*vikalpa*)—which, following those [sets of names], adhere to essential natures and specific qualities.

Some maintain that the grasping of signs and conceptualization (*manaudgrahavikalpa*) is the cause (*nimitta*) of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), because it nourishes the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) therein.

Others, however, consider it to be the cause of designation (*prajñapti*), because it makes known the specific characteristics of intrinsic nature; for it is said that perception (*saṃjñā*) consists in the grasping of signs.

The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which comprises the basis, the body, and objects of enjoyment, is the causal sign (*nidānanimitta*) because it nourishes the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
The mind (*manas*), as well as apprehension and conceptualization, are the objective signs (*ālambananimitta*) in the sense that they take [the storehouse consciousness] as their objective sign.
And the objective-sign-of-the-objective (*ālambanālambananimitta*) is so called because it takes both [the storehouse consciousness and the objective sign] as signs in a dual manner.
In that context, "mind" (*manas*) is that which always has the aspect of cogitation (*manyanā*). That which constantly cogitates "I" and "mine" is called the "mental faculty" (*matam*).

And it is associated with the five [defilements]—self-delusion, self-view, self-love, and self-pride—as well as with the five omnipresent factors: feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention.

Apprehension (*udgraha*) refers to the five groups of sensory consciousness; because their characteristic is the grasping of the specific nature of objects, they cannot be described as self-cognized, and thus they are called apprehension.
Conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is mental consciousness;
this is because its characteristic is the conceptualization of the specific and general characteristics of phenomena (*dharma*).
All of this—the sign (nimitta) together with its conceptual designations and causes—is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) because it is produced by karma and the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Furthermore, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) consists of cessation (*nirodha*), which is peace (*praśama*), and suchness (*tathatā*), which is the object of that peace. It is logical that cessation has the nature of peace, because its characteristic is the pacification of suffering along with its signs. How is suchness said to be the "object of peace"? Because it is the object (*artha*) of peace.

But surely, there is no connection whatsoever between cessation (*nirodha*) and suchness (*tathatā*); how then can it have the sense of "quiescence" (*praśama*)? Because suchness is the objective support (*ālambana*) of the path.
Furthermore, how is the path itself quiescence? Because one is quiesced by means of it.
Nirvana is quiescence because it is the state of being quiesced.
And because it brings about pacification, the path is called "pacification" (praśama).
Thus, through this analysis of the compound, both Nirvana and the path are grasped by the single term "pacification.
Furthermore, is the truth of the path conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? It is conditioned, because it is something to be produced.
If one were to say that it is "unconditioned" because it is not produced by karma and afflictions, and because it is characterized by the unconditioned, there would be no fault.
For this reason, it should be understood that skill regarding the aggregates and so forth is knowledge concerning the aggregates and so forth.
From the beginning, [this knowledge] has the purpose of [understanding] multiplicity, condensation, and delimitation.
Thus it should be stated in detail in all instances.
{The Summary Meaning of Reality} The summary meaning of reality:
in brief, reality is twofold;
in detail, it is said to be tenfold.
Therefore, he says that in brief it is twofold: the mirror-like reality (ādarśatattva) and the object-of-vision reality (dṛśyatattva).
Among these, the fundamental reality (mūlatattva) is the mirror-like reality;
furthermore, that consists of the three natures (svabhāva).
Why, then, is that called the reality of the mirror (*ādarśatattva*)? Because the remaining realities, such as the reality of characteristics (*lakṣaṇatattva*) and so forth, are seen therein.

As for the ninefold reality of the visible (*dṛśyatattva*), which was previously specified as beginning with the reality of characteristics—why is it called the reality of the visible? Because it is seen within the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*); thus, the reality of characteristics is the reality of the visible free from conceit (*nirabhimāna*).
Therefore, one becomes free from conceit.

The reality of the visible, characterized by non-perversion, consists in the absence of the perversions of superimposition and denial regarding the person and phenomena, the grasped and the grasper, and existence and non-existence.
For that [reality] serves as the antidote to the perversions such as [the notion of] permanence and so forth.

The reality to be perceived for departure via the Śrāvaka vehicle is the reality consisting of cause and fruit; the departure of the Śrāvaka occurs through the cultivation of the penetration of the four noble truths. The reality to be perceived for departure via the Mahāyāna is the subtle and coarse reality.

One departs by means of the Mahāyāna because of maturing sentient beings through the coarse conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) and liberating them through the subtle ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Regarding the reality of what is to be seen for the purpose of refuting opponents and the reality of what is established, it is asked: "How so? To this it is said: "Because of refutation by means of reasoning based upon examples."
The example for refutation is that which is well-known in the world;
reasoning is based on words established through logic;
and the reality to be perceived by illuminating the Mahāyāna is the reality that is the domain of pure knowledge.
For that scripture which elucidates what is other than the domain of the knowledge that purifies the obscuration of afflictions is the Mahāyāna. Furthermore,
it is the reality of the entry into and the reality of the comprehension of all aspects of the knowable.
And that consists of five entities because it penetrates all that is knowable therein:
the reality of the visible as the illumination of non-falsity, and the reality of differentiation;
for by means of these, there is the illumination of both the non-false suchness and the non-other suchness of phenomena.
And the reality of the visible as the entry into all the underlying intentions regarding the basis for the grasping of a self is the reality of skillfulness.

For by means of that, one enters the basis for the grasping of a self through the gateway of all underlying intentions; as was previously stated, the occurrence of the grasping of a self with respect to the aggregates and so forth is due to ten underlying intentions.
The statement of the summarized meaning of the realities is for the sake of easy retention, as it draws out the text from its meaning.

And for the sake of non-delusion and non-exhaustion: for one who has clearly observed the limits of the subject matter, neither exhaustion arises nor does delusion, since [knowledge] is produced through the comprehension of the detailed explanation according to the initial summary.
Thus, reality has been explained.
The third chapter, on Reality, in the Madhyāntavibhāga-ṭīkā following the Āgama, composed by the venerable master Sthiramati, is completed.

The Fourth Chapter: The Analysis of the Cultivation of the Antidotes, the States, and the Results. Regarding the cultivation of the antidotes (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*): immediately after the exposition of reality (*tattva*), the cultivation of the antidotes must be explained, as well as its states and the attainment of its results. Therefore, this fourth chapter is commenced for the purpose of explaining those.
Because it was mentioned immediately after reality, and because it is connected to the cultivation of the antidotes, the states and the attainment of the results are also listed here.

In order to demonstrate that the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣa*) are intended as the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) in the Sūtra, it is said: "The cultivation of the antidotes consists in the nature of the factors conducive to awakening. For these, when cultivated, are capable of abandoning the aforementioned opposing obstructions; thus they are called "antidotes.
Furthermore, they are thirty-seven, ranging from the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the noble eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

Cultivation (*bhāvanā*), nourishment (*bṛṃhaṇā*), application (*āropaṇā*), practice (*abhyāsa*), and frequent performance (*bahulā-kriyā*) are synonyms. This [cultivation] must now be explained, as it was indicated immediately after reality (*tattva*).

For what reason is the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) alone mentioned first, and not the other cultivations of the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*)? It is said: "In that regard, first of all, because of coarseness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and because it is the cause of craving (*tarṣa*)," and so forth.
"In that regard" means in the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
The meaning of the word "first" (*tāvat*) is the sense of sequence.
First, the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is explained.
"Subsequently, for others as well" means that because they do not understand the virtues of nirvāṇa and the defects of saṃsāra,
fools— due to their clinging to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as being pleasant, pure, permanent, and a self— have a longing for the enjoyment of existence and fear the goal of nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, this lack of understanding regarding virtues and faults, as well as the attachment to pleasure and so forth, ceases through the vision of the truths; therefore, for the sake of generating weariness toward saṃsāra and for the sake of turning one toward nirvāṇa, the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) alone is taught at the beginning in order to enter the four truths.
For it is through the body that dysfunction (dauṣṭhulya) is manifested;
dysfunction is a state of being ill-situated.
For in this way, since the body is indeed subject to transformation as it is conditioned day by day, corruption is manifested through the body;
and thus, by means of the investigation of the body, one enters into the Truth of Suffering.
To the question "For what purpose is this?", he says: "Because it has the characteristic of formations accompanied by corruption."

Because the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) consists of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) accompanied by dysfunction (*sadauṣṭhulya*), and because dysfunction is manifested through the body, one enters into the truth of suffering by means of examining the body. Since dysfunction is not understood, it is said: "Dysfunction is indeed the suffering of conditioning (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).
Conditioning refers to the arising of formative forces (*bhāvanā*).
And that total ruin is itself the "suffering" (*duḥkhatā*) of the noble ones (*ārya*), because it is disagreeable due to its being a state of corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*).
As it has been said: "This birth is a misfortune, for when there is birth, there exist enemies such as old age, death, disease, calamity, and bondage.
Those misfortunes would not exist if you did not exist; for if a tree does not arise, there can be no destruction by fire, forest fires, or wind."

"By that" refers to the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), and not to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) or the suffering of suffering itself (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), because those two do not pervade [all things] and because they have the suffering of conditioned formations as their cause.

Noble ones perceive every contaminated (*sāsrava*) entity as suffering, but not the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), because the Truth of the Path is the antidote to the arising of birth; however, ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) do not perceive it so, because they rely on a basis for cognitive inversion (*viparyāsa*).
It is also stated in the Sūtra: "In brief, the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandhāḥ*) are suffering."
Others say that the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is lack of functional flexibility (*akarmaṇyatā*).
Still others maintain that it is not lack of flexibility, but rather *dauṣṭhulya* (corruption).

What is the reason? Because lack of functional flexibility is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), one must necessarily admit that its state of being associated with outflows arises from a causal seed.
However, that [state] occurs occasionally within the continuum of objects even without seeds due to the improper consumption of food and so forth;
yet it cannot be considered *dauṣṭhulya* because it is not associated with outflows (*anāsrava*).
Therefore, it is held that the seed of the phenomena associated with outflows, which resides within the *ālayavijñāna*, is what constitutes *dauṣṭhulya*.
This body, accompanied by pleasure, pain, and neither-pleasure-nor-pain, is the fruit [of that].
Therefore, by means of this body—which arises moment by moment and provides the occasion for pleasure and so forth—that *dauṣṭhulya* (corruption) is manifested; the meaning is that it is made known.
It is just as a seed within a granary hole is [made known] by its sprout.
Therefore, one enters into the Truth of Suffering through the investigation of the body.

Regarding this, the reason is stated: "Because it has the characteristic of conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) accompanied by corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*)," which means that its nature consists of conditioned factors together with their seeds.

Indeed, the suffering inherent in conditioned factors (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is called "corruption" because it is permeated by and is the cause of both the corruption of change (*vipariṇāma-dauṣṭhulya*) and the corruption of suffering itself (*duḥkha-dauṣṭhulya*).
For this very reason, because of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), the Noble Ones perceive every contaminated thing as suffering.

Thus, through the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāya-smṛtyupasthāna*), one enters into the Truth of Suffering. This is with the intention that feeling (*vedanā*) born from contact associated with ignorance is the cause of craving; for that which is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) is not its cause.
In this regard, pleasant feeling is the cause for craving for union with and non-separation from it; painful feeling is the cause for craving for non-union with and separation from it;
and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the cause for craving for its continued state, as well as for craving for union with and non-separation from it, upon the completion of some [experience].

Because of the statement, "Touched by painful feeling, he delights in sensual pleasure," even painful feeling becomes a cause for craving for pleasure. By examining that [feeling], one enters into the truth of the origin (*samudaya-satya*).

For, while thoroughly examining feeling in terms of its intrinsic nature, its cause, its effect, its impermanence, and its suffering, one enters into the truth of the origin; the meaning is that one understands craving to be its effect.

For craving is stated in the Sūtra to be the truth of origination. What is the origination of suffering? It is recited: "Craving, which leads to renewed existence, is accompanied by delight and passion," and so forth.
In this way, one enters into the truth of origination through the application of mindfulness to feeling.
"The mind is the basis for the adherence to a self.
Since there is no other self characterized by qualities such as permanence, the mind alone is the objective support for the adherence to a self.
Therefore, through the investigation of that [mind], one enters into the Truth of Cessation as being peaceful.
He states the reason for this very point: "because of the removal of the fear of the annihilation of the self.
For, through the investigation of impermanence and so forth regarding the mind, attachment to a self is turned away and the perception of suffering arises.
Consequently, because the fear of the annihilation of the self has been removed, one enters into the truth of cessation as peace, since it is merely suffering that is being annihilated.
Thus, through the application of mindfulness to the mind, one enters into the truth of cessation.
Through the examination of phenomena (*dharmaparīkṣā*), by means of the absence of delusion regarding phenomena that are defiled and those that are purified, one enters into the truth of the path.
In this context, defiled phenomena (*sānkleśika-dharma*) are the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
The purifying [factors], however, are those such as love (*prema*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which serve as the antidotes to the afflictions and secondary afflictions.

Having understood the relationship of adverse factors and their antidotes between those defiled and those purifying states, one becomes oriented toward the Truth of the Path, which is the means for the absolute abandonment of all calamities.
Thus, through the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), one enters into the Truth of the Path.
In this context, "entry" refers to the realization of the specific characteristics of each truth.

Therein, the cultivation of the application of mindfulness to the body is performed by way of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; also by way of its nature as consisting of many impure substances, its impure seed, its impure outflow, its cause for the persistence of impurity, and its transformation into impurity; and also by way of its lack of essence like a mass of foam, its destination, and its mode of birth.

Furthermore, the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness regarding feelings, mind, and phenomena is practiced by way of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; also by way of their specific characteristics, causes, results, realms, stages, and locations; and also by way of being wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, as well as by way of the discordant factors and their antidotes.
For Bodhisattvas, however, the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness is likewise performed through the aspect of non-apprehension for the purpose of abandoning conceptual construction.

Although the foundations of mindfulness have wisdom as their intrinsic nature, they are called "foundations of mindfulness" because these wisdoms are established by the power of mindfulness; thus, they are termed "foundations of mindfulness."
{The Four Right Efforts} Immediately after the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness, the cultivation of the right efforts is taught.
For what reason? To this he says: "Because, when the adverse factors have been fully understood," and so forth.
[This is] by means of the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness.
Even though it is stated without distinction, it should be understood as being through the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) alone.

This is because, when the adverse factors (*vipakṣa*) and their remedies (*pratipakṣa*) have been thoroughly known in every way—by means of the realms (*dhātu*), stages (*bhūmi*), and locations (*avakāśa*); by means of the aspects (*ākāra*) such as the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and so forth; likewise by means of the aspects of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) realms, stages, those in training (*śaikṣa*), and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and so on; and by means of the distinctions between the contaminated and uncontaminated realms, stages, those in training, those beyond training, and so forth—for the purpose of abandoning the adverse factors.
The departure from the adverse factors (*vipakṣa*) here consists in the severance of the continuity of those [factors] already arisen and the non-arising of those not yet arisen.
And for the sake of approaching the remedies (*pratipakṣa*):
the approach to the remedies consists in the continuation of the continuity of those [remedies] already arisen and the arising of those not yet arisen.
"Vigor functions in four ways" means that the operation of vigor is fourfold, distinguished by whether the adverse factors and their antidotes have already arisen or have not yet arisen.
The phrase "for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen," and so forth, demonstrates through scripture that vigor itself functions in these four ways.
By this detailed statement, the connection with the remainder of the text is established.
In this regard, the remaining summary is as follows: "He generates desire for abandonment, he exerts himself, he arouses energy, he upholds the mind, and he correctly applies himself.

Thus, the detailed explanation is: "He generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil and unwholesome states," and so forth; likewise, the detailed explanation is: "He generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states," and so forth.
For the stability, increase, non-forgetfulness, and fulfillment of wholesome states that have arisen, one generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses energy, uplifts the mind, and applies right effort;
this constitutes their stability and non-decline once they have arisen.
"Increasing further" means arising in a continuous succession;
"fulfillment" means reaching the highest excellence.
"He generates desire" indicates the perfection of energetic effort characterized by reverence and earnestness.
