Likewise, "knowledge, the formative forces, and the unconditioned—which is their remedy—are the grasped and the grasper" is an extreme.
And here, by the inclusion of the limit "up to old age and death," consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth are implied.
Consciousness as the grasped and the grasper is an extreme.
Likewise, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and old age and death—as the grasped and the grasper—are extremes.
Among these, ignorance consists in the non-comprehension of the truths and the jewels.
Volition (*cetanā*)—whether meritorious, non-meritorious, or neutral—is called "formative forces" (*saṃskāra*) because it conditions rebirth.
In this way, following the explanation of the characteristics of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the other factors should also be explained in detail.
Knowledge (*vidyā*) is untainted cognition (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
The knowledge of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) itself is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
Alternatively, he says "that is the antidote" in order to distinguish it from other unconditioned things.
Others, however, consider that because it possesses the quality of non-arising, all eight kinds of the unconditioned are included here.
The antidote, however, is untainted volition (*anāsravā cetanā*), because it performs the formative activity of cultivation (*bhāvanābhisaṃskaraṇa*).
The view that its cessation is either the apprehended object (*grāhya*) or the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*) constitutes an extreme.
By the word "that" (*tat*), the factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) and ending with old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are connected.
It is not known whether cessation is an entity or a cause; therefore, he says: "by which that name-and-form is ceased.
But by what, then, is that name-and-form ceased?
By the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) which is the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to name-and-form.
Knowledge and ignorance—these two are non-dual and indivisible; this very thing, together with its retinue, is here the path.
And because cessation occurs by means of this, it is called "cessation" (*nirodha*). But what, then, is the "extreme" (*anta*) in this context?
This very thing is the adherence to the grasped and the grasper.
What is the reason? Because it proceeds by superimposing a non-existent duality upon ignorance and the other factors, which are by nature non-dual.
Thus, the extreme of the grasped and the grasper is twofold, distinguished by the black and white sides.

In that regard, within the dark side (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), there are twelve factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*), from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). Likewise, within the bright side (*śuklapakṣa*), there are also twelve types through the distinction of the cessation (*nirodha*) of ignorance and so forth, namely, the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death. And here, because ignorance and the others are ceased by means of it, the path (*mārga*) which serves as their antidote is itself expressed by the word "cessation" (*nirodha*).
The phrase "for the sake of abandoning that" refers to the Middle Way as being taught for the sake of abandoning the extremes of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).
Since that [Middle Way] is not understood, he says: "Knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*)—these two are non-dual.

To the question, "How are knowledge and ignorance, up to old age and death and their cessation, non-dual? he replies: "Because knowledge, ignorance, and the rest lack the nature of the grasped and the grasper."
The non-existence of those [factors] such as ignorance and so forth, however, is due to their having non-duality as their fundamental nature (*advaya-prakṛti*).

Alternatively, "knowledge" (*vidyā*) and "ignorance" (*avidyā*) are of an imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); therefore, by the equality of the non-existence of knowledge and ignorance—which both possess an imagined nature—knowledge and ignorance are non-dual.

In this same way, it should be stated for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and the unconditioned, for consciousness (*vijñāna*) and its cessation, and so on up to old age and death (*jarā-maraṇa*) and its cessation.
What, then, is the middle way here?

It is this very knowledge that "knowledge and ignorance are non-dual; they are not to be divided. Thus, knowledge is not to be produced, nor is ignorance to be ceased; the formative factors (*saṃskāra*) and so forth are not to be abandoned.
The knowledge that "this cessation is not to be attained" is precisely what constitutes non-differentiation.
Regarding the statement "defilement is threefold":

therein, affliction (*kleśa*) is called defilement because it is the cause of the defilements of karma and birth, because it is itself afflicted, and because it is the cause of harm to both oneself and others. Karma, too, is called defilement because it is produced under the sovereignty of affliction, because it is the cause of birth, and because it is itself afflicted in some cases.
Birth, too, is a defilement because it is caused by karma and afflictions, and because it serves as the locus for all calamities.

Furthermore, in order to demonstrate the threefold division of the defilement of afflictions, he says: "The defilement of afflictions is threefold," and so forth. In that context, "views" refers to the five views, beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Attachment, aversion, and delusion alone are the cause, because they are the cause of sorrow and so forth, and because they are the cause of renewed existence (*punarbhava*).

Others, however, say: the cause of attachment and the rest consists of sense-objects favorable to them, improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), and the latencies (*vāsanā*) of attachment and so forth residing in the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
They describe it thus: the cause of attachment and the rest is that which appears as such.
Furthermore, the aspiration for renewed existence and the longing for renewed existence—
of which the antidote is the emptiness of knowledge (*jñāna-śūnyatā*), as explained in detail—
therein, the emptiness of knowledge is the antidote for those [afflictions] already seen.
Knowledge whose object is emptiness is the emptiness of knowledge (*jñāna-śūnyatā*).
Knowledge that is signless (*jñānānimitta*) is the antidote to the signs of passion and so forth, because of the departure from all signs;
or alternatively, knowledge whose object is the signless is the signlessness of knowledge.
Because its object is the emptiness of imagined passion and so forth, the knowledge that is wishless is the antidote to the aspiration for renewed existence (*punarbhava*).
Knowledge free from the aspiration for renewed existence, or having the emptiness of renewed existence as its object, is the "wishless knowledge" (*jñānāpraṇihita*).

Karmic affliction (*karma-saṃkleśa*) is the formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) of wholesome and unwholesome actions; it is the accumulation, the production, and the formative activity of those wholesome and unwholesome karmas which project renewed existence.
The antidote to this is the non-conceptualization of knowledge (*jñānānabhisaṃskāra*).
That knowledge by which one does not perform karma that leads to renewed existence is "the non-conceptualization of knowledge.
Furthermore, its object is suchness (*tathatā*).
The defilement of birth (*janmasaṃkleśa*) consists of: (1) birth in a new existence (*punarbhavajāti*), which is the mind at the moment of linking (*pratisandhicitta*);
(2) the moment-by-moment arising of the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) for one who has been born, from the point after the connection of the rebirth-linking until death;
and (3) the continuity of renewed existence (*punarbhavaprabandha*), which is the state of existence at death (*maraṇabhava*) accompanied by the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, immediately following that is the intermediate state (*antarabhava*);
from that, in turn, arises the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*).
However, for one who has attained the formless meditative absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the state of rebirth follows immediately after the state of death (*maraṇabhava*) itself.
The antidote to this consists of the non-arising of knowledge (*jñānājāti*), the non-production of knowledge (*jñānānutpāda*), and the lack of intrinsic nature in knowledge (*jñānāsvabhāvatā*).
In that regard, the knowledge that all phenomena are unarisen by virtue of their being of an imagined nature—that is, the knowledge whose object is emptiness—is "the non-arising of knowledge.
Knowledge whose object is the emptiness of imagined phenomena is "the non-production of knowledge," because through it one penetrates that non-production.
The knowledge that the continuity of entities (bhāvaprabandha) lacks intrinsic nature because it is non-existent, like the son of a barren woman—that is the "lack of intrinsic nature of knowledge.
This sevenfold knowledge, beginning with the emptiness of knowledge, is the antidote to the aforementioned sevenfold opposition consisting of views and so forth.
The removal of this very threefold defilement of afflictions, karma, and birth, which is divided into seven types, is purification.
"Removal" (*apagama*) means abandonment (*prahāṇa*).

Others, however, consider that suchness (*tathatā*), the path (*mārga*), and nirvāṇa are purification (*vyavadāna*); for through different analyses of the compound, such as "that in which [defilements] depart" (*apagacchati asmin*) or "the departure itself" (*apagatiḥ eva*), suchness and the others are said to be purification.

In that context, by the phrase "by means of the emptiness of knowledge (*jñāna-śūnyatā*) and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes the emptiness of knowledge, the signlessness of knowledge (*jñānānimitta*), the wishlessness of knowledge (*jñānāpraṇihita*), the non-conditioning of knowledge (*jñānānabhisaṃskāra*), the non-arising of knowledge (*jñānājāti*), the non-production of knowledge (*jñānānutpāda*), and the lack of intrinsic nature of knowledge (*jñānāsvabhāvatā*).

Regarding the phrase "the phenomena of the emptiness of the knowable (*jñeya-śūnyatā*) and so forth," here too the word "and so forth" includes the emptiness of the knowable, the signlessness of the knowable (*jñeyanimitta*), the non-conditioning of the knowable (*jñeyānabhisaṃskāra*), the non-arising of the knowable (*jñeyājāti*), the non-production of the knowable (*jñeyānutpāda*), and the lack of intrinsic nature of the knowable (*jñeyāsvabhāvatā*); these are the characteristics of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).
By means of these three kinds of defilements, as appropriate, emptiness and so forth are not produced;

that is to say, by the aforementioned defilements of afflictions, karma, and birth, the phenomena such as the emptiness of objects of knowledge—which exist as distinct entities—are not produced by the emptiness of cognition and so forth.
What is the reason they are not produced?

Because they are, by their very nature, emptiness and so forth; that is to say, they have, by their very nature, the intrinsic character of being free from [wrong] views and the like. Why is this? To this he says: because the *dharmadhātu* is by nature undefiled.
Therefore, the phenomena such as the emptiness of the knowable (*jñeya-śūnyatā*) are empty by their very nature; they are not produced by the emptiness of knowledge (*jñāna-śūnyatā*) and so forth.
"According to what is appropriate" (*yathāyogam*) is the meaning of "appropriateness" in this context.

By means of the emptiness of knowledge, the emptiness of the knowable—which is liberated from and devoid of the defilement of views—is not produced, because the emptiness of views is itself by nature the absence of views.

Thus, by means of the signlessness of knowledge (*jñānānimitta*), the signlessness of the object of knowledge (*jñeyānimitta*)—which is devoid of the signs of passion and so forth—is not produced, because emptiness is itself signless by its very nature. By means of the wishlessness of knowledge (*jñānāpraṇihita*), the wishlessness of the object of knowledge is not produced, because emptiness is by its very nature characterized by wishlessness. By means of the lack of formative activity of knowledge (*jñānānabhisaṃskāra*), the lack of formative activity of the object of knowledge is not produced, because emptiness is by its very nature characterized by the absence of formative activity.
The non-arising of the object of knowledge is not produced by the non-arising of knowledge, because arising is, by its very nature, characterized by the emptiness of arising.

The non-arising of activity is not produced by the non-arising of knowledge, because the moment-to-moment arising of mind and mental factors is, by its very nature, characterized by non-arising through emptiness.
The lack of intrinsic nature in the object of knowledge is not produced by the intrinsic nature of knowledge, because rebirth is, by its very nature, without intrinsic nature due to emptiness.
Alternatively, [the phrase] "according to the appropriate [application] by means of the threefold affliction" is the detailed explanation.

By means of the sevenfold division of the afflictions of defilement (*kleśa*), karma, and birth, whichever phenomenon among the knowable phenomena such as emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is associated with whichever specific division of affliction, that phenomenon is not produced by the cognitions of emptiness and so forth; rather, it is realized.

In this regard, there is the association of the cognition of emptiness with the affliction of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃkleśa*); and so on, up to the association of the cognition of the lack of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatā*) with the continuity of renewed existence (*punarbhava-prabandha*).
What is the reason it is not performed? Because those phenomena, such as emptiness and so forth, are by their very nature [empty]; this is because the *dharmadhātu* is by its very nature undefiled.
In that regard, views are not made empty by the emptiness of knowledge, because they have emptiness as their very characteristic by nature.
The sign of passion and so forth is not made signless by the signlessness of knowledge, because the *dharmadhātu* is by its very nature signless.

In this way, up until the continuity of further existence (*punarbhava-prabandha*), its lack of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatā*) is not produced by means of knowledge, because even when the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*) has not yet arisen, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is simply non-existent.

And since this is so, if one imagines that the *dharmadhātu* is either defiled or purified, that is an extreme (*anta*). Why? To this he says: "Because for that which is by nature undefiled, there is neither defilement nor purification, just like space."

In order to avoid this extreme, there is the Middle Way, which does not make phenomena empty—such as the emptiness of the unknowable (*ajñeyaśūnyatā*) and so forth—which consist of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), by means of their opposite, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) consisting of views and the like;
rather, even when knowledge (*vidyā*) has not yet arisen, phenomena themselves are empty by way of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which is the very form of views.

Thus, when one does not make phenomena signless by means of a signless [agent], but rather phenomena themselves are signless; and so on, until when one does not make phenomena selfless by means of selflessness, but rather phenomena themselves are selfless—this kind of discernment, Kāśyapa, is called the "correct discernment of phenomena" (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*).

In this way, by illuminating the existence of knowledge and the existence of its opposite as being devoid of an imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*), the rejection of the extremes of superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*) is accomplished.
This other sevenfold duality of conceptual extremes follows from the variety of conceptual distinctions just enumerated.
To demonstrate this variety of conceptual distinctions, he says: "For example, conceptualization regarding existence is an extreme, and conceptualization regarding non-existence is also an extreme.
To the question "How so? he replies: because of the conceptualization that "the person exists for whose destruction emptiness [is taught]," or that "selflessness does not exist."
If one does not make phenomena empty because they are empty by nature through means of emptiness, then there must exist a person (*pudgala*) for whose destruction emptiness exists;
or else, selflessness (*nairātmya*) would not exist either, due to the absence of a person.
For there is no counteragent that exists without an object of negation.
Therefore, one must necessarily either accept the existence of a person (*pudgala*) or the existence of selflessness (*nairātmya*);
the conceptualization of their existence or non-existence is an extreme.
For the purpose of avoiding these two extremes of the conceptualization of existence and non-existence, this is the middle way (*madhyamā pratipad*).
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, emptiness is certainly not for the sake of destroying a person;
rather, it is emptiness itself that is empty—such is the detailed reading of the Sūtra.

In this regard, emptiness is not for the destruction of a defiled person, nor for the production of a purified person, because the person exists only as a conceptual designation (*prajñapti-sat*), like an army or similar constructs, and thus lacks both production and destruction. Rather, it is emptiness itself that is empty, and not by means of a "person" superimposed by the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), since that [person] is absolutely non-existent.
And having established it thus, emptiness is not a non-entity in the sense of being devoid of the self-nature of persons and phenomena, because it is free from those [imputed natures].

Nor is it a mere absence in the sense of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*), for he explains that the perfected nature is the very essence of emptiness by demonstrating its existence in exactly the same way throughout the three times—namely, as "emptiness of the past limit," "emptiness of the future limit," and "emptiness of the present.
Alternatively, it is because its existence is demonstrated in the same way across the states of ordinary beings, those in training (*śaikṣa*), and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

In this context, the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is the prior limit, the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is the subsequent limit, and the state of one in training (*śaikṣa*) is the present.

Because the intrinsic nature of existence and non-existence is thus empty, it is said: "Kāśyapa, rely upon emptiness," because it is the object of non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), and not upon the person (*pudgala*), because that is a mere designation.
The phrase "conceptualization regarding cessation is an extreme; conceptualization regarding pacification is an extreme" follows [from the previous context].
To the question "How so?", he says: "Because of the fear of emptiness arising from the conceptualization of that which is to be abandoned and its abandonment.
In this context, "that which is to be abandoned" (*praheya*) refers to what is to be pacified, and "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) refers to the act of pacifying.
Having conceptualized phenomena as being that which is to be abandoned and emptiness as being the abandonment, fear of emptiness arises.
How so? For the threefold defilement is that which is to be abandoned.
If it were empty by nature, then, like a person (*pudgala*), it would not be something to be abandoned.
Consequently, due to the absence of anything to be abandoned, there would be an absence of abandonment; thus, fear arises regarding emptiness.
This too is indeed an extreme.

Why? Because beings are attached to the idea that phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and feeling (*vedanā*), which merely revolve within the nature of consciousness, exist substantially (*dravyataḥ*). Not knowing that these imagined forms—form and so forth—are by their very nature non-existent like a self (*ātman*), they fear their emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Therefore, the simile of space is given in order to avoid these two extremes of conceptual construction.
For example, Kāśyapa, suppose a certain man were terrified of space and, beating his breast, were to cry out and say, "Remove this space!
What do you think, Kāśyapa, is it possible to remove space? He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "In just this way, Kāśyapa, these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are terrified of emptiness; I declare that they have fallen into a state of great distraction."
For what reason? Because, Kāśyapa, they wander in emptiness itself and yet are afraid of that very thing.
This is what is meant: just as space cannot be removed because it pervades all forms, so too emptiness is established at all times within all phenomena and cannot be removed.
Nor can emptiness be established by the abandonment of phenomena; therefore, he shows that this is a groundless fear.
Conceptualization is also the end of that which is to be feared; and therefore, conceptualization is also the end of the fear arising from that which is to be feared.
What [is meant]? It is understood that "conceptualization is the end. That from which fear arises is called "that which is to be feared" (*trāsya*).
"Bhaya" (fear) is that from which one fears;
therefore, regarding that which has an undesirable result, one will be terrified of it, and regarding that fear, whoever conceptualizes it constitutes an "extreme.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Because of being terrified by imagined form and so forth, due to a dread of suffering."
For the foolish, having conceptually imagined forms and so forth as real entities, imagine fear and undesirable results arising from them;
consequently, out of a dread of suffering, they tremble with fear of those forms and their signs.
To avoid these two extremes of conceptual construction, the analogy of the painter is given.

For example, Kāśyapa, it is as if a painter, having himself created the terrifying form of a yakṣa, were to fall headlong, terrified and trembling by that very form, and fall into a state of delusion.

In the same way, Kāśyapa, all foolish common people, having themselves created forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles, wander in saṃsāra because of them, and do not understand those phenomena as they truly are.
Just as a painter, having superimposed the state of a real yakṣa upon a terrifying yakṣa-form created by himself through false conceptualization, becomes afraid of it and falls into delusion;
so too all fools, flowing with false conceptualizations, wander in saṃsāra due to their own conceptual constructions, because moments, states, and homogeneous classes of beings are unstable.
The previous example was intended for the śrāvakas, whereas this one is for the bodhisattvas.
For the śrāvaka, because he has not cultivated familiarity with emptiness, is terrified of emptiness;
whereas the bodhisattva, some say, is afflicted by the conceptualization of imagined phenomena because his afflictions consist of conceptualization.
Others, however, maintain that there is no difference in meaning between these two, but rather they are designated as two on account of their belonging to two distinct classes.
Others say that the Śrāvaka does not attain what is to be attained because of fear of emptiness, whereas the Bodhisattva does not [fail to attain it] because of fear of conceptualized phenomena.
Some maintain that the former [is taught] as an antidote to the grasping at a self, while this [latter] is an antidote to the grasping at phenomena.

Conceptualization regarding the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is an extreme, and conceptualization regarding the subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*) is also an extreme; this is the context. How so? These objects of apprehension, such as form and the rest, and their subjects, the groups of consciousness, when grasped by way of their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and by way of their function, will—like the self and so forth—be of a superimposed nature. Thus, the intended "extreme" is the conceptual construction of the object and subject as real entities.
To avoid these two extremes of conceptual construction, there is the analogy of a magician. For instance, Kāśyapa, it is like a magician who creates a magical illusion;
then that magically created being might devour the magician himself.
In the same way, Kāśyapa, whatever object a practitioner of yoga (yogācāra) monk attends to, all of that appears to him as empty—so it is said at length.

How does one avoid these two extremes of conceptual construction by means of this? To this he says: "For the knowledge of the non-existence of objects is produced by the knowledge of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

And that very knowledge of the non-existence of objects causes that same knowledge of representation-only to cease, because in the absence of an object, representation is impossible. This is the point of similarity here.
The knowledge of representation-only (vijñaptimātratā) is like the magician; the knowledge of the non-existence of objects is like the conjured yakṣa,
because the knowledge of the non-existence of objects is brought about by the knowledge of representation-only.
Just as a created being might devour its creator, so too will the knowledge of the non-existence of objects devour that very knowledge of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
This is because, in the absence of an object, representation-only is impossible, since representation is defined as the apprehension of an object.
It has been stated that conceptual construction regarding correctness is an extreme, and conceptual construction regarding falsity is also an extreme.

In the stage conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), one who conceptualizes the discernment of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*) as either "correctness" (*samyaktva*) or "falsity" (*mithyātva*) falls into the two extremes.

How so? Correctness consists of the untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena, while falsity consists of the tainted (*sāsrava*) ones. In that regard, if one determines the discernment of reality as being exclusively correctness, then wholesome tainted phenomena would not be the discernment of reality.
Furthermore, if it were characterized by a lack of correctness, then even so, falsity would result, just like the wholesome [states] associated with the three realms.
To avoid these two extremes, there is the analogy of fire from two pieces of wood.
For example, Kāśyapa, fire is produced in dependence upon two pieces of wood; once produced, it consumes those very two pieces of wood.

In the same way, Kāśyapa, depending upon the correct analytical investigation (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*), the noble faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) arises; and once arisen, it consumes that very same correct analytical investigation.

This is the meaning of "without self" (*amama*). Just as fire, which does not possess the characteristics of the two pieces of wood, is produced from those two pieces of wood and, once produced, consumes both pieces of wood;

even so, from the correct analytical investigation—which does not possess the characteristic of non-perfection—there arises the noble faculty of wisdom, which possesses the characteristic of perfection.
Once born, it consumes that very same contemplation of reality;
the meaning is that it causes it to vanish. For it is said to be "as if burnt" precisely because of its vanishing, due to the observation of its transformation.
And although this discernment of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*) is still associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is called "discernment of reality" because it is conducive to correctness.
It is understood that conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is an extreme whether there is activity or whether there is non-activity.
To the question "How so?", he says: "One imagines either an action preceded by cognition for knowledge, or its lack of efficacy.
If one proceeds toward the abandonment [of ignorance] after determining, "This is knowledge; I shall abandon this ignorance," such conceptualization regarding activity is an extreme.
Because knowledge is momentary, it cannot exist at the time of the activity of abandonment.
Therefore, the claim that the abandonment of ignorance is devoid of efficacy is an extreme of conceptual construction regarding non-activity.
To avoid these two extremes of conceptual construction, there is the analogy of the oil lamp.
For example, Kāśyapa, when an oil lamp is lit, the blinding darkness disappears; yet, Kāśyapa, it does not occur to the oil lamp, "I am dispelling all this darkness."

Moreover, Kāśyapa, it is in dependence upon an oil lamp that the thick darkness disappears. In the same way, Kāśyapa, when knowledge arises, ignorance disappears. Yet, Kāśyapa, it does not occur to knowledge, "I am dispelling ignorance.
Rather, it is simply in dependence upon knowledge that ignorance disappears.

This is what is meant: just as a lamp, though devoid of activity and lacking the intention to dispel the darkness of gloom, yet causes all the darkness of gloom to vanish from whatever place it is brought simply by its mere presence in that place;

even so, when non-conceptual knowledge arises in a mental continuum, ignorance departs from that continuum by the mere fact of its existence, because knowledge is non-conceptual and thus lacks [deliberate] activity.
Thus, because cognition lacks activity and lacks causal efficacy—just like a lamp—it dispels its opposite by its mere existence; therefore, there is an absence of causal efficacy.
Even in the case of non-arising, conceptualization is an extreme; even in the case of simultaneity, conceptualization is an extreme.
The phrase "conceptualization is an extreme" is understood to carry over [from the previous context].

To explain how this is so, he says: "If one imagines the non-arising of the antidote—thinking that just as the antidote has never arisen before for such a long time, so too it will not arise now—this conceptualization regarding non-birth is an extreme.
Or [one imagines] the long duration of affliction;
for as long as ignorance, which is the counter-agent to knowledge, remains established, knowledge is not capable of arising."
Moreover, even if it were somehow to arise, because ignorance has persisted for a long time, its removal by momentary knowledge would not be possible;
consequently, defilement and purification would be simultaneous.
To avoid these two extremes of conceptualization, there is the second illustration of the oil lamp.
It is just as if, Kāśyapa, in a house, a dwelling, or a chamber, after the passing of a thousand years, no one had ever brought an oil lamp.
Suppose then that some man were to light an oil lamp there.
What do you think, Kāśyapa? Would it occur to the blinding darkness that, "I have accumulated for a thousand years; I will not depart from here"?

He said: “No, Blessed One. Indeed, once an oil lamp has been lit, darkness has no power not to depart; it must necessarily depart. The Blessed One said: “In the very same way, Kāśyapa, even the afflictions of karma accumulated over hundreds of thousands of aeons vanish through a single instance of proper mental attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*).
“Oil lamp,” Kāśyapa—this is now the occasion for the exposition of the supremacy of the object (*ālambana-anuttarya*). Therefore, he asks: “What is the supremacy of the object?”

Therefore, in order to determine that, he says: "The establishment, as well as the element," and so forth. This twelvefold object of focus (ālambana)—beginning with the object of focus as establishment and ending with the object of focus as excellence—is called the "supremacy of the object" because it is superior to all other objects of focus.

In this context, first, those phenomena such as the perfections (*pāramitā*) and so forth are also established by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; thus, they are "establishments" (*vyavasthāna*).
Demonstrating this very point, the author of the Commentary also says: "The objective support is the establishment of the designation of phenomena" (*dharmaprajñaptivyavasthānālambana*).

The "designation of phenomena" (*dharmaprajñapti*) refers to the designation of phenomena such as the perfection of generosity, the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), the noble truths (*āryasatya*), and so forth.
By means of that [designation], one establishes [the dharma], or that [designation] itself is the establishment here; thus, it is the "establishment of the designation of dharmas.
Furthermore, because it conforms to clear realization (*abhisamaya*), the sequence of the establishments, their objects, and so forth, should be understood here.
The second is *tathatā* (suchness), because it is a synonym for the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm).
Regarding "the third and the fourth":
therein, the third has the object of proof (*sādhya*) as its focal point, and the fourth has the means of proof (*sādhana*) as its focal point.
"Those two alone" refers to the first and the second.
"Respectively" means that the first has the goal (*sādhya*) as its object and the second has the means (*sādhana*) as its object.
He states the reason for this very point: "Because through the penetration of the *dharmadhātu*, there is the realization of the qualities such as the perfections (*pāramitā*).
Since one realizes the untainted perfections through the penetration of the *dharmadhātu*, the first has the goal as its object and the second has the means as its object.
The fifth is the objective support for retention (*dhāraṇālambana*). It pertains to the knowledge consisting of hearing (*śrutamaya-jñāna*);
because one retains the dharmas such as the perfections (*pāramitā*) and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) by means of mere hearing, the knowledge consisting of hearing is called "retention."
The objective support of retention (*dhāraṇā*) is the "retention-object" (*dhāraṇālambana*).
Furthermore, that is precisely the first pair: the object of establishment (*vyavasthānālambana*) and the object of the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātvālambana*).
The sixth [type of wisdom] is so called because one retains [the truth] after having understood it through the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*).

Having understood [the truth] through the reasonings of dependence, cause and effect, logical proof, and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-yukti*), one retains the meaning of what has been heard; thus, "ascertainment" (*avadhāraṇā*) refers to knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya-jñāna*). Its object is the "object of ascertainment. The seventh [type of object] is the object of knowledge consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya-jñāna*), as is the context here.

"Because of retaining it within oneself" (*pratyātmaṃ dhāraṇāt*): because of retaining the meaning within oneself, "firm retention" (*pradhāraṇā*) is the knowledge consisting of cultivation that serves as the preparatory application for entering the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, beginning from the foundations of mindfulness up to the powers,
its object is the "object of sustained application" (pradhāraṇālambana),
which pertains to the path of seeing on the first stage.
It is the penetration of the all-pervading nature of the non-dual realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) within each individual;
or alternatively, it is the piercing that acts as the antidote to the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing and to the non-afflicted ignorance whose object is the all-pervading meaning.
Furthermore, this is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Its object is the object of penetration;
it is the ninth [stage] of the path of cultivation, extending up to the seventh ground.

Through the repeated practice of that very penetration of the dharmadhātu, its progression toward ever-increasing excellence and its expansion constitutes the path of cultivation, up to the seventh ground.
The objective support (*ālambana*) of that path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is the pervasive objective support (*pratānatālambana*).
It is the tenth [type of objective support], which, in this context, is the objective support for both the mundane and supramundane paths;
this is because of the realization of phenomena (*dharma*) according to their specific modes (*prakāraśas*).
On that very stage, because of the realization of the Dharma by way of the departure from attachment to all types of signs of phenomena, such as those found in the sūtras, it is called "progression.
That itself is said to be the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) on the seventh stage. The object of this progression is the "object of progression" (*pragamālambana*).
The eleventh [moment] occurs on the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).

For on the eighth stage, because that very path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) flows forth naturally and effortlessly for one who is free from the mental engagement of striving toward all signs (*nimitta*), it is called "the effortless object" (*praśaṭhālambana*); that is, the object of the effortless state.
The twelfth [perfection] pertains to the three stages beginning with the ninth: because on the ninth stage one attains the excellence of the knowledge of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*);
on the tenth stage, because one attains the excellence of mastery over karma;
and on the Buddha stage, because one attains the excellence of the purification of all afflictive obscurations and cognitive obscurations without exception.

Thus, because one attains the excellence of the purification of knowledge and activity across the three stages beginning with the ninth, the object of focus for one established in those stages is called the "object of excellence.
Another, however, says that the "object of excellence" is taught in relation to the three stages by making a distinction of weak, medium, and intense within the excellence of the path itself;
for it is that same first pair which receives its respective name as an object of focus in each particular state.
And this object of focus consists of the object of focus that is the systematic arrangement of phenomena (*dharmavyavasthāna*) and the object of focus that is the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Furthermore, these two objects of focus receive their respective names according to each specific stage of knowledge:
at the stage of knowledge consisting of hearing (*śrutamaya-jñāna*), it is the "object of retention," because what has been heard is the domain of the knowledge of retention.
And by that, the knowledge of retention is called "retention" (*dhāraṇā*).
In this manner, it should be explained up to the "object of excellence.
On the ninth and tenth stages, as well as on the Buddha-stage, there is supramundane knowledge that has reached excellence, as well as the mundane knowledge subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*).
Its objective support is the preeminent objective support.
Thus, the supremacy of the objective support has been explained.

{The Unsurpassedness of Realization} Now, in order to determine the unsurpassedness of realization (*samudāgamānuttarya*) which has reached its proper occasion, he asks: "What is realization? Realization (*samudāgama*) is that which is fully accomplished through various modes of practice (*pratipatti*). It is called "unsurpassed" because it is superior to other realizations, and because there is no other realization superior to it.
To demonstrate that, he says: "The non-deficiency [of conditions], the non-rejection, distraction, and fulfillment," and so forth in detail.
In this regard, starting from the non-deficiency of conditions up to the manifestation of enlightenment—this is the tenfold realization (*samudāgama*).
In this context, "the non-deficiency of conditions" means the complete gathering of the lineage (*gotra*).

The non-deficiency of conditions refers to the presence of all [conditions] in their entirety. When these have been brought together, the lineage is fully realized; the meaning is that it becomes flourishing and even more distinguished.

Furthermore, these consist of attending upon virtuous persons, hearing the true Dharma, proper mental attention (*yoniśo-manaskāra*), and so forth. Their deficiency arises from a lack of those [conditions], such as the spiritual lineage and friends.
The non-rejection of the Mahāyāna is the full realization of resolute faith (*adhimukti*).

If one does not reject the Mahāyāna Dharma characterized by profundity and magnanimity, then there occurs the nourishment of this resolve, which consists of the retention of such conviction (*adhimukti*). This is the non-distraction from the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and the full attainment of the arousal of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*). That is to say, even when conditions for the turning back of the thought of awakening are present, if his mind does not stray toward the Śrāvaka Vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, then his thought of awakening attains nourishment.

"The fulfillment of the perfections is the realization of practice" means that for those who have generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), through the power of that [thought], the perfection of giving and the other perfections are fulfilled, whereby there is the nourishment of the practice of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). "The arising of the noble path is the realization of the entry into certainty (*nyāmāvakrānti*)."
The very first arising of the unprecedented Noble Path is the entry into *nyāma*.
"Raw" (*āma*) refers to a fault or exhaustion;

that state where such [faults] do not exist is *nyāma*, a ground free from outflows like a place sheltered from the wind. Entry into *nyāma* is "entry into *nyāma*" (*nyāmāvakrānti*), which means "entrance."
Even in the reading "entry into certainty" (*niyamāvakrānti*), "certainty" (*niyama*) itself is the certainty;
for one who has produced the path of seeing becomes fixed in a happy rebirth and in *nirvāṇa*.
The firm rooting of the roots of virtue through long-term cultivation is the full attainment of the ripening of sentient beings.

For those who have attained the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), there is an increase of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) and a firm rooting of those roots through the practice and long-term cultivation of the subsequently attained path of meditation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
By means of that, one becomes capable of maturing sentient beings.
Therefore, the firm rooting of the roots of virtue is the realization (*samudāgama*) of the maturation of sentient beings.

But others say: "In this way, his maturation of sentient beings is fully accomplished; that is, if, through long-term practice, he has strengthened the roots of virtue within the mental continuums of sentient beings, then the pliancy of the mind (*citta-karmaṇyatā*) constitutes the full accomplishment of the purification of the field.

Thus, for those whose roots of virtue have increased through such cultivation, there arises the pliancy of the mind due to the disappearance of both the signs (*nimitta*) and the exertion (*ābhoga*) which are the adversaries of the path to the single sphere (*ekāyatana*).

Through the sovereignty of pliancy of action, one displays a buddha-field composed of crystal and so forth according to one's wish; thus, the pliancy of the mind is the realization of the purification of the field.
{The Summary Meaning of the Unsurpassed Vehicle} Regarding the summary meaning of the unsurpassed vehicle, the purpose for stating the summary meaning is first explained:
in brief, there are three kinds of unsurpassedness, while in detail, they are infinite.
As for "practice," it is said that unsurpassedness resides in practice; as for "the basis of practice," it is further said to reside in the objective support (*ālambana*).
Regarding what was stated as "the fruit of practice is designated as full realization," that practice is such that it is supreme; thus it is said: "The supreme consists of twelve aspects."
"By which" means by the mental attention toward the Mahāyāna Dharma as it has been prescribed;
"and so forth" refers to the Bodhisattva’s constant application of the three types of wisdom.
Because of this statement:
"And likewise, it should be known that she is further endowed with the ten religious practices."
In what manner and by what means: it is transformed through non-distraction by the cultivation of *śamatha*, due to the absence of the six kinds of distraction;
and it is transformed through non-perversion by the cultivation of *vipaśyanā*, due to the absence of perversion regarding the ten [factors] such as the letter (*vyañjana*).
And for what purpose: for the sake of deliverance by way of the middle way, which is the practice consisting in the avoidance of the two extremes.
Regarding the phrase "and wherein": this refers to those ten stages (*bhūmi*).
To the question "In what way?", he says: "both distinguished and undistinguished.
This is the summary meaning of the non-perversions (*aviparyāsa*).
Furthermore, through non-perversion regarding the phrasing (*vyañjana*), one penetrates the sign of calm abiding (*śamatha-nimitta*) and realizes that which is devoid of the nature of conjunction.
Through non-perversion regarding the meaning (*artha*), one penetrates the sign of insight (*vipaśyanā-nimitta*) as being nothing but delusion in both respects.

Through non-perversion regarding mental attention (*manaskāra*), one abandons the seed of adherence to duality, which is the cause of perversion and is deposited within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Through non-delusion regarding non-distraction, one brings the cause of delusion under control by means of non-adherence to existence or non-existence, as in the case of an illusion and so forth.

Through non-delusion regarding specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), one cultivates the path which has the specific characteristics of phenomena (*dharmasvalakṣaṇa*) as its object—being non-conceptual and free from verbal expression—as the antidote to that [delusion].
Through non-delusion regarding general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), one penetrates the nature of purification through the commonality of all phenomena.

Through the non-perversion of mental attention regarding impurity and purity, one discerns whether those obscurations have been abandoned or not abandoned, because the naturally luminous *dharmadhātu* is defiled by adventitious secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

Through the non-perversion of their adventitious nature, one discerns defilement and purification, because otherwise defilement and purification would be impossible for that which is naturally luminous.
Through the non-perversion of fearlessness and lack of pride, one emerges free from obscurations by way of non-attachment to persons and phenomena.
And thus concludes this Commentary on the *Madhyāntavibhāga* following the scriptures, composed by the Master Sthiramati.
